title: OpenDFX for Printed Circuit Boards: recommendations
author: Chris Denney
attribution: OpenDFX for Printed Circuit Boards by Chris Denney, https://opendfx.org
citation: Denney, C. (2026). OpenDFX for Printed Circuit Boards (Version 1.0). https://opendfx.org
note: These are recommendations, not rules. Each record links to its page in the book, which has the full text, drawings and sources. Records with a `checks` field are also checked by the OpenDFX KiCad design-rules file (https://opendfx.org/opendfx.kicad_dru): run KiCad's design rule check with it after placing and routing a board, and look up each report by its recommendation's permanent address. See https://opendfx.org/kicad/.

recommendations.title: Send one complete fabrication package, in one format, from one revision
recommendations.why: Every file in the archive has to be opened and checked for instructions. Extra files waste that time, and two copies of the same board in different formats (Gerber and ODB++, say) force the CAM engineer to compare them and ask which one is right. Native design files need the same design software to open, and the fab builds from fabrication data, not from them. IPC-2581 and ODB++ carry the netlist and layer structure inside them, which is their advantage, but each design tool exports them a little differently and each CAM system reads them a little differently.
recommendations.typical_values: Gerber files with the standard `.gbr` extension and Gerber X2 attributes. Even if top and bottom solder masks are identical, send both.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Questions, a day's delay for each, and occasionally a board built from the wrong one of two conflicting files.
recommendations.example: One assembler that imports IPC-2581 from several design tools found that each tool writes the same standard slightly differently, and had to handle each one separately. Practitioners have reported pads silently missing and thermal reliefs rotated after an ODB++ import, caught only by comparing against known-good artwork. Open your outputs in a viewer that is not part of your design tool before you send them.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Which of Gerber, ODB++ and IPC-2581 to send varies by fab; ask yours.

sources.text: *PCB Fabrication Data: Design to Fabrication Data Transfer*, V6 (Sept 2015), the guide published by the maintainers of the Gerber format: chapters 14 to 16 (one board per archive, nothing superfluous, no duplicate formats, both masks); Gerber Layer Format Specification, revision 2026.05; KiCad 10 documentation, fabrication outputs (Gerber, IPC-2581, ODB++, IPC-D-356); [“Building the factory of the future with CircuitHub CEO, Andrew Seddon”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19621440-building-the-factory-of-the-future-with-circuithub-ceo-andrew-seddon) (Aug 2026), [38:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19621440?t=2280)–39:00; [“The PCB assembly process”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4364141-the-pcb-assembly-process) (Jun 2020), [08:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4364141?t=480); Chris Denney (author).

recommendations.title: Always send a netlist, made from the same revision as the Gerbers
recommendations.recommendation: Export an IPC-D-356 netlist from your design tool every time you export Gerbers, and send it with them. If you send ODB++ or IPC-2581, the netlist is already inside.
recommendations.why: The first thing a CAM engineer does is build a netlist from your Gerbers and drill files, and they re-check against it every time they edit the data. Your netlist comes from the schematic connections in your design tool, not from the images. Comparing the two catches a Gerber that didn't import correctly, a trace or hole deleted by mistake, and copper that shorts two nets you meant to keep apart. Without your netlist, the fab can only test the boards against a netlist built from your images, so a wrong image is built and passes electrical test anyway. Many design tools only regenerate the netlist when you tick a separate box, so it's easy to send an old one.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: An error in the data is built faithfully, passes the fab's electrical test, and is found only after the board is assembled. A stale netlist does the opposite: dozens of false mismatches, and questions back to you.
recommendations.example: CAM engineers report receiving netlists that contained only half the board, because the netlist was not re-exported after the layout changed. A fab's quoting engineer gives the classic case: if the Gerbers show a plated slot where there shouldn't be one, and there's no netlist, you get a plated slot.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Fabs can work without a netlist; that doesn't make it a good idea.

sources.text: *PCB Fabrication Data: Design to Fabrication Data Transfer*, V6 (Sept 2015), chapter 11, "Always include the netlist"; one large fab's published data guidance (checks the supplied IPC netlist against its own); [“The PCB CAM Process w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431-the-pcb-cam-process-w-dave-wilcox) (Mar 2021), [12:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431?t=720)–19:00; [“What factors influence PCB quotes w/ Brett Babilonia”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855-what-factors-influence-pcb-quotes-w-brett-babilonia) (Feb 2024), [09:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855?t=540)–11:00.

recommendations.title: Tell the fab where you join nets on purpose
recommendations.recommendation: If your copper deliberately joins nets that stay separate in the schematic (a star point joining analog and digital ground, a net-tie, a shorting jumper), list them in your fabrication notes. Better still, use your design tool's net-tie feature so the netlist knows about them.
recommendations.why: The fab compares its netlist, built from the copper, with yours. A deliberate join looks exactly like a short.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: The netlist check fails, and the job stops while the CAM engineer asks you whether each join is meant to be there.

recommendations.title: Separate plated and non-plated holes, and use an unambiguous drill format
recommendations.recommendation: Put plated and non-plated holes in separate drill files. Export them as Gerber X2 drill files if your fab accepts them. If you send Excellon (NC drill) files, use one of the two safe formats, 2:4 inch or 3:3 metric, with the units and zero suppression stated in the header. Make the drill files from the same origin as the Gerbers, so the holes land on their pads.
recommendations.why: If plating isn't stated, the CAM engineer guesses from the copper: a hole through a pad is plated, a hole in bare laminate is not. A large hole you wanted plated, with no copper around it, comes back bare. Excellon has no standard way to say where the decimal point is, so the fab has to work out the number of digits and which zeros were left off. Formats with too few decimal places, such as 3:2 metric, round every hole position to the nearest 0.01 mm, which shifts holes off their pads. Gerber X2 drill files have none of these problems, and they also say which layers a blind or buried via spans.
recommendations.typical_values: 2:4 inch or 3:3 metric for Excellon; avoid 3:2 metric, 5:1, 1:5 and other unusual formats. Metric is preferred where you have the choice. A format that writes every coordinate with a decimal point, such as KiCad's decimal format, can't be misread either, so it is also safe.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Holes plated that shouldn't be, or not plated that should, and drill files that need hand-work to line up with the copper.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Many fabs still ask for Excellon. KiCad 10's drill dialog writes plated and non-plated holes to separate Excellon files by default, but its command-line export puts them in one file unless you ask for separate files.

recommendations.title: Dimension the holes that matter, with their real tolerance
recommendations.recommendation: If a hole's size or position matters (a press-fit pin, a connector whose datasheet says +0.1/−0 mm, a hole sized for current, a mounting hole that must line up with an enclosure), dimension it on the drill drawing with its true tolerance. Design the hole to the middle of the allowed range, not to the nominal value. Don't create extra hole sizes just to split the difference; a drawing callout does the job.
recommendations.why: Fabs adjust hole sizes to suit their process: they drill plated holes larger to allow for plating, and may enlarge an awkward size within the standard tolerance without telling you. IPC-6012F says only holes dimensioned in the procurement documents are inspected for position; the rest are checked only through annular ring. A one-sided tolerance such as +0.1/−0 mm is invisible in the data: a 0.7 mm hole looks like any other 0.7 mm hole.
recommendations.typical_values: IPC-6012F default finished hole tolerances, when the drawing says nothing: ±100 µm for plated component holes, +80 µm with no lower limit for via-only holes (they may be plugged), ±80 µm for non-plated holes. One large fab aims for the middle of any tolerance band you give it. Tighter than standard tolerances are possible, but cost more, because every hole has to be measured and out-of-range boards scrapped.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A connector that won't go in, or falls out; a press-fit pin that sits loose in a hole drilled too large.
recommendations.example: Small connectors whose datasheets call for 0.7 mm +0.1/−0 holes have repeatedly caused trouble when the footprint simply used a 0.7 mm hole, because the fab had no way of knowing the hole must never be smaller.

recommendations.title: Put your intent in the data, not in a note that contradicts it
recommendations.recommendation: Make the layer files show the board you want. If you want vias tented, export the solder mask with no openings over them, rather than leaving openings and adding a note saying "tent all vias". Don't export component values or other assembly text onto the legend layer unless you want it printed. Keep title blocks, frames and notes out of the layer files; put them on the drawing.
recommendations.why: A CAM engineer treats the data as what you want. When a note contradicts the data, they have to stop and ask which one is right. A note like "tent all vias" also leaves them to decide which holes are vias, which is hard when a board has several via sizes and small component holes. Value text exported to the legend lands on pads and gets clipped off, or prints as an unreadable mass of overlapping text.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A question and a day's delay, or a board built to the data when you meant the note.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Most design tools can tent vias in the export settings; in some it takes a design rule on hole size.

recommendations.title: Put everything the Gerbers can't say on the fabrication drawing
recommendations.why: Gerbers only show shapes. Thickness, material, finish, class and impedance can only come from you. When the drawing is silent, IPC-6012F fills the gap with defaults the fab will build to, which may not be what you meant. Many fabs' software can read specifications from a plain-text file automatically; none can read them from a drawing. The same goes for the AI tools now used to check designs and prepare quotes: a text file is read exactly, a drawing has to be interpreted.
recommendations.typical_values: IPC-6012F defaults when nothing is specified: Class 2; epoxy-glass laminate; ENIG finish for designs first released on or after 1 October 2023 (tin-lead for older ones); 1/2 oz starting copper on every layer; the hole tolerances in [PCB-DFM-012](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/01-fabrication-data/#pcb-dfm-012-dimension-the-holes-that-matter-with-their-real-tolerance). IPC-6012F gives no default board thickness tolerance; other dimensional tolerances fall back to the IPC-2220 design standards. Fabs commonly quote ±10% on thickness for boards 0.8 mm and thicker, but this varies, so state the tolerance you need. Controlled impedance is commonly held to ±10%, and ±5% on request.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Boards that are the wrong thickness, the wrong finish, or the wrong class, and no claim against the fab, because they built what was ordered. If controlled impedance isn't on the drawing, the fab doesn't control it, and a board that doesn't perform is still a good board as far as they're concerned.
recommendations.example: At one assembler that builds bare boards to what is entered on its order form, boards have come back the wrong thickness because the thickness wasn't set there. Wrong thickness can't be reworked: it means new bare boards and a new assembly.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. IPC-2611 and IPC-2614 cover fabrication documentation in full.

recommendations.title: Check a copied fabrication drawing line by line
recommendations.recommendation: When you start a new board from an old one's drawing or stack-up, read every note again. Remove impedance callouts, reference planes, finishes and special processes the new board doesn't need, and add the ones it does.
recommendations.why: Drawings are usually copied from the last project. Notes that were right for the old board stay on, and requirements for the new one get left off.
recommendations.typical_values: Under IPC-6012F, a drawing first released before 1 October 2023 with no finish callout defaults to a tin-lead finish; one released after defaults to ENIG. State the finish rather than rely on the date.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Impedance requirements for traces that no longer exist, with questions to match, or a missing reference plane and a board that doesn't work even though it passed every inspection.
recommendations.example: One fab's engineers regularly find impedance callouts copied from an earlier drawing that don't apply to the new board, or reference planes left out.

recommendations.title: Clear every design-rule error before you make the outputs
recommendations.recommendation: Run your design tool's design-rule check (DRC) and resolve every error, above all unconnected nets, before you export anything. Then compare the release with the previous one, so you know exactly what changed.
recommendations.why: Design tools will happily export Gerbers from a board with unrouted connections. Treat DRC errors like compiler warnings: each one is either fixed or understood. A comparison between versions (a schematic, layout or BOM diff, not just "this file changed") catches values and net names changed by accident.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A board with a missing connection, fixed with a wire on the prototype and a new revision afterwards.
recommendations.example: A first-time designer's board had a dead display because one power pin was never routed to the microcontroller. A mentor found it from the design files, and a single wire fixed the prototype.

recommendations.title: Always send the XY file, and send native design files and the schematic when you can
recommendations.why: Gerbers show pads, not parts. Without the XY file, someone has to find and type in the position of every part by hand. Do-not-place locations stay in because a BOM change on a later order can fill them, and the assembler then already has their positions. With the schematic and design files, the assembler can answer their own questions about polarity, pin 1 and which part goes where, instead of putting the job on hold to ask you.
recommendations.typical_values: Millimeters, with the origin and units stated in the header. Rotations positive counter-clockwise, as most assemblers expect. Plain text or CSV. Without the file, making placement data by hand takes about 3 minutes a part: about 5 hours for a 100-part board (one assembler).
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A job put on hold while someone asks you a question the schematic would have answered; a four-day turn can become something like seven days. With no XY file at all, extra programming time and cost.
recommendations.example: One assembler says the XY file is the one file new customers most often don't know about, because a board soldered by hand on the bench never needs one. Assembly inspectors say the schematic is what they open when they can't work out a part's orientation from the placement viewer.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Online assemblers vary in whether they want through-hole parts in the file; listing every location and marking the type works for all of them.

recommendations.title: Draw footprints to the IPC zero rotation, and write your convention down
recommendations.recommendation: Draw every footprint in your library at the zero rotation shown in IPC-7351B, Figure 16-1, and write the convention into your library's rules so everyone who adds a footprint follows it. Expect the assembler to check every rotation anyway.
recommendations.why: The rotation in the XY file is the part's angle relative to how its footprint was drawn. If footprints are drawn in different orientations, the same rotation number means different things on different parts. The current standard, IPC-7352 (2023), no longer lists zero rotations; it says each organization's library standard should define them. IPC-7351B's figure is still the convention most libraries follow. Parts on reels sit in many orientations, depending on the maker, so the assembler always matches each reel to your footprint by hand; a consistent library means one correction per package type instead of one per part.
recommendations.typical_values:
IPC-7351B zero rotation, by package (drawn in D44):

| Package | Zero rotation |
|---|---|
| Chip resistors, capacitors, inductors; molded and MELF parts; aluminum electrolytics | Horizontal, pin 1 on the left. Pin 1 is the positive pin, or the cathode for diodes. |
| SOT, SOT-23, SOT-223, DPAK, SOIC, TSSOP, SON, DFN, QFP, QFN, chip arrays | Pin 1 at the upper left |
| BGA, LGA | Pin A1 at the upper left |
| PLCC, LCC, bumpered QFP with pin 1 at the center of a side | Pin 1 at the top center |

For example, a part that sits on its tape with pin 1 at the lower left is 90° counter-clockwise from its zero rotation.

![D44 is drawn to scale: six footprints at their IPC zero rotation: a horizontal 0603 chip with no polarity mark; a horizontal SOD-123 diode with the cathode on the left; a SOT-23 with pins 1 and 2 on the left, pin 1 at the top, and no mark; an 8-pin SOIC with pin 1 at the upper left; a 3 × 3 mm QFN with pin 1 at the top of the left side; a BGA with ball A1 at the upper left. Each has a cross at its center.](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/images/zero-rotation.svg)
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: More time spent lining up rotations before the first board can be built, and more chances to place a part backwards.
recommendations.example: At one assembler, lining up rotations from customers' XY files commonly takes about half an hour per job. Because the rotations are at least consistent within a package type, the usual fix is "turn every 0402 by 90°", and the rest follow. LEDs are the hardest: each maker orients them differently in the tape and uses different polarity marks.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. If you use a different convention, that's fine; the assembler will work it out. Use one convention throughout the library.

sources.text: IPC-7351B, section 16 and Figure 16-1; IPC-7352 (May 2023), section 7; [“All the Tricks and Gotchas in Surface Mount Assembly (Repost from the Coriolis Effect)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453-all-the-tricks-and-gotchas-in-surface-mount-assembly-repost-from-the-coriolis-effect) (Jul 2022), [07:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453?t=420)–11:00; Chris Denney (author).

recommendations.title: Give every part a unique reference designator, placed next to its own part
recommendations.recommendation: Give every part on the board its own reference designator (R1, U4), with no duplicates and no suffixes like U4_1 and U4_2 left over from copied schematic blocks. Use only letters and numbers. If the legend shows reference designators, place each one where it clearly belongs to its own part.
recommendations.why: The reference designator is how everyone talks about a part: the BOM, the XY file, the inspection report and every email. Duplicates make every conversation ambiguous. Some inspection and programming software can't handle unusual characters in designators. Printed designators nudged around to fit can end up beside the wrong part, and the assembler uses them to check placement.
recommendations.typical_values: Up to about 8 characters is safe; at least one inspection machine's software fails on longer ones.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A question that takes half an hour to answer instead of seconds; in the worst case, the wrong part soldered to a pad because its designator sat beside the neighboring footprint.
recommendations.example: One assembler's inspection machine crashes outright on some unusual designators; they now run their own check on every job for long or odd designators before it reaches the machine.

recommendations.title: Put everything the data can't show on an assembly drawing
recommendations.why: Placement data says where a part goes and which way it faces, not how its leads are formed or how tight a screw is. "Tight" means something different to every operator; a torque value can be set on a torque driver and checked. Assemblers are wary of choosing a torque for you, because they don't know your materials and loads. Branded solder pastes, wires and other materials get discontinued or go out of stock, and a drawing that names one product can stop a build.
recommendations.typical_values: Torque in N·m (or in·lb), from the fastener maker, a calculation, or a pull test on a few samples.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Parts fitted the way the data shows, which may not be what you meant, and a second build to fix it.
recommendations.example: A customer wanted a through-hole LED bent at 90° and lined up with another feature, but sent no drawing; the LEDs were fitted the way the design appeared to call for, and the customer was disappointed. Screenshots and marked-up 3D renders of tricky areas help fabs and assemblers as much as formal drawings.

recommendations.title: Give every BOM line the designators, quantity, maker and full part number
recommendations.why: The assembler matches each line to the XY file by its designators, buys by the maker's part number, and checks what arrives against it. A distributor's own stock number, or a description alone, leaves the buyer to guess. One character in a part number can mean a different packaging (R for reel, T for tube), or a different part entirely. CSV files use commas to separate fields, so a comma inside a part number splits it into two.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Questions before parts can be bought, and parts received that don't match the BOM by one character, each of which has to be confirmed before it can be used.
recommendations.example: Some part makers do use commas in their part numbers; one assembler had to write software to quote every part number so that its files wouldn't break.

recommendations.title: Say which lines are locked to one part, and why; list alternates for the rest
recommendations.recommendation: Mark each BOM line as either "this exact part only" or "equivalents allowed". For a locked line, say which parameter makes it critical (for example, low ESR, a particular tempco, a qualified part). For the others, list one or more approved alternate part numbers, especially for anything that's scarce, single-source, or not a simple resistor or capacitor (LEDs, diodes, connectors).
recommendations.why: When a part is out of stock, the assembler's buyers need to know whether they may substitute, and what a good substitute must match. Many lines are more flexible than designers expect, and an alternate you've already approved can be bought at once. A locked line with a reason tells them what to protect, and stops them suggesting a substitute you'll have to refuse.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Emails back and forth, a job held waiting for a part, or a substitute chosen by someone who doesn't know which parameter mattered.

recommendations.title: Check every value and part number before release, and check each part is still made
recommendations.recommendation: Before you release a BOM, check each value and part number character by character against what you meant, and check every part's lifecycle status and stock with a distributor. Replace parts that are obsolete or not recommended for new designs.
recommendations.why: Part numbers are long, and one character can change the value, the tolerance, or how the part is mounted. Libraries age: a BOM generated today from an old library can be full of parts that stopped being made years ago.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Boards built exactly to a wrong BOM, which don't work and have to be reworked; or a quote that can't be completed until obsolete parts are replaced.
recommendations.example: A customer's boards wouldn't power up; the BOM had the wrong value for 20 to 30 ceramic capacitors, one zero out. A one-character difference in another capacitor part number selects a version made for epoxy mounting instead of soldering; the two look identical and have the same electrical ratings. One assembler received a freshly generated BOM with 16 obsolete part numbers on it.

recommendations.title: Mark do-not-place and customer-supplied lines clearly
recommendations.recommendation: Give every location the BOM leaves empty its own line or column marked DNP (do not place), rather than deleting it. Mark parts you'll supply yourself as CONSIGNED, and confirm with the assembler that they'll use your parts and not buy their own. If you'll fit the through-hole parts yourself to save cost on a prototype, mark those lines DNP too.
recommendations.why: A location missing from the BOM looks like a mistake; one marked DNP is a decision. Assemblers buy from the BOM unless told otherwise, so a consigned part that isn't marked may be bought again, and the wrong one fitted. Through-hole parts are slow and costly to fit at low volumes, and leaving them off is a common, easy saving.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A question for every empty footprint, or parts fitted that you meant to leave off; a consigned, pre-programmed chip replaced with a blank one.
recommendations.example: A designer consigned pre-programmed bootloader chips, and the assembler bought and fitted blank ones instead; the boards had to be shipped back and forth to put it right.

recommendations.title: For small builds, keep the number of unique BOM lines down
recommendations.recommendation: When you'll build only a few boards at a time, use as few different part numbers as you can: one resistor value where several would do, the same capacitor for all decoupling, the same connector family throughout.
recommendations.why: Every unique part has to be loaded onto a feeder and set up on the machine, however many boards you build. On a run of a few boards, that set-up time is most of the cost.
recommendations.typical_values: About 3 to 5 minutes to load each feeder. A 100-line BOM spread over 5 boards carries the set-up cost of all 100 feeders.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Prototype and small-batch prices that are much higher than they need to be.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice; matters most for prototypes and small batches.

recommendations.title: Use proven footprints for chip resistors and capacitors
recommendations.recommendation: Use the footprints in the table below for chip resistors and capacitors. They are strongly recommended for industrial and consumer products. You can adjust them, but do it knowingly, and keep the gap between the pads (see the warning below).
recommendations.why: For small chip parts, the gap between the two pads matters most. If the pads sit too far apart, the part's metal ends don't both rest on solder: one end lifts while the other wets, and the part stands up on end (tombstoning), or one end looks soldered but never wetted (head-in-pillow). Many library footprints have gaps that are too wide for 0402 and smaller parts.
recommendations.typical_values:
Footprints proven over millions of placements at one assembler (Worthington Assembly, Rev E). All dimensions in mm; pad length runs along the part, pad width across it.

| Size (inch / metric) | Pad length × width | Pitch (pad center to center) | Gap between pads | Solder mask expansion |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 008004 / 0201 | 0.20 × 0.20 | 0.30 | 0.10 | 0 (untested footprint) |
| 01005 / 0402 | 0.25 × 0.23 | 0.41 | 0.16 | 0.025 maximum |
| 0201 / 0603 | 0.25 × 0.35 | 0.55 | 0.30 | 0.05 maximum |
| 0402 / 1005 | 0.60 × 0.70 | 1.00 | 0.40 | |
| 0603 / 1608 | 0.70 × 1.00 | 1.40 | 0.70 | |
| 0805 / 2012 | 0.90 × 1.40 | 1.80 | 0.90 | |

⚠️ **If you change these, keep the gap.** On 0201 parts, a gap just 0.1 mm wider than shown causes serious tombstoning and head-in-pillow problems, and 0402 parts are nearly as sensitive. 0603 and larger parts are much more forgiving.

The other sizes in the table, each enlarged and drawn to scale:

*D12. 008004 (0201 metric): pads 0.2 mm long and 0.2 mm wide, 0.3 mm pitch, 0.1 mm gap; the part is 0.25 × 0.125 mm. Solder mask expansion 0 (untested footprint).*

*D13. 01005 (0402 metric): pads 0.25 mm long and 0.23 mm wide, 0.41 mm pitch, 0.16 mm gap; the part is 0.4 × 0.2 mm. Solder mask expansion 0.025 mm maximum.*

*D14. 0201 (0603 metric): pads 0.25 mm long and 0.35 mm wide, 0.55 mm pitch, 0.3 mm gap; the part is 0.6 × 0.3 mm. Solder mask expansion 0.05 mm maximum.*

*D22. 0402 (1005 metric): pads 0.6 mm long and 0.7 mm wide, 1.0 mm pitch, 0.4 mm gap; the part is 1.0 × 0.5 mm.*

*D15. 0603 (1608 metric): pads 0.7 mm long and 1.0 mm wide, 1.4 mm pitch, 0.7 mm gap; the part is 1.6 × 0.8 mm.*

*D16. 0805 (2012 metric): pads 0.9 mm long and 1.4 mm wide, 1.8 mm pitch, 0.9 mm gap; the part is 2.0 × 1.25 mm.*
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Tombstoned and half-soldered small parts, found at inspection and reworked by hand, or missed and found in the field.
recommendations.example: Since about 2017, every tombstoning problem at one assembler has traced back to the footprint. The usual cause was a default library footprint, or one downloaded and never checked.
recommendations.applies_to: Industrial, consumer and similar products. Mission-critical designs (space, aviation and similar) should follow the IPC land-pattern rules their customers require. These footprints are offered as a downloadable KiCad library; the 0402 and 0201 are also available for two other design tools.

recommendations.title: Use one footprint per package size, not one per part maker
recommendations.recommendation: Keep one footprint for each chip size (one 0402, one 0603, and so on) and use it for every resistor and capacitor of that size, whoever makes the part.
recommendations.why: Assemblers design stencil openings and program inspection machines footprint by footprint. Two parts of the same size from two makers, each with its own downloaded footprint, look like two different footprints and need two sets of work.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Extra engineering time on every new job, and more chances for a mistake.
recommendations.example: Designs regularly arrive with as many as 16 different 0402 footprints on one board.

recommendations.title: Check every footprint you didn't draw yourself, against the datasheet and a real part
recommendations.recommendation: Check every downloaded or library footprint before you use it. Compare it with the part maker's recommended land pattern, and print it 1:1 and lay a real part on it, or measure the part with calipers. Read the datasheet drawing carefully: many leadless parts are drawn from the bottom, and a footprint drawn from a bottom view comes out mirrored.
recommendations.why: Downloaded footprints are often wrong: off grid, the wrong pad sizes, or mirrored. Datasheet drawings are often made by people who never handled the part, and part tolerances only show up over many builds.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A part that doesn't fit, a mirrored chip that can't be fitted at all, or a board respin.
recommendations.example: One assembler catches a footprint drawn from a bottom view about once a month.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Treat a new footprint as proven only after it has been soldered about 100 times.

recommendations.title: Put a solder mask dam between every pad of a fine-pitch part
recommendations.recommendation: Give every pad of a fine-pitch part (0.5 mm pitch and finer) its own solder mask opening, so a thin strip of mask (a dam) separates each pad from the next. Never use one large mask opening around a whole row of pads. If your fab says the dams are too thin, ask what they can do rather than accept their removal. What's easy for the fab may make the assembler's work very difficult.
recommendations.why: During reflow, solder flows wherever there's bare copper. A dam between the pads keeps each joint separate. Without it, the solder runs together along the row into one long bridge.
recommendations.typical_values: 0.25 mm (10 mil) between copper pads, made up of 0.075 mm (3 mil) of mask registration on each side and a 0.1 mm (4 mil) dam in the middle. Green solder mask can hold a 0.075 mm (3 mil) dam, but 0.1 mm is recommended for every color. Where the pitch is too fine for 0.25 mm between pads (0.4 mm pitch, for example), trim the copper pads, or use a fab that images solder mask with a laser, which needs less registration: 0.2 mm copper and a 0.3 mm opening leaves the same 0.1 mm dam. Never give up the dam itself.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Solder bridges across a whole row of pins, which then have to be cleared by hand on every board.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Laser-imaged solder mask varies by fab; check with yours.

checks.check: Solder mask web between pads, and between a via and a pad

recommendations.title: Set the solder mask expansion of fine-pitch pads yourself
recommendations.recommendation: For parts of 0.5 mm pitch and finer, set the solder mask expansion of each footprint by hand instead of using your design software's default. Where a pad connects to a copper pour, set its mask opening so the exposed copper matches the other pads of the same part.
recommendations.why: Default mask expansions suit coarse parts and swallow the dam on fine-pitch ones. A pad inside a copper pour is defined by its mask opening, not by its copper, so a default expansion makes that pad bigger than its neighbors, and the part gets uneven solder.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Missing dams, uneven pads, and an assembler who has to guess what you meant.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Above 0.5 mm pitch the default is usually fine.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale, plan view of the corner of a 0.5 mm-pitch QFN, three times. Every pad has the same mask opening. On the left, the two ground pads at the corner each have a single trace to a via, and bare FR4 shows around them inside their openings, like every other pad. In the middle, the ground pads are tied straight into a copper pour, and copper fills their openings, so they look larger than the other pads. On the right, the ground pads join the pour through thin thermal spokes, and they look like the other pads again.

recommendations.title: Make pin 1 impossible to miss
recommendations.recommendation: Make pin 1 of every IC a square or rectangular pad, with the other pads rounded. Put a pin-1 mark in silkscreen right beside pin 1, outside the part's body, where it can still be seen after the part is placed. Avoid putting a pin-1 or polarity mark under the part: once the part is placed, the information is lost. A mark under the part is still better than no mark at all. Use one kind of mark throughout the board, and don't use a symbol (such as an asterisk) that could mean something else. Parts that aren't polarized (chip resistors and ceramic capacitors), and parts whose pads only fit one way (SOT-23, SOT-23-5, SOT-223, DPAK), don't need a mark.
recommendations.why: The assembler sets the orientation of every part from your data, then checks it by eye against the board. A mark hidden under the part disappears once it's placed; an ambiguous mark gets read the wrong way.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Parts placed backwards, often on every board in the batch.
recommendations.example: A designer used an asterisk beside a diode as a footnote marker, because the reference designator wouldn't fit. The assembler read it as the diode's polarity mark, and every board in the batch was built with that diode backwards.

recommendations.title: Mark diode and LED polarity so it can't be misread
recommendations.recommendation: Name diode and LED pins K (or C) for the cathode and A for the anode, not 1 and 2. Mark the cathode in silkscreen beside the cathode pad, not under the part: a K, or a short bar about as long as the pad is wide (one mark is enough). On through-hole diodes and LEDs, make the cathode the square pad (pin 1). Check the silkscreen mark against the schematic and the datasheet.
recommendations.why: Part makers mark polarity inconsistently: some LEDs are marked only underneath, some makers mark the anode on one part and the cathode on another, and some datasheets call the pins 1 and 2 without saying which is which. Some designers use the square pad for the anode, so a square pad alone isn't proof. A pin name, a visible mark and the schematic that agree leave nothing to guess.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: LEDs and diodes fitted backwards, which inspection machines can't always catch.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale: an 8-pin IC footprint with a rectangular pin-1 pad and a silkscreen dot right beside pin 1, beside one with identical pads and the dot inside the part's outline; two 0603 LEDs on the recommended 0603 footprint, one marked with a K and one with a short bar beside the cathode pad, beside the same footprint with the bar under the part, where it is hidden once the part is placed.

recommendations.title: Draw the real outline of each part in silkscreen, including anything that hangs over the edge
recommendations.recommendation: Give every footprint a silkscreen outline of the part's real body. It doesn't have to be detailed, just accurate. Draw the overhang of any part that hangs past the board edge (connectors, antennas, modules) in silkscreen, past the edge, as it would look if it could print over empty space. Don't trim it to the board outline; the fab trims silkscreen that falls outside the board itself. Attach a 3D model where you can.
recommendations.why: The assembler lays out the panel and checks for collisions from your data. An outline of the real body shows how much room a part needs; an overhang drawn past the edge tells them to keep the next board in the panel clear. The fab trims silkscreen that falls outside the board, and it sees the overhang first: the drawing is the warning that tells them to adjust the panel.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A connector that collides with the next board in the panel or a rail, found only after the boards are made.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale, plan view of a connector footprint at a board edge, twice. On the left, the connector's silkscreen outline stops at the board edge. On the right, the outline continues 3 mm past the edge, over the area outside the board, showing the overhang.

recommendations.title: Size plated through-holes and their pads from the lead
recommendations.recommendation: Size each plated hole from the part's largest lead, and each pad from the hole. For a square or rectangular lead, measure corner to corner. If the datasheet gives a hole tolerance like "+0.1 / −0 mm", make the hole 0.1 mm larger than the datasheet's recommended size (for a recommended 1.0 mm hole, make it 1.1 mm).
recommendations.why: A hole sized to the nominal lead can be too tight for the largest leads in a batch; a pad sized without allowance for drilling and registration can lose its ring of copper.
recommendations.typical_values:
Hole = largest lead diameter + a hole allowance. Pad = hole + 2 × (0.05 mm minimum annular ring + a pad allowance). The allowances depend on the IPC density level; level A is the easiest to build and the usual choice when there's room.

| IPC density level | Hole = lead + | Pad = hole + 2 × (0.05 + …) | Example: 0.5 mm lead |
|---|---|---|---|
| A (least dense, easiest to build) | 0.25 mm | 0.3 mm | 0.75 mm hole, 1.45 mm pad |
| B (moderately dense) | 0.20 mm | 0.25 mm | 0.70 mm hole, 1.30 mm pad |
| C (most dense, hardest to build) | 0.15 mm | 0.2 mm | 0.65 mm hole, 1.15 mm pad |
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Parts that won't go into their holes, or that need forcing, and pads with too little copper around the hole.

figures.alt: Enlarged and drawn to scale, three steps: measure the lead (a 0.5 mm round lead across, a rectangular lead corner to corner); the hole is the lead plus 0.25 mm, 0.75 mm; the pad is the hole plus twice 0.35 mm, 1.45 mm.

recommendations.title: Don't put copper on non-plated holes
recommendations.recommendation: Remove the copper pad from every hole that isn't plated, and give its solder mask opening a proper clearance. Where the hole sits in a copper pour, keep the pour back from the hole's edge.
recommendations.why: A copper ring on a non-plated hole leaves the fab guessing whether the hole should be plated. A pour that runs right up to the hole shows as a ring of copper at its edge, which looks just like the ring of a plated hole. A mask opening only a hair larger than the hole leaves a sliver of mask too thin to hold.
recommendations.typical_values: Copper pour kept at least 0.2 mm (8 mil) from the edge of the hole, the minimum fabs list; more with heavy copper, so check with your fab. Mask clearance of about 0.1 mm (4 mil) around the hole, not 0.025 mm (1 mil).
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Questions from the fab, a delay, or a hole plated that shouldn't be.
recommendations.example: Designs arrive with pads on half their non-plated holes and none on the other half.

checks.check: Copper on another net to the edge of a drilled hole, on every layer

figures.alt: Drawn to scale, plan view of a 3.2 mm non-plated hole in a ground pour, twice. On the left, the pour runs right up to the hole, so a ring of copper shows at its edge, like the ring of a plated hole. On the right, the pour is kept 0.2 mm back, so a ring of bare FR4 shows instead. Enlarged views below show the edge of the hole in each.

recommendations.title: Let your manufacturer design the panel, and approve it before you order bare boards
recommendations.page_title: Why boards are built in panels
recommendations.recommendation: Don't panelize the board yourself. Send a single board and let the assembler's engineering team design the panel around their own equipment. If you buy bare boards separately and send them to an assembler, get the assembler to approve the panel drawing before you place the board order.
recommendations.why: Every factory's machines, conveyors, board racks and clamps are slightly different, and only the factory knows what works best on its line. A panel that suits one assembler can be awkward or unbuildable for another.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Boards arrive that the assembler can't run without extra handling. Sometimes it costs more to handle them than to order new boards. One assembler estimates that only about two out of five "we already bought the boards" requests can be accommodated, usually at extra cost.
recommendations.example: A customer arrived with bare boards and parts already in hand for a board half an inch by one inch, too small for the factory's machines to hold. It could not be built as designed.

recommendations.title: Make sure small boards can be panelized, and never send them loose
recommendations.page_title: Why boards are built in panels
recommendations.recommendation: If your board is shorter than about 100 mm (4 in) in the direction of travel, expect it to be built in a panel, and make the panel at least 100 mm long. Don't order loose single boards for automated assembly.
recommendations.why: Assembly lines are a row of machines joined by conveyors. Each conveyor end may leave a gap of up to 19 mm, so two machines side by side can leave 38 mm, and real-world alignment brings that to about 50 mm. A board has to be longer than twice the gap: anything shorter hangs more than halfway off one conveyor before it reaches the next, tips and falls. PCBA cleaning machines are also built for panels; a single small board needs to be set inside of a cage or some kind of fixture instead.
recommendations.typical_values: 19 mm allowed gap per conveyor end · about 50 mm (2 in) real gap between machines · boards and panels at least 100 mm (4 in) long in the direction of travel. From the SMEMA conveyor interface standard (IPC-SMEMA-9851) and one factory's experience.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Boards drop between machines, or parts near the edge have to be hand-soldered instead of machine-placed.
recommendations.example: Conference badges, 3 × 4 in, arrived as loose single boards on a tight deadline. They fell through the gaps between conveyors. The team had to mask off and hand-solder the edge components that got covered by the machine clamps.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale, plan view of the end of one machine's conveyor and the start of the next, about 50 mm apart. A 15 by 10 mm board on its own has left the first conveyor and has nothing under it. The same board in a 120 by 50 mm panel, longer than twice the gap, rests on both conveyors at once.

recommendations.title: Expect panels of about 200 × 150 mm, and plan quantities in whole panels
recommendations.page_title: Why boards are built in panels
recommendations.recommendation: Assume your assembler will aim for a panel about the size of a sheet of letter or A4 paper. Order quantities, first articles and delivery batches in multiples of the number of boards on a panel.
recommendations.why: The panel is the unit the factory works in. Setting up a run (stencil, feeders, oven profile) builds at least one full panel, so even a request for "one first article" usually means one panel's worth.
recommendations.typical_values: About 200 × 150 mm is a common target size. One factory's example; other factories differ.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Odd quantities leave partly built panels, and a one-up panel of a large order means every board is handled one at a time.
recommendations.example: A customer ordered more than 2,000 boards on a one-up panel. Switching to a three-up panel on the next order made the run dramatically faster. Another long-running customer orders in batches that match the panel: first 27 boards (a 3 × 3 panel), later 10 after a redesign to a 10-up panel.
recommendations.applies_to: Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

recommendations.title: Keep panels stiff: small panels for thin boards, and no long floppy rows
recommendations.page_title: Why boards are built in panels
recommendations.recommendation: If your board is thinner than the standard 1.6 mm, expect smaller panels. Avoid board shapes that force a long, narrow panel held only at its short ends. For large, heavy, double-sided panels, ask whether the assembler will need a support fixture in the reflow oven.
recommendations.why: A panel behaves like a beam: the longer and thinner it is, the more it sags, and a heavy load makes it worse. In the reflow oven, a double-sided panel can't lie on a belt, so it hangs by its edges on narrow rails while the board is at its softest.
recommendations.typical_values: 1.6 mm is the standard thickness. Oven pin rails grip only about 3 mm of board edge. Sag problems seen on panels over 200 mm.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Bowed panels cause trouble in optical inspection and selective soldering, and in the worst case a panel drops off the oven rails. The assembler has to build custom support tooling, which adds cost and time to your job.
recommendations.example: A 16 in (about 400 mm) long, 5 × 2 panel held only at its short ends flexed "like a diving board". Panels fell apart just from being picked up, and the job needed custom tooling.

figures.alt: End-on views of a 1.6 mm panel on the oven's pin rails, which grip about 3 mm of each edge. A panel 200 mm across the rails sags in the middle; one 100 mm across sags one sixteenth as much. The sag is exaggerated by the same factor in both.

sources.text: [“How PCB panelization methods inform depanelization”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685-how-pcb-panelization-methods-inform-depanelization) (Sep 2022), [22:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685?t=1320)–23:00; [“An Answering Your Questions Grab Bag”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902-an-answering-your-questions-grab-bag) (Oct 2023), [41:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902?t=2460)–42:00; [“Custom tooling to the rescue”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10804740-custom-tooling-to-the-rescue) (Jul 2022), [10:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10804740?t=600)–12:00.

recommendations.title: Expect rails along the long edges unless you design them out
recommendations.recommendation: Assume your assembler will add a rail of about 10 mm along each long edge of the panel and will put the global fiducials there. If you can keep every component and exposed copper well clear of the board edges (see [PCB-DFA-015](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/04-edge-clearance/#pcb-dfa-015-keep-parts-and-exposed-copper-at-least-3-mm-from-the-edges-5-mm-if-you-can)), tell your assembler: they may be able to skip the rails.
recommendations.why: Conveyors and machine clamps grip the board edge. Rails give them a strip to hold that carries nothing of yours. Skipping rails saves panel material and a depaneling step, but needs a board designed for it from the start.
recommendations.typical_values: About 10 mm per rail is common. For one assembler, 95–99 % of jobs need rails. A large panel may also get a 10 mm rail down the middle so the reflow oven's center support has somewhere to sit. Some assemblers, Worthington Assembly among them, put 10 mm rails on all four sides and between the boards, with the global fiducials on the short-edge rails (D48, [PCB-DFA-076](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/02-rails-tooling-holes-fiducials/#pcb-dfa-076-make-each-fiducial-show-which-side-and-which-corner-it-is)). Tooling holes in the rails are now largely a legacy feature: one assembler used 3/16 in (about 4.8 mm) holes for years and, as of 2026, has stopped using them altogether. Others still use them, in various sizes.
recommendations.example: One designer laid out a 2 × 2 panel with no rails at all: edge clearances and fiducials designed in, nothing to break off, zero waste.
recommendations.applies_to: Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

recommendations.title: Make fiducials simple copper dots, round or square, with a clear ring around them
recommendations.recommendation: Make each fiducial a round copper dot 1 mm in diameter, with the solder mask pulled back to a circle 2 mm in diameter, so a 0.5 mm ring of bare board surrounds it. You can use squares too. But crosses and other shapes are less common. A clever practice is to use rounds on the top side and squares on the bottom side. Silkscreen labels are not necessary.
recommendations.why: Cameras need a high-contrast target. Glossy solder mask next to the dot, especially white or yellow, reflects light and confuses them. Modern vision systems don't need unusual shapes, and every assembler recognizes a plain dot as a fiducial.
recommendations.typical_values: 1 mm dot · 2 mm mask opening. Common industry practice.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: The machine can't find the board. The operator has to teach it by hand, and placement accuracy can suffer.

sources.text: [“What are fiducials and why you should use them”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9355465-what-are-fiducials-and-why-you-should-use-them) (Oct 2021), [23:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9355465?t=1380)–26:00; [“Small PCB layout decisions that have a significant impact on assembly”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623-small-pcb-layout-decisions-that-have-a-significant-impact-on-assembly) (Aug 2021), [27:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623?t=1620)–31:00.

episodes.title: What are fiducials and why you should use them
Small PCB layout decisions that have a significant impact on assembly

recommendations.title: Put at least two fiducials on each board, far apart, on every side that has surface-mount parts
recommendations.recommendation: Place two fiducials near opposite corners of the board itself, not only on the panel rails. Use three on large boards. If both sides of the board carry surface-mount parts, put fiducials on both sides. Keep the center of every fiducial's copper dot about 5 mm in from the edge of the panel.
recommendations.why:
Two fiducials give the machine position and rotation. A third lets it correct for the board stretching or shrinking slightly. Fiducials on the board itself mean it can still be built if it comes out of its panel, and an operator can fix a setup mistake at the machine without calling an engineer. Most machines clamp the outer 3 mm or so of the panel edge, so any part of a fiducial inside that strip will probably be covered.

*D2. The close-up is enlarged and drawn to scale. A copper dot 1 mm in diameter sits in a solder mask opening 2 mm in diameter, leaving a 0.5 mm ring of bare board. The outer 3 mm of the panel edge is shaded: that's where machine clamps grip. The center of the copper dot is 5 mm in from the panel edge, so the clamps can't hide it.*
recommendations.typical_values: 2 minimum, 3 preferred · center about 5 mm in from the panel edge; clamps cover the outer ~3 mm. If the board runs without rails, its own edge is the panel edge, so give the fiducials more room: one rail-less design used about 10 mm.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Most designs arrive without fiducials (about 19 out of 20 at one factory), so assemblers add them to the rails. That works, but only while the board stays in its panel.
recommendations.example: A conveyor fault once broke a panel into its individual boards. Because each board had its own fiducials, the machine was reprogrammed and the boards were built anyway.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Very small boards (about 10 × 15 mm) have been built successfully without fiducials by putting them in a panel.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale, enlarged: a 1 mm copper fiducial dot inside a 2 mm solder mask opening, its center 5 mm from the panel edge, outside the shaded 3 mm clamp zone.

recommendations.title: If there's room, add local fiducials beside expensive or very fine-pitch parts
recommendations.recommendation: If there's room and it's easy, add a pair of fiducials right beside high-value BGAs, very fine-pitch parts and dense clusters of very small parts, such as 0201 and 01005. This is a low priority. Leave them out if they get in the way of anything else on the board.
recommendations.why: Local fiducials let the placement machine re-check its position right at that part, instead of relying on fiducials far away across the panel. But modern placement machines are accurate enough with the board's own fiducials. They also use their own cameras to find each part's leads or balls before placing it. So on most boards today, local fiducials add little.
recommendations.example: A board carrying a single FPGA worth about $6,000 has fiducials at the corners of the BGA.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale, plan view of a 0.8 mm-pitch BGA on a board, with its inner balls fanned out to vias and its outer ring escaping straight out. A local fiducial, FID1 and FID2, sits just outside two opposite corners of the BGA.

recommendations.title: Don't use drilled holes instead of fiducials
recommendations.recommendation: Use etched copper fiducials for machine alignment, even if the board already has tooling or mounting holes.
recommendations.why: Holes are drilled in a separate step from copper etching, so they never line up with the pads quite as precisely. Fiducials are etched at the same moment as the pads they help place.

sources.text: [“What are fiducials and why you should use them”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9355465-what-are-fiducials-and-why-you-should-use-them) (Oct 2021), [19:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9355465?t=1140)–20:00.

recommendations.title: Make each fiducial show which side and which corner it is
recommendations.recommendation: Give the panel three global fiducials of different sizes, 1, 2 and 3 mm, and make them round on the top side and square on the bottom side. Put them on the rails at three corners: the 1 mm at one corner, and the 2 mm and 3 mm at the two ends of the opposite long edge. Give each the clear ring of bare board described in [PCB-DFA-006](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/02-rails-tooling-holes-fiducials/#pcb-dfa-006-make-fiducials-simple-copper-dots-round-or-square-with-a-clear-ring-around-them).
recommendations.why: A machine's camera finds each fiducial by its shape and size. If every fiducial is the same, a panel loaded the wrong way round, or upside down, still shows the camera what it expects, and the machine prints or places on the wrong side or rotated by 180°. With three sizes and a different shape on each side, the camera finds a 1 mm dot where it expected a 3 mm one, or a square where it expected a circle, and stops before anything is built.
recommendations.typical_values:
Copper dots 1, 2 and 3 mm, each in a solder mask opening about twice its size. Round on the top side, square on the bottom. At one assembler: on the short-edge rails, centered in the 10 mm rail and 15 mm from the long edges (D48).

![D48 is drawn to scale: the top and bottom of a 150 by 110 mm panel of four boards with 10 mm rails on all four sides and between the boards. Each side has a 1 mm, a 2 mm and a 3 mm fiducial on the short-edge rails, round on top and square on the bottom; the long-edge rail carries the side and the part number in silkscreen. An enlarged row shows the six fiducials.](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/images/panel-style.svg)
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A panel loaded rotated or upside down that the machine accepts anyway: paste printed on the wrong side, or parts placed 180° out across the whole panel.
recommendations.applies_to: Varies by assembler; this is Worthington Assembly's panel style. Many assemblers design the panel themselves ([PCB-DFA-001](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/01-why-panels/#pcb-dfa-001-let-your-manufacturer-design-the-panel-and-approve-it-before-you-order-bare-boards)); if yours does, ask for this.

sources.text: Worthington Assembly Panel Design Guidelines v1.1; Chris Denney (author).

recommendations.title: Print the board's part number and the side on the panel rails
recommendations.recommendation: Put the board's part number and the word "Top" or "Bottom" in silkscreen on a rail on each side of the panel. At one assembler, both go on the long-edge rail opposite the 2 mm and 3 mm fiducials (D48).
recommendations.why: Anyone handling a panel, at any station, can see at a glance what board it is and which side is facing them. That catches the wrong job on a machine, or a panel turned over, before it's built.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Boards that look alike mixed up between jobs, or a panel run on the wrong side.
recommendations.applies_to: Varies by assembler; this is Worthington Assembly's panel style.

sources.text: Worthington Assembly Panel Design Guidelines v1.1; Chris Denney (author).

recommendations.title: Give the board its own tooling holes if it will go into a test fixture
recommendations.recommendation: If the board will be tested in a fixture (for example a bed-of-nails or functional test fixture), include tooling holes on the board itself so the fixture can locate it. Don't rely on the board outline.
recommendations.why: Tooling holes on the rails are gone once the board leaves the panel. A routed edge is accurate to within about 0.1 mm, but a V-scored edge varies a lot more, so it's a poor reference for a fixture.
recommendations.typical_values: There's no single standard, but one contract manufacturer's guide is a good starting point. Make each tooling hole 3 mm to 4 mm in diameter. A 2 mm hole is possible if you really need it. Drill them to a tolerance of +0.05 mm, −0.0 mm, and don't plate them. Use two holes per board, ideally in diagonally opposite corners, as far apart as you can, and at least 3 mm from the edge of the board. Keep an area at least 5 mm in diameter around each hole free of parts and tracks on the underside, so the board sits flat and the tooling pins can't short anything. Check the size and position with whoever builds the fixture.

recommendations.title: Use straight-edged, rectangular board outlines when you can
recommendations.page_title: Breakaway methods: V-score, tabs and mouse bites
recommendations.recommendation: Keep the board outline rectangular, or at least made of straight edges, unless the product really needs another shape.
recommendations.why: A straight-edged board can be V-scored, which is the cheaper and faster method. Any curved or irregular edge forces tab routing, which needs a slower router pass and leaves stubs that may need filing or sanding.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Higher board cost, slower depaneling, and manual finishing of the tab stubs.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale, two 80 by 70 mm panels. Four rectangular boards are separated by V-score lines that run straight across the whole panel. Four round boards are each cut out by a routed slot and held by four tabs with mouse bites.

recommendations.title: Keep overhanging parts away from breakaway edges, and draw the overhang on the silkscreen
recommendations.page_title: Breakaway methods: V-score, tabs and mouse bites
recommendations.recommendation: Avoid connectors, antennas or modules that hang past the board edge on an edge that will be V-scored or tabbed. Never put overhangs on opposite edges facing each other across the panel. If an overhang is unavoidable, show its full outline on the silkscreen or assembly drawing so the panel designer can leave room.
recommendations.why: Separating a V-score means bending the panel along the groove, and an overhanging part blocks that bend. The panel designer usually works from the board outline and won't read every datasheet; a visible outline makes them check and add a cut-out (relief) in the panel at that spot.
recommendations.typical_values: Example: a coax connector overhanging by 7 mm needed about 10 mm of clearance. Some fiber optic connectors overhang the edge by more than 1 in (25 mm).
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Panels that are nearly impossible to separate, parts snapped off during depaneling or shipping, and boards that have to be cut apart by hand.
recommendations.example: An ethernet port on the bottom of one board and a USB port on the top of its neighbor overlapped across the panel rail with no clearance. The boards could not be separated without removing and re-soldering a part. On another design, a module on top and a USB port directly beneath it pinched the panel material; hundreds of boards had to be cut free by hand.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale, plan views with side views below. Boards A and B meet at a V-score, and a coax connector on board A hangs 7 mm past it, over board B; bent to snap the score, board B meets the connector before the score breaks. With board A's edge routed and held by tabs, and a routed relief cut-out leaving 10 mm from its edge, nothing is in the way.

Drawn to scale, three side views of two boards joined by a V-score. A connector on board B's top hangs 7 mm over board A, and a connector on board A's underside hangs 7 mm under board B. Bending board B up drops its own connector onto board A; bending it down lands board B on board A's connector. The score can't be snapped either way.

recommendations.title: Mark critical edges on a drawing, and leave room around the board in the enclosure
recommendations.page_title: Breakaway methods: V-score, tabs and mouse bites
recommendations.recommendation: Don't draw the board to the exact inside size of its enclosure. Leave about 1 mm all round (0.5 mm at the very least). If an edge really must be held tightly, mark it as a critical dimension on a mechanical drawing so the assembler routes that edge instead of scoring or tabbing it.
recommendations.why: Even good fabs hold board edges to only about ±0.1 mm, and boards change size slightly through reflow and other heating steps. A V-scored edge is less precise than a routed one, and tab stubs stick out past the edge.
recommendations.typical_values: Fab edge tolerance about ±0.1 mm (routed) · enclosure clearance about 1 mm, 0.5 mm minimum.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Boards that don't fit their case, or that need every tab stub filed off by hand.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Tighter tolerances may be possible but would need to be confirmed with the fab and assembler in advance.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale, plan view of a 50 by 30 mm board inside an enclosure with 1 mm of room all round. A 0.5 mm tab stub on the left edge, shown enlarged, fits in that room. The right edge is marked as critical, to be routed to about plus or minus 0.1 mm.

recommendations.title: If you need tabs and a clean outline, recess the edge where each tab joins
recommendations.page_title: Breakaway methods: V-score, tabs and mouse bites
recommendations.recommendation: For a tab-routed board that must fit its enclosure closely, add a small notch in the board outline at each tab location. Agree on the tab positions with your assembler.
recommendations.why: After breaking, the tab stub sits inside the notch, flush with the rest of the outline, so nobody has to file or sand it off.
recommendations.typical_values:
Tabs are typically about 3–6 mm wide. Mouse-bite holes are 0.5 mm non-plated holes, pulled back 0.1 mm from the board edge. Keep traces, pads and plated holes at least 0.5 mm from the mouse-bite holes, which puts them at least 1.1 mm from the board edge. One assembler's guideline.

*D5. The close-up is enlarged and drawn to scale. Non-plated holes 0.5 mm in diameter run along the board edge, each pulled back 0.1 mm from the edge. The nearest trace, pad or plated hole is at least 0.5 mm from the holes, which puts it at least 1.1 mm from the board edge.*
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Every board needs its tab stubs filed, sanded or ground flush. If your assembler does not have an automated depaneling router, then it's slow manual work, and you pay for it whether or not it's on the quote.
recommendations.example: A consumer product with a distinctive non-rectangular enclosure, ordered in the thousands. The customer suggested recessing the edge at each tab instead of having every unit filed by hand. The assembler now recommends it to other customers.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale: four close-ups of a board edge at a breakaway tab. Without a recess, the broken tab leaves a stub sticking out past the board outline. With a 1 mm recess, the stub stays below the outline.
Drawn to scale, enlarged: 0.5 mm mouse-bite holes pulled back 0.1 mm from the board edge, with the nearest trace at least 0.5 mm from the holes and 1.1 mm from the edge.

recommendations.title: Agree the number and position of tabs on round or odd-shaped boards
recommendations.page_title: Breakaway methods: V-score, tabs and mouse bites
recommendations.recommendation: For non-rectangular boards, decide with your assembler how many tabs to use and where they go. Tell them about any keep-out areas, such as an antenna, where a tab must not be placed.
recommendations.why: Too few tabs and a large board can fall out of the panel during handling or reflow. Too many, or in the wrong place, and separating the board risks damaging it.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Example: a 6 in (about 150 mm) round board with only two tabs, which is clearly not enough to hold it securely.
recommendations.applies_to: Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

recommendations.title: Talk to your assembler before panelizing boards thicker than about 2 mm
recommendations.page_title: Breakaway methods: V-score, tabs and mouse bites
recommendations.recommendation: If your board is 2 mm thick or more, discuss depaneling with your assembler before you order.
recommendations.why: Standard depaneling tools are made for boards around 1.6 mm thick. Thicker boards are too stiff to snap cleanly along a score, and too thick for the usual round-blade cutter.
recommendations.typical_values: 1.6–1.8 mm depanels normally · 2.0–2.4 mm and up gets difficult.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: If your assembler does not have an automatic depaneling router then boards are broken by hand or cut apart one at a time with special cutters. That's slow, it adds labor cost, and the extra force puts parts near the edge at risk.
recommendations.example: Boards a quarter of an inch (about 6 mm) thick could not be separated by any normal method and had to be cut apart by hand with a rotary tool.

recommendations.title: Keep parts and exposed copper at least 3 mm from the edges, 5 mm if you can
recommendations.page_title: Clearance near board and panel edges
recommendations.recommendation: Keep every component and every piece of exposed, solderable copper at least 3 mm from the board's long edges, and preferably 5 mm. This is generally not possible, but very convenient when possible. If you manage this, plus fiducials on the board, tell your assembler: they may be able to run the board without rails.
recommendations.why: Equipment built to the SMEMA conveyor standard (IPC-SMEMA-9851) grips about 3 mm of the board edge, and the standard allows a conveyor to use up to 5 mm. Anything in that strip can be crushed, hidden from cameras or kept from getting solder paste. Without the clearance, the assembler has to add rails, which costs panel material and depaneling time.
recommendations.typical_values: 3 mm minimum · 5 mm recommended. Copper that is covered by solder mask can come much closer (see PCB-DFM-002).
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Rails on every panel, a depaneling step on every board, and extra handling stress on the parts near the edge.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Most assemblers add rails by default anyway; ask yours whether they'll run your board without them.

recommendations.title: Keep copper back from the board edge, further for V-score than for routing
recommendations.page_title: Clearance near board and panel edges
recommendations.recommendation: Keep traces and copper pours, on every layer, at least 0.5 mm (20 mil) from a V-score line, and 1.0 mm if you have room. On routed edges, 0.25 mm (10 mil) is a common minimum. Some fabs can route closer, down to about 0.13 mm (5 mil), if you agree it with them first.
recommendations.why: The V-score blade cuts a groove into the board, and its position varies by a few tenths of a millimeter. Copper too close to it gets cut, exposed or cracked when the board is snapped apart. Routing is more precise and puts less stress on the edge.
recommendations.typical_values: V-score: 0.45–0.5 mm minimum in published fab rules (one European fab: 0.45 mm on all layers; one US fab: 20 mil), with some fabs asking for up to 1.0 mm · routed: about 0.25 mm on outer layers (some fabs ask 0.4 mm on inner layers). Copper right up to the edge can't be V-scored at all.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: The fab flags the design and puts it on hold, or rejects it.
recommendations.applies_to: Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

checks.check: Copper to the board edge

recommendations.title: Keep components back from breakaway edges, and ceramic capacitors further still
recommendations.page_title: Clearance near board and panel edges
recommendations.recommendation: Keep components at least 1.3 mm (50 mil) from any edge that will be V-scored or tab-routed. Keep multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) at least 5 mm (0.2 in) from a V-scored edge and from each breakaway tab, and 10 mm if you have room. If an MLCC has to sit closer than 5 mm, use a flexible-termination MLCC, or ask for a routed slot between the part and the break line.
recommendations.why: Breaking a panel apart bends the board along the break line, and the strain is highest right next to it, and highest of all at a tab. Most parts can take it. MLCCs are ceramic: they don't bend, they crack.
recommendations.typical_values: Components 1.3 mm (50 mil) · MLCCs 5 mm (0.2 in) minimum, as two capacitor makers advise · MLCCs 10 mm better, as a third maker advises for board edges, screw holes and connectors. Flexible-termination MLCCs are rated for up to 5 mm of board bending in the standard bend test, against the usual 2 mm minimum. Near an MLCC, a routed slot is a gentler break line than a row of mouse bites. Some assemblers accept MLCCs as close as 3.2 mm (125 mil) on low-volume boards, at higher risk.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Cracked capacitors are hard to catch. Many pass test and fail weeks or months later in the field, sometimes as a short that can overheat. On a run of 50 boards you may never see it; at automotive volumes, you will.
recommendations.example: Ceramic capacitors placed close to the edge cracked during depaneling, and many boards had to be reworked.

recommendations.title: Turn ceramic capacitors and other chip parts near a break line parallel to it
recommendations.page_title: Clearance near board and panel edges
recommendations.recommendation: Where a chip part (especially an MLCC) has to sit near a V-score line or breakaway tab, turn it so its long axis runs parallel to the line, not across it. If you can't, ask your assembler about a routed slot between the part and the line.
recommendations.why: Snapping a panel bends the board along the break line, and the strain runs across the line. A part lying across the line is stretched end to end, which is how MLCCs crack. A part lying along the line sees much less of that strain. Capacitor makers rank parallel placement as the lowest-stress option.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Cracked capacitors that may pass test and fail later in the field. A cracked MLCC can short and overheat.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Distance from the line (PCB-DFA-016) still matters most.

recommendations.title: If copper must run to the board edge, say so
recommendations.page_title: Clearance near board and panel edges
recommendations.recommendation: If your design really needs copper right up to the edge (for example an edge connector or an edge-plated shield), state it clearly in the fabrication notes.
recommendations.why: Fab engineers are trained to pull copper back from the edge by default, because routing through copper wears out router bits faster. They can do it, but only if they know you mean it.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: The fab quietly pulls your copper back, or puts the job on hold with questions.

recommendations.title: Accept X-outs unless you have a real reason not to
recommendations.page_title: X-outs: accepting panels with a bad board
recommendations.recommendation: Allow your fab and assembler to use panels with X-outs. If your process truly can't handle them (for example a test fixture that needs every position filled), say so up front and expect to pay for it.
recommendations.why: The other boards on the panel are perfectly good. Refusing X-outs means the fab scraps whole panels, and that cost is passed on to you.
recommendations.typical_values: Refusing X-outs can cost about 20–30 % more per board (one assembler's estimate, as of 2023).
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: You pay a premium for every board, often without seeing it on the quote.
recommendations.applies_to: Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

recommendations.title: Design with margin above the fab's minimums to avoid X-outs in the first place
recommendations.page_title: X-outs: accepting panels with a bad board
recommendations.recommendation: Don't design right at the fab's stated minimum trace width and spacing. Use 6 mil (0.15 mm) as an everyday minimum and 8 mil (0.2 mm) where you have room. Design for the copper weight you'll actually order: 2 oz copper needs wider gaps than 1 oz.
recommendations.why: Tight features are fine on one small board but get much harder to make perfectly when they're repeated many times across a large panel. Margin lets the fab hit its tolerances every time, so fewer boards fail.
recommendations.typical_values: Most fabs' practical limit is about 4 mil (0.1 mm) · 6 mil (0.15 mm) everyday minimum · 8 mil (0.2 mm) comfortable, and recommended for 2 oz copper.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: More boards fail at the fab. Panels arrive full of X-outs, the fab has to make extra panels to fill your order, and the cost and delay come back to you.
recommendations.example: A power-supply board designed with 1 oz spacing but ordered in 2 oz copper came back with so many X-outs that about 400 panels had to be made to deliver an order that should have needed 250. Redesigning to 8 mil trace and gap fixed it. The other way round, a designer who chose 8 mil instead of the fab's 6 mil minimum reported zero X-outs across many thousands of boards.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Exact limits vary by fab.

recommendations.title: Prefer smaller panels for designs that are hard to make
recommendations.page_title: X-outs: accepting panels with a bad board
recommendations.recommendation: If your design pushes the fab's limits, ask for a smaller panel (for example 3- or 4-up) rather than a large one (for example 15-up).
recommendations.why: A large panel collects more bad boards per panel. Some fabs resist shipping panels with many X-outs, and a panel that is mostly X-outs wastes assembly time.
recommendations.applies_to: Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.
