recommendations.title: Use standard FR-4 unless the product needs something else
recommendations.recommendation: Specify standard FR-4 epoxy-glass laminate unless your product has a real need for something else: sustained high temperature, very high frequencies, or a customer requirement. If you need a particular material or certification, name it by its IPC-4101 specification sheet (the "slash sheet") and confirm with your fab that they stock it.
recommendations.why: Standard materials are in stock at every fab, in every thickness. Exotic laminates can take about eight weeks to arrive and come with minimum order quantities, and some are harder to drill, plate and laminate. Tg (glass transition temperature) is the temperature at which the laminate starts to soften; a higher-Tg material stays stiffer and flatter through reflow, rework and hot service. UL flammability approval belongs to a particular fab's process with a particular material, so a different material or a custom build may not carry it.
recommendations.typical_values: Standard FR-4 has a Tg of about 135 °C; mid-Tg is about 150 °C and high-Tg about 170 °C. Fabs don't treat mid- or high-Tg as standard, and it usually costs more. If you don't specify Tg, expect the cheapest material, most likely about 135 °C, but the fab may use anything reasonable it has on the shelf. So if your product needs mid- or high-Tg, say so on the drawing; if it doesn't, don't pay for it.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Weeks added to the lead time and a higher price for a material the product didn't need; or, the other way round, a board that softens and warps in a hot product.

recommendations.title: Start from your fab's standard stack-up, or give them what they need to build one
recommendations.recommendation: Use your fab's standard stack-up for your layer count and thickness if it meets your needs. If you need a custom one (for controlled impedance, say), don't work it out alone: give the fab the signal frequencies, the target impedances, which layers each impedance trace runs on and references, and how much the material may cost, and let their engineers propose the stack-up before you place the order.
recommendations.why: The fab knows which cores and prepregs it actually stocks, and how much each one thins when it's pressed. A stack-up built from someone else's materials list will be adjusted anyway. Fabs are allowed to tune dielectric thicknesses (by about ±20%) to hit a stated impedance, but a large change should come back to you for approval.
recommendations.typical_values:
- Minimum dielectric thickness between copper layers, when the drawing doesn't say: 65 µm (2.56 mil) under IPC-6012F.
Older guidance, including IPC-6012E, gave 3.5 mil (90 µm).
- One sheet of prepreg between the outer layer and the next layer is fine for most boards; use two for products that will see heavy shock and vibration.
- Avoid stacking more than three sheets of prepreg in one gap.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A stack-up that can't be built from stock material, a week lost going back and forth, or impedances that are off because the fab had to change your dielectrics.
recommendations.applies_to: Varies by manufacturer; standard stack-ups are fab-specific.

recommendations.title: Specify controlled impedance fully, make the traces easy to find, and leave room to widen them
recommendations.why: Gerbers show trace widths, not which traces are impedance-controlled. An odd width lets the fab select every impedance trace at once. Etching leaves traces narrower at the top than the bottom, and the fab adjusts widths and dielectrics to suit its own materials; if the traces are hemmed in, they can't.
recommendations.typical_values: Tolerance ±10% is common; ±5% costs more. Common targets: 50 Ω single-ended, 90 or 100 Ω differential. Ask for a TDR test of the impedance coupon, or the fab's stack-up calculation, if you want proof.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Traces that can't reach the impedance you need, discovered after the board is built.
recommendations.example: A board revision added an 85 Ω differential pair in a space that allowed only 3 mil traces with 3 mil gaps; the impedance was physically unachievable in that space, and the design sat stuck for over a week.

recommendations.title: Size traces and gaps for the finished copper weight
recommendations.recommendation: Set your trace width and spacing rules for the copper weight the board will really have, and set the clearance from copper pours to the same values.
recommendations.why: Copper is etched from the side as well as from the top, so thicker copper needs wider gaps to etch cleanly. Outer layers also gain plated copper on top of the foil. A pour clearance left at a tight default undoes every other rule.
recommendations.typical_values:
| Finished copper | Minimum trace and space | Recommended |
|---|---|---|
| 1 oz (35 µm) | 0.1 mm (4 mil) | 0.15 mm (6 mil) |
| 2 oz (70 µm) | 0.2 mm (8 mil) | 0.25 mm (10 mil) |

On 2 oz copper, 6 mil can be built, but with very poor yield, so avoid it. Finer than about 0.075 mm (3 mil) needs thinner starting foil and a fab that specializes in it.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Shorts and opens, lower yield, X-outs, and a higher price; heavy-copper boards drawn to 1 oz rules may not be buildable at all.
recommendations.example: A motor controller needed 2 oz copper for its current but was laid out with fine 1 oz rules; the fab's advice was to open trace and gap up to 8 mil. On another board, trace and space were set to 6 mil, but the pour clearance was left at 2 mil.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice; exact capability varies by fab.

checks.check: Trace width
Spacing between copper on different nets, including pours

recommendations.title: Use as few layers as the circuit needs
recommendations.recommendation: Use two layers when the circuit genuinely allows it, and add layers only when routing, power or signal integrity need them.
recommendations.why: Every extra pair of layers adds lamination, drilling depth, registration risk and cost. Above about 12 to 16 layers, many fabs reach the limit of their equipment and need very thin cores and tighter process control.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A higher price and a longer lead time than the board needed; at high layer counts, fewer fabs that can build it.

recommendations.title: Expect thin boards to need a carrier during assembly
recommendations.recommendation: Choose the board thickness the product needs; any thickness can be assembled, even double-sided flexible boards. For boards 0.6 mm or thinner, expect the assembler to run them on a carrier (a rigid tray that holds the board through printing, placement and reflow), and ask what it costs.
recommendations.why: Thin boards sag on conveyors and under the stencil, and warp in the oven. A carrier holds them flat, but it has to be made for the board.
recommendations.typical_values: 0.6 mm or thinner: carrier needed. About 0.8 mm: sometimes needed. 1.0 mm and thicker: generally not needed.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A carrier charge and lead time you didn't plan for.
recommendations.applies_to: Varies by assembler; thresholds from Worthington Assembly and CircuitHub (2026).

recommendations.title: Keep copper 0.25 mm or more from drilled holes on every layer
recommendations.recommendation: Keep at least 0.25 mm (10 mil) between the edge of any drilled hole and the nearest copper it isn't meant to connect to, on every layer, including plane clearances. Go down to 0.2 mm (8 mil) only in a tight area, and avoid going below 0.15 mm (6 mil).
recommendations.why: Layers move during lamination, and the drill has its own positional tolerance. The gap between a hole and nearby copper is what absorbs both. Measure it edge to edge: from the edge of the hole to the edge of the copper.
recommendations.typical_values: 0.25–0.3 mm (10–12 mil): good boards every time. 0.2 mm (8 mil): possible, harder. 0.15 mm (6 mil): in one small, tight area only; below that, few fabs will build it.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Shorts between a hole and an inner-layer trace or plane, found at electrical test as scrapped boards, or worse, not found until later.

checks.check: Copper on another net to the edge of a drilled hole, on every layer

recommendations.title: On very large boards, expect the fab to scale the outer layers, and tell the assembler
recommendations.recommendation: If your board is very large (about 400 mm or longer), ask the fab whether they had to scale the outer layers, and make sure the stencil is made to match the boards as built.
recommendations.why: On a large board, the movement in the press adds up from one end to the other. To keep the holes on their pads, the fab may scale the drill data and then scale the outer-layer artwork to match. A stencil cut from your original data is then slightly too small or too large for the board.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Paste prints that are on the pads at one end of the board and off them at the other.
recommendations.applies_to: Large boards; panels are usually kept small enough to avoid it.

recommendations.title: Give hole sizes as finished sizes
recommendations.recommendation: Give every hole in your design as the finished size you need after plating and surface finish, not the size of drill you think the fab should use.
recommendations.why: The fab drills plated holes larger, by an amount that depends on its plating process, copper weight and finish, so that the finished hole comes out at your size. They can only do that if your sizes are finished sizes.
recommendations.typical_values: A 1.0 mm finished plated hole is typically drilled at about 1.1 to 1.15 mm. One large fab enlarges plated holes of 0.5 mm and up by 0.15 mm, and non-plated holes by 0.05 mm.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Holes too small for the leads, if you've already allowed for plating and the fab allows for it again.

recommendations.title: Keep the aspect ratio at 8:1 or less, and holes 0.25 mm or larger where you can
recommendations.recommendation: Keep the ratio of board thickness to the smallest plated hole's drill size at 8:1 or less, and no more than 10:1. Use 0.25 mm (10 mil) or larger for the smallest drilled holes where the design allows, and avoid going below 0.2 mm.
recommendations.why: Plating solution has to flow all the way down a hole to plate its walls. The deeper and narrower the hole, the harder that is, and the thinner the copper in the middle of the barrel. Small drills also bend and break more easily, and fabs can't stack as many panels on the drill at once, which makes drilling slower and more expensive.
recommendations.typical_values:
(see D47)

| Aspect ratio (thickness : drill) | What it means |
|---|---|
| 8:1 or less | Recommended; any good fab |
| 8:1 to 10:1 | Possible; pushing the limits |
| Over 10:1 | Difficult; ask first |

For a 1.6 mm board, a 0.2 mm drill is 8:1. At 0.25 mm, a fab can drill two 1.6 mm panels stacked together; some fabs can't drill below 0.2 mm at all.

![D47 is drawn to scale: a 1.6 mm board with a 0.2 mm drilled hole, an aspect ratio of 8 to 1; and top views of a 0.6 mm pad on a 0.3 mm hole, with a 0.15 mm annular ring when centered and 0.05 mm left on one side when the drill is 0.1 mm off center.](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/images/aspect-ratio-annular-ring.svg)
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Thin or missing copper in the middle of the hole, which may pass electrical test and then crack open in thermal cycling.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice; capability varies by fab.

checks.check: Finished diameter of a drilled hole, except laser microvias

recommendations.title: Use as few different hole sizes as you can
recommendations.recommendation: Standardize on one or two via sizes, and avoid hole sizes that differ by only a few hundredths of a millimeter.
recommendations.why: Every hole size is another tool change on the drilling machine. Near-duplicate sizes usually come from footprints made by different people, not from a real need.
recommendations.typical_values: About 40 to 60 seconds per tool change, on every panel.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Longer drilling time and a higher price for no benefit.

recommendations.title: Give every plated hole an annular ring with margin above the IPC minimum
recommendations.recommendation: Design every pad on a plated hole with an annular ring (the copper between the edge of the hole and the edge of the pad) of 0.15 mm or more on outer layers where you can. Never end a trace at a plated hole without a pad.
recommendations.why: The drill never lands exactly in the center of the pad: layers move in the press, and the drill has its own tolerance. The annular ring is the margin that keeps the hole inside the pad. IPC-6012 sets what the finished board must meet; your design needs more than that, so the board still meets it after the drill wanders.
recommendations.typical_values:
Design target: 0.15 mm (6 mil) on outer layers; 0.125 mm is a common fab minimum for design; 0.2 mm or more for high-reliability products.
IPC-6012F, finished board, external plated holes:
- Class 2: the hole may break out of the pad by up to 90°, as long as the trace joining the pad isn't narrowed too far; with no teardrop, at least 25 µm of ring where the trace joins.
- Class 3: at least 50 µm of ring all round.

Internal layers, Class 3: at least 25 µm. Teardrops (fillets where a trace meets a pad) are acceptable for Class 2 unless you prohibit them, and must be agreed for Class 3.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Holes that break out of their pads, X-outs, and boards that fail Class 3 inspection.

checks.check: Annular ring on plated holes and vias

sources.text: IPC-6012F (Sept 2023), section 3.4.2 and Table 3-7; [“Advanced Drilling w/ CAM Engineer, Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991-advanced-drilling-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (May 2022), [26:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991?t=1560)–28:00 and [35:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991?t=2100)–36:00; [“Inner Layer Production w/ CAM Engineer Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9018673-inner-layer-production-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (Aug 2021), [01:03:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9018673?t=3780)–01:04:00; fabs' published annular ring guidance (0.125–0.15 mm).

recommendations.title: Use microvias and blind or buried vias only when you need them
recommendations.recommendation: Use plain through-hole vias unless the design really needs blind, buried or micro vias (for example, to fan out a very fine-pitch BGA). If you use laser microvias, make each one span a single layer (layer 1 to 2, for example), and stack them only if you must.
recommendations.why: Each blind or buried via structure adds drilling and lamination cycles. A laser can only drill a hole about as deep as it is wide, so microvias reach only to the next layer, and need electroless copper plating to cover their walls.
recommendations.typical_values: Laser microvias: below about 0.15 mm; depth about equal to diameter (0.1 mm wide, about 0.1 mm deep).
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A board that costs many times what it should.
recommendations.example: A design expected to cost $30–40 per board was quoted at hundreds of dollars, because it used stacked and blind vias and via fill it didn't need; removing them brought the price down sharply.

recommendations.title: Know what plating does to your holes and outer copper
recommendations.why: Plating adds copper to the hole walls and the outer surfaces in one step. Getting the minimum thickness in the middle of a deep, narrow hole means the surface gets more than that. Very small microvias are plated with a slower electroless copper process that covers their walls more reliably than the faster direct-metallization lines.
recommendations.typical_values:
IPC-6012F minimum copper in plated holes:

| Copper plating thickness | Class 2 | Class 3 |
|---|---|---|
| Through-holes, blind and buried vias: average | 20 µm | 25 µm |
| Through-holes, blind and buried vias: thinnest spot | 18 µm | 20 µm |
| Microvias: average / thinnest | 12 / 10 µm | 12 / 10 µm |
| Copper cap over a filled via (minimum) | 5 µm | 12 µm |

The outer surfaces gain at least as much copper as the hole walls, often more, so a 1 oz finished outer layer is usually reached from thinner starting foil plus plating.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Outer-layer gaps too tight once the copper has grown, or holes that are too small.

sources.text: IPC-6012F (Sept 2023), section 3.6.2.11 and Tables 3-10, 3-11 and 3-13; [“Outer Layer Imaging w/ CAM Engineer Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11724857-outer-layer-imaging-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (Nov 2022), [18:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11724857?t=1080)–19:00 and [30:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11724857?t=1800)–38:00.

recommendations.title: Avoid acute angles, keep pour clearances to your trace rules, and fan out fine-pitch parts through vias
recommendations.recommendation:
- Avoid acute (sharper than 90°) inside corners in traces and copper pours.
- Set the clearance between copper pours and other copper to at least your trace spacing.
- To escape the inner pads of a fine-pitch BGA or QFN, drop to an inner layer through a via, rather than squeezing a trace between pads on the outer layer.
recommendations.why: Etchant pools in acute corners and eats into the copper; CAM software fills them in automatically, which changes your copper. A pour clearance tighter than your trace rules becomes the tightest gap on the board. A trace between fine-pitch pads leaves almost no room for etching tolerance or solder mask.
recommendations.typical_values: Pour clearance equal to trace spacing, for example 0.15 mm (6 mil) on 1 oz copper.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Artwork changed by the fab without your knowing; shorts in the narrowest gaps; bridges between fine-pitch pads.

checks.check: Spacing between copper on different nets, including pours

recommendations.title: Tent vias by default, on both sides, if they're 0.3 mm or smaller
recommendations.recommendation: Tent every via that doesn't need to be open, on both sides of the board, by leaving it out of the solder mask openings in your data. Keep tented vias to 0.3 mm (12 mil) finished size or smaller; plug or fill larger ones. Tent or plug vias under BGAs, and never leave an open via right beside a solder joint on a different net.
recommendations.why: A tented via can't steal solder from a nearby pad or bridge to it, lets legend print cleanly over it, and makes the board much easier to inspect. Solder mask can only bridge a small hole; above about 0.3 mm it may not cover, or may crack as it cures. Tenting one side only traps air and process chemistry in the hole (see [PCB-DFA-075](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/06-via-treatments/#pcb-dfa-075-never-put-solder-mask-on-thermal-vias-under-a-qfn)). Tenting is not a seal: if air or liquid must not pass through, plug or fill the via instead.
recommendations.typical_values: Tented: 0.3 mm or smaller, both sides. Larger vias: plugged or filled.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Solder bridges between a pad and a nearby open via; solder drawn away from joints; a busy board that's hard to inspect.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice; check your fab's tenting limit.

sources.text: [“Vias, Tenting, and Tiny Fireworks”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15957877-vias-tenting-and-tiny-fireworks) (Oct 2024), [05:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15957877?t=300)–06:00 and [15:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15957877?t=900)–20:00; [“Small PCB layout decisions that have a significant impact on assembly”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623-small-pcb-layout-decisions-that-have-a-significant-impact-on-assembly) (Aug 2021), [10:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623?t=600)–14:00; fabs' published via-tenting guidance (0.3 mm or smaller, both sides); Chris Denney (author).

recommendations.title: Plug or fill vias that must be sealed, or that would trap chemistry
recommendations.recommendation: Plug or fill a via, rather than tent it, when air or liquid must not pass through the board, or when an open-on-one-side via could trap process chemistry (on boards with a gold finish, for example). Say on the drawing which you want: plugged (partly filled from each side) or filled (completely).
recommendations.why: A tent is a thin film over a hollow hole; it isn't airtight. A via left open on one side through fabrication can hold plating chemicals that spoil the gold finish nearby ("skip plating"). Plugged and filled are often used as if they meant the same thing, but a plugged via can still have an air gap in the middle.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Leaks through the board where it must be sealed; patches of missing finish on pads.
recommendations.example: A gas-sensor maker used the board itself as the barrier between the gas being measured and the outside air, so every via had to be filled. In testing, the fill wasn't strong enough to hold back the pressurized gas. So the vias were left open, solder paste was printed over them along with the rest of the board, and reflow filled them with solder. Filling vias with solder is rare, but here it stopped pressurized gas passing from one side of the board to the other.

recommendations.title: For via-in-pad, fill with non-conductive epoxy and plate over it
recommendations.recommendation: If a via sits inside a pad you'll solder to, specify it filled with non-conductive epoxy and copper-capped (IPC-4761 Type VII). Use conductive fill only if you need its extra heat or current capacity and the volume justifies the cost; a larger via with standard fill is often enough. Keep filled vias within your fab's size limit, and if many vias need filling, consider asking for all of them to be filled and capped.
recommendations.why: An open via in a pad drains solder from the joint and traps gas under the part. Fill and cap gives a flat, solid pad. A plugging compound (similar to solder mask) is fine for vias you won't solder to, but not under a cap. Filling every via can be simpler and barely more expensive than choosing which ones.
recommendations.typical_values: Filled vias up to about 0.5 mm (20 mil), depending on the fab. IPC-6012F limits for a capped filled via: copper cap at least 5 µm (Class 2) or 12 µm (Class 3); dimple no deeper than 127 µm (Class 2) or 76 µm (Class 3); bump no higher than 50 µm.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Voids and starved joints under fine-pitch parts and BGAs; with conductive fill, a higher price for little gain.

recommendations.title: Never put solder mask on thermal vias under a QFN
recommendations.recommendation: Never put solder mask on the thermal vias in a QFN's (or similar part's) ground pad, on either side of the board, and never plug them from one side only. Leave them open on both sides, or have them filled and capped (IPC-4761 Type VII). If a part's datasheet recommends tenting or plugging these vias from one side, the datasheet is wrong. If some vias of the same size need a different treatment from the rest, flag them one by one in your design tool, or on a separate layer or note.
recommendations.why: The top of these vias is the pad you solder to, so it can't be tented. Mask on the bottom closes the hole at one end. In the oven, the air and flux trapped inside expand with nowhere to go: they blow voids into the joint, or lift the part right off the board. Open vias let gas escape; filled and capped vias leave nothing to trap. Many design tools only apply a via treatment by hole size, so a thermal via the same size as your ordinary vias gets tented with them unless you say otherwise.
recommendations.typical_values:
Open thermal vias: about 0.3 mm (as in D46).

![D46 is drawn to scale: three cross-sections through a QFN's ground pad on a 1.6 mm board with three 0.3 mm thermal vias: open on both sides (correct), filled and capped (correct), and masked on the bottom with air and flux trapped inside (wrong).](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/images/qfn-thermal-vias.svg)
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Parts that come out of the oven displaced, or pop off the board during rework.
recommendations.example: A board's large QFN had thermal vias masked on the bottom and open on top. The QFNs came out of reflow scattered, and when the assembler tried to rework them with hot air, they shot off the board like popcorn: the flux trapped in the vias was boiling.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. One of the few places this book says "never".

recommendations.title: Choose green solder mask and white legend unless you have a reason not to
recommendations.recommendation: Use green solder mask with white legend unless the product needs another color. If it does, any common color can be built; expect the effects below, and choose a legend color that stands out against the mask: white on green, blue, red or black, and black on white or yellow.
recommendations.why: Green mask lets the most ultraviolet light through when it's exposed, so it holds the finest dams between pads. Some fabs can hold a 0.075 mm (3 mil) dam in green, against about 0.1 mm (4 mil) in other colors. Green also gives cameras and people the best contrast with solder and copper. Black mask hides black parts and reflects little light back to optical inspection machines, so it's harder to rework by eye, and 3D inspection machines handle it far better than 2D ones. Red mask can confuse inspection machines that light the board with red LEDs, because the red light coming back from the mask looks like light from a solder joint. Some white masks turn yellow or brown after several trips through the oven, and not every fab stocks white; ask for a white made to survive repeated reflow if appearance matters, as it does on LED boards.
recommendations.typical_values: Smallest dam between pads: about 0.075 mm in green at some fabs, 0.1 mm in black, red, blue, yellow and white; 0.1 mm is recommended for every color (see [PCB-DFA-032](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/04-footprints/#pcb-dfa-032-put-a-solder-mask-dam-between-every-pad-of-a-fine-pitch-part)).
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Coarser limits on fine-pitch parts, slower inspection programming, and parts that are hard to see during rework. None of these makes a board unbuildable.
recommendations.example: Some widely used inspection machines light boards with red LEDs, so red mask adds programming time on them. A designer with two near-identical boards that differed by a couple of parts used a different mask color for each, with matching kit labels, so the two could never be mixed up on the line.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Color limits vary by fab and by inspection machine.

recommendations.title: Keep a solder mask web between every via and the pad beside it, or tent the via
recommendations.recommendation: Where an open via sits next to a pad, leave a strip of solder mask (a web) between the via's copper and the pad. If there isn't room for the web, tent the via (see [PCB-DFM-030](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/06-via-treatments/#pcb-dfm-030-tent-vias-by-default-on-both-sides-if-theyre-03-mm-or-smaller)) or move it. The exception is thermal vias in a QFN's ground pad, which stay open on purpose (see [PCB-DFA-075](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/06-via-treatments/#pcb-dfa-075-never-put-solder-mask-on-thermal-vias-under-a-qfn)).
recommendations.why: Molten solder flows over any bare copper it touches. With no mask between them, solder from the pad runs onto the via ring and down the hole, and the joint is left short of solder. A very thin web over a long run is hard for the fab to hold and may break away.
recommendations.typical_values: Web at least 0.1 mm (4 mil) wide, and only over short distances at that width; wider is better.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Starved joints and solder balls on the far side of the board, which need rework.

checks.check: Solder mask web between pads, and between a via and a pad

Left: the via has its own mask opening, leaving a 0.15 mm web of mask between it and the pad. Middle: the via is tented. Right: the via's opening runs into the pad's, with no web between them.

recommendations.title: Clear solder mask from non-plated holes by about 0.1 mm, with no thin ring left
recommendations.recommendation: Give every non-plated hole a mask opening about 0.1 mm (4 mil) larger than the hole all round. Don't leave a mask opening only a hair bigger than the hole.
recommendations.why: The fab drills the hole after the mask is on, and the drill and the mask never line up perfectly. A mask opening barely larger than the hole leaves a ring of mask about 0.025 mm wide that either gets drilled into, so mask chips into the hole, or is too thin to stay put.
recommendations.typical_values: Mask clearance about 0.1 mm per side on non-plated holes. Copper is kept back from non-plated holes too (see [PCB-DFM-007](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/04-footprints/#pcb-dfm-007-dont-put-copper-on-non-plated-holes)).
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A query from the fab, or flaking mask in and around mounting holes.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale, plan views of a 3.2 mm non-plated hole. Left: the mask opening is 0.1 mm larger than the hole all round, leaving a thin ring of bare board. Right: the opening is only 0.025 mm larger, and with the drill 0.08 mm off center the drill cuts into the mask on one side, leaving chipped mask at the edge.

recommendations.title: Expect the fab to trim pads to keep mask dams, and check what they changed
recommendations.recommendation: Expect the fab's CAM engineers to adjust your data so it can be built, most often by shaving a little off fine-pitch pads to keep the dam between them. Ask the fab to send you its questions and changes (an engineering query) before it builds, and check them, especially on a first order. If you plan to tighten mask registration, first ask whether the fab images its mask with a laser.
recommendations.why: The fab needs a little clearance between each pad and its mask opening, plus a dam between openings. When your pads are too close for both, it either trims the copper or drops the dam, and a dropped dam is worse (see [PCB-DFA-032](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/04-footprints/#pcb-dfa-032-put-a-solder-mask-dam-between-every-pad-of-a-fine-pitch-part)). Changes made in CAM are silent unless you ask to see them, and some (legend resized, pads trimmed, mask opened up) change what the assembler gets. Laser-imaged mask lines up more accurately than mask exposed through film, so it needs less clearance.
recommendations.typical_values: About 0.05 mm (2 mil) between a pad and its mask opening on each side, leaving a dam of about 0.1 mm (4 mil); pads trimmed by tens of microns.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Boards that don't match your files, discovered at assembly.
recommendations.applies_to: Varies by manufacturer; check with yours.

figures.alt: Enlarged and drawn to scale, plan views of three pads of a 0.4 mm-pitch part. Left: pads 0.25 mm wide, 0.15 mm apart, with openings 0.05 mm larger on each side leave a 0.05 mm dam, too thin to hold. Middle: the fab has made one opening round all three pads, with no dam. Right: pads 0.2 mm wide leave room for a 0.1 mm dam.

recommendations.title: For BGAs, use copper-defined pads unless the part maker says otherwise
recommendations.recommendation: Draw BGA pads as copper-defined (non-solder-mask-defined, NSMD): the copper pad sets the size, and the mask opening is a little larger, so the mask doesn't touch the pad. Use mask-defined pads (the mask overlaps the copper and sets the opening) only where the BGA maker's land pattern calls for them, usually on the finest pitches. Say on the drawing which you've used.
recommendations.why: A copper pad's size is held by etching, which is more accurate than the mask's position, so every pad comes out the same. Solder wraps around the pad's sides as well as its top, which anchors the joint. Mask-defined pads hold their size by the mask, leave a notch where mask meets ball that can start cracks, but give the most even paste volume at very fine pitch, which is why some makers specify them.
recommendations.typical_values: Mask opening about 0.05–0.075 mm larger than the pad on each side; follow the BGA maker's land pattern where one is published.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Uneven joints across the array, or cracked joints in products that see heat cycling or shock.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice; the part maker's land pattern wins.

figures.alt: Enlarged and drawn to scale, cross-sections through one ball of a 0.8 mm-pitch BGA after reflow. Left, copper-defined: a 0.35 mm pad with the mask opening larger, so solder wraps round the pad's sides. Right, mask-defined: a 0.45 mm pad with the mask over its edge, leaving a 0.35 mm opening and a notch where mask meets solder.

sources.text: BGA makers' land-pattern notes (two semiconductor makers' BGA application notes recommend NSMD pads); fabs' published BGA pad guidance. Not covered in the podcast.

recommendations.title: Join BGA and leadless pads to copper pours with a short trace, not straight into the pour
recommendations.recommendation: Where a pad of a BGA, QFN, DFN or other leadless part connects to a copper pour, keep the pour back from the pad and join them with a short, narrow trace, as you would a pad on its own. Don't let the pour run straight into the pad. This is the BGA and leadless-part version of [PCB-DFA-033](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/04-footprints/#pcb-dfa-033-set-the-solder-mask-expansion-of-fine-pitch-pads-yourself) and D26.
recommendations.why: A pad inside a pour has no copper edge of its own: the mask opening sets its size instead. Every mask opening is a little larger than its pad, so pads tied into the pour come out bigger than their neighbors, and they sit wherever the mask lands rather than where the copper was etched. On a BGA or leadless part, every joint is under the part and can't be touched up, so those few oversized pads take more solder, pull the part off center, and leave neighboring joints thin. A pad joined by a short trace keeps its copper edge, so all the pads come out the same size.
recommendations.typical_values: Trace about 0.15–0.2 mm wide, or no wider than about half the pad; pour kept back from the pad by your usual clearance.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Uneven joints, opens or bridges under BGAs and leadless parts, found only by X-ray; it's one of the most common design flaws assemblers see.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale, plan views of the corner of a 0.8 mm-pitch BGA with 0.35 mm pads and 0.45 mm mask openings on a ground pour. Left: three ground pads sit straight in the pour, so their whole openings show copper and they come out bigger than the rest. Right: the pour is kept back from every pad and each ground pad is joined to it by a 0.15 mm trace, so every pad shows the same copper.

recommendations.title: Always name the surface finish on the fabrication drawing
recommendations.recommendation: State the surface finish on the fabrication drawing and in the order, every time, even when you'd be happy with the fab's default. For ENIG, ENEPIG, immersion silver and immersion tin, citing the IPC finish standard (IPC-4552, IPC-4556, IPC-4553, IPC-4554) fixes the thicknesses too.
recommendations.why: Fabs and standards fill gaps with defaults, and those differ. IPC-6012F, the standard most fabs build to, says that if the finish isn't specified, drawings first released on or after 1 October 2023 get ENIG, and older drawings get "X": a solder coating or fused tin-lead. An old drawing reused without a finish can therefore legally come back with tin-lead on it.
recommendations.typical_values: IPC-6012F Table 1-2 default: ENIG (drawings from 1 October 2023), "X" before that.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A finish you didn't expect, which may not suit your parts, your lead-free process or your price.

sources.text: IPC-6012F (Sept 2023), Table 1-2 and Table 3-3.

recommendations.title: Choose ENIG for most boards; lead-free HASL only for coarse pitch; OSP or immersion silver for high volume with tight process control
recommendations.recommendation: Use ENIG unless you have a reason to choose something else. Use lead-free HASL only on boards whose finest parts are about 0.65 mm pitch or 0603 and larger, with no BGAs or QFNs. Consider OSP or immersion silver for high volumes where the assembler controls handling, storage and time between steps closely. Choose ENEPIG for wire bonding, and hard gold only for contacts that wear.
recommendations.why: Small parts need flat pads: a domed HASL pad lets a tiny part tilt or a QFN rock, and makes paste printing uneven. ENIG is flat, solders well, and keeps for about a year sealed, which suits small batches that may wait between bare board and assembly. OSP and immersion silver are cheaper and flat, but much less forgiving: fingerprints, humidity and time all spoil them, and OSP weakens with every trip through the oven, which matters on double-sided boards.
recommendations.typical_values: HASL: down to about 0.65 mm pitch and 0603. See the table above for shelf lives.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: With HASL on fine pitch, bridges, tombstones and open joints; with OSP stored too long or handled carelessly, poor wetting and open joints on the second side.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice; prices and shelf lives vary by fab.

recommendations.title: Give edge-connector fingers hard gold and a bevel, with mask and legend kept off them
recommendations.recommendation: For fingers that plug into a card-edge connector, specify hard (electroplated) gold over nickel, and a bevel on the inserting edge. Keep solder mask and legend off the fingers, keep plated holes and other pads away from them, and round or chamfer the board corners beside them. Put the gold thickness, bevel angle and bevel depth on the fabrication drawing.
recommendations.why: Fingers slide in and out of a connector, and the soft, thin gold of ENIG wears through after a few insertions; hard gold is made for wear. A bevel lets the board slide into the connector instead of stubbing on its contacts. The fingers are plated through a strip that's removed at the edge, so the fab needs them to run cleanly to the edge with nothing else in the way.
recommendations.typical_values: Hard gold at least 0.8 µm (Class 1–2) or 1.25 µm (Class 3) over at least 2.5 µm of nickel (IPC-6012F Table 3-3). Bevel 30° or 45°, commonly 30°, about 0.5–1.0 mm deep; keep other plated features about 1 mm from the fingers.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Fingers that wear through or scratch the connector, boards that won't insert cleanly, and fab queries about mask or holes in the plating area.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice; bevel limits vary by fab.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale. Plan view of a board edge with six hard-gold fingers, 1.5 mm wide on a 2.54 mm pitch, ending 0.6 mm from the edge, with the solder mask cleared from the whole finger area and the corners beside them chamfered. Below, enlarged 2.5 times, a side view of the 1.6 mm board beveled at 30 degrees on both faces over the last 0.5 mm, with the fingers stopping before the bevel.

sources.text: IPC-6012F (Sept 2023), Table 3-3; fabs' published edge-connector and gold-finger guidelines. Not covered in the podcast.

recommendations.title: Keep bare boards sealed, use them within the finish's shelf life, and expect a bake if they've taken on moisture
recommendations.recommendation: Expect bare boards to arrive dry-packed: heat-sealed in a moisture barrier bag with desiccant and a humidity indicator card, and only lightly evacuated, not vacuum-packed hard. Keep them sealed until assembly, and build them within a year (six months for OSP). Once a bag is opened, the boards should be built promptly, or go back into dry storage. If the bag was damaged, the card shows moisture, or the boards are older than that, tell the assembler, and expect them to be checked, dried in dry storage or baked just before assembly, or rejected. Don't ask the fab to bake boards before shipping. If your board is unusually sensitive to moisture (polyimide, or thick and many-layered), say so on the drawing; IPC-1602A leaves it to the designer or user to set how much moisture the board can tolerate.
recommendations.why: Laminate absorbs moisture from the air. In the reflow oven that moisture turns to steam and can blister or delaminate the board. Finishes age too, and solder wets an old finish poorly; dry packing slows the moisture but doesn't stop the finish aging. Squeezing all the air out of the bag stops the desiccant working, can warp boards and lets sharp corners puncture the bag. Baking drives the moisture out but ages the finish further, so it's done only when needed and as late as possible. A humidity card shows the air in the bag, not the moisture in the boards, so a card that has changed color after a short exposure doesn't always mean a bake: dry storage can be the safer fix.
recommendations.typical_values: IPC-1602A, unless you specify otherwise: boards packed with no more than 0.2% moisture by weight, in a moisture barrier bag with desiccant and a three-spot humidity card (5%, 10%, 60% RH); this keeps them at least 12 months at up to 40 °C and 90% RH, and double-bagging at least two years. Check solderability after 6 months for OSP and 12 months for other finishes. An opened bag: boards into dry storage at 10% RH or less within an hour, or resealed with the same desiccant and card within 30 minutes. Handle boards by the edges, with clean gloves if needed. Immersion silver also needs sulfur-absorbing paper in the bag.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Blistered or delaminated boards, and poorly wetted joints, often found only after assembly.

sources.text: [“All the Tricks and Gotchas in Surface Mount Assembly (Repost from the Coriolis Effect)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453-all-the-tricks-and-gotchas-in-surface-mount-assembly-repost-from-the-coriolis-effect) (Jul 2022), [01:16:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453?t=4560)–01:17:00; IPC-1602A, Standard for Printed Board Handling and Storage (Nov 2024), sections 4.1–4.2 and 5.1–5.8; a European PCB industry association's recommendations on IPC-1601 (bake just before assembly, not at the fab).

recommendations.title: Make legend text about 1 mm tall, with lines of 0.15 mm or more
recommendations.recommendation: Make legend text about 1 mm tall and 1 mm wide, with a line width of 0.18–0.2 mm. Don't go below 0.15 mm line width or about 0.8 mm text height. If text doesn't need to be small, don't make it small.
recommendations.why: The legend ink spreads and the printer has a resolution limit. Lines thinner than the fab's minimum are removed or come out broken, and small text fills in until it can't be read. Text sized generously costs nothing and is read by people at every step after.
recommendations.typical_values: Line width 0.15 mm (6 mil) minimum, 0.18–0.2 mm recommended; text 1 mm tall, 0.8 mm minimum. Some fabs print down to 0.1 mm lines, but readability suffers below about 0.8 mm text.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Designators and marks that can't be read, so assembly and rework take longer and mistakes get through.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice; minimums vary by fab and printing method.

recommendations.title: Send only the legend you want printed, keep it off exposed copper, and expect the fab to clip and resize it
recommendations.recommendation: Export only the legend layers you mean to print: no component value or name layers unless you want them on the board. Keep the legend off pads, exposed copper and holes, with a small clearance. Expect the fab's CAM engineers to clip legend that runs over pads, holes or off the board, and to resize text too small to print: lots of small legend edits are normal. They aim to keep it legible and printable, and they shouldn't move it; if they must, ask them to check with you first.
recommendations.why: Ink on a pad stops solder wetting it, so fabs clip any legend that crosses exposed copper. Legend can't print over a hole or past the board edge either. When a designator or polarity mark sits over copper, clipping can cut it in half, so place marks where they'll print whole. Some design tools export value and name layers by default, which crowds the board with text nobody asked for.
recommendations.typical_values: About 0.1 mm clearance from exposed copper and holes.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Unreadable, clipped or missing marks, and a board that doesn't look like your design.

checks.check: Legend to exposed copper and holes

recommendations.title: Leave legend out where it won't fit, but keep it complete in your data
recommendations.recommendation: Where the board is too dense for legible legend, such as around 0.4 mm-pitch BGAs or on very small boards, leave it off the printed board rather than squeezing it in. Keep every designator and mark complete and correct in your design data anyway, and put them on the assembly drawing. Check designators against the netlist and BOM, not by where the text happens to sit.
recommendations.why: Tiny legend can't be read and may be printed over pads. The assembler and inspector still need to know which part goes where and which way round, and an assembly drawing gives them that without printing it on the board. When designators are crowded, text drifts onto the wrong part, so only the data can be trusted.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Illegible marks, legend over pads, or the wrong part placed because a designator sat beside the wrong footprint.

recommendations.title: Keep legend off vias, even tented ones
recommendations.recommendation: Place legend text and marks on flat solder mask, clear of vias. This applies to tented vias as well as open ones. If there's no other room, printing legend over tented vias is acceptable. Avoid printing legend over open vias, because the fab will clip it.
recommendations.why: A tented via is covered by a thin film of solder mask, and that film sags a little into the hole. Legend printed across the via follows the dip, so the character comes out slightly distorted. It still prints and is usually legible, and a small mark such as a dot works fine. An open via is different. Legend can't print over a hole, and the fab keeps it back from exposed copper (PCB-DFM-040). So the fab cuts the legend away around every open via, and a designator printed across a row of them is cut into pieces.
recommendations.typical_values: Over tented vias, legend can come right up to the via, or even cross it: 0 mm is acceptable. Over open vias, keep legend back from the exposed copper by the fab's clearance, which is about 0.1 mm (PCB-DFM-040). The recommended position is on flat mask, clear of every via.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Over tented vias, designators and marks that look uneven and are harder to read. Over open vias, designators clipped into pieces or removed.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Whether a via is tented is set by your data and fab notes (PCB-DFM-030).

*D68 is drawn to scale. On the left, the designator sits on flat mask beside the part and prints cleanly. In the middle, it is printed across tented vias: it prints, but the ink dips into each via, so the characters come out wavy and thinner there. On the right, the vias are open, so the fab clips the legend back from their copper and the designator is cut into pieces. The enlarged cross-section below shows why the middle case is distorted: the mask sags into the hole, and the legend ink follows it down.*

recommendations.title: Turn legend text so it reads from only two edges of the board
recommendations.recommendation: Keep all horizontal designators and labels the same way round, reading left to right. Where text has to turn 90° to fit, turn all of it the same way. Reading from bottom to top is the most common choice. It matches engineering drawings, where text reads from the bottom or the right-hand side of the sheet, and it's what a 90° turn gives in most design tools. Then a person can read the whole board while holding it in one of only two ways: square on, or turned a quarter turn. Avoid text that reads upside down, or that reads from top to bottom. Bottom-side legend follows the same rule, as seen with the board turned over.
recommendations.why: Assemblers, inspectors and repair technicians read designators all day. If the text faces all four directions, they have to keep turning the board, which is slow and handles it more. Text read upside down is easy to misread, and some characters such as 6 and 9 swap meaning. Turning a designator to match its part doesn't help, because a person matches a designator to its part by position, not by angle.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Slower assembly, inspection and rework, and more misread designators.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale, two copies of the same area of a board with eight 0603 parts, some horizontal and some vertical. Left: horizontal designators read left to right and vertical ones read bottom to top, so the board reads from the bottom and right edges. Right: designators face all four ways, some upside down, so the board must be turned to all four sides.

sources.text:
Chris Denney (author); published silkscreen design guides, which recommend only 0° and 90° text, read from the bottom or right edge of the board; engineering drawing practice (the aligned system, with text read from the bottom or right-hand side).

![D69: Drawn to scale, two copies of the same area of a board with eight 0603 parts, some horizontal and some vertical. Left: horizontal designators read left to right and vertical ones read bottom to top, so the board reads from the bottom and right edges. Right: designators face all four ways, some upside down, so the board must be turned to all four sides.](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/images/legend-orientation.svg)

*D69 is drawn to scale. On the left, every horizontal designator reads from the bottom edge, and every vertical one reads from the right edge. A person only ever holds the board one of two ways. On the right, the same designators face all four ways, so the board has to be turned to every side to read them.*

recommendations.title: Use a callout box where parts are packed too tightly for their designators
recommendations.recommendation: Where a group of parts is packed too tightly to fit a designator beside each one, draw a legend box round the group. Then draw a second box nearby, as a map of the group. In the map, put each designator in the same position as its part, turned the same way. Make the map larger than the group, so the designators can be 1 mm tall (PCB-DFM-039). Put it as close to the group as you can, on the same side of the board. Join the two boxes with a legend line. Make the line as straight as you can, and where it has to bend, use 45° and 90° bends. If there's no room for a map either, leave the designators off and put them on the assembly drawing (PCB-DFA-081).
recommendations.why: Groups of small parts, such as decoupling capacitors round a chip, often leave no room for their designators. Designators squeezed in between the parts end up on pads, where the fab clips them, or beside the wrong part. A callout box keeps every designator on the board and legible. A person finds a part by matching its position in the group to the same position in the map. The line between the boxes shows which map belongs to which group, which matters when a board has several.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Designators clipped, unreadable or next to the wrong part, or left off the board, so everyone has to work from the assembly drawing.
recommendations.applies_to: Dense areas, such as decoupling capacitors beside a BGA or QFN, or parts on the back of a BGA.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale, a QFN, U3, with eight 0402 capacitors packed 0.25 mm apart beside it. A legend box surrounds the capacitors. Beside it, a larger legend box holds their designators, C11 to C18, each in the same position and orientation as its capacitor, and a straight legend line joins the two boxes.

sources.text:
Chris Denney (author); published silkscreen design guides, which show designators grouped in a box and arranged to match the parts.

![D70: Drawn to scale, a QFN, U3, with eight 0402 capacitors packed 0.25 mm apart beside it. A legend box surrounds the capacitors. Beside it, a larger legend box holds their designators, C11 to C18, each in the same position and orientation as its capacitor, and a straight legend line joins the two boxes.](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/images/legend-callout-box.svg)

*D70 is drawn to scale. The eight capacitors beside U3 are 0.25 mm apart, so there's no room for a designator beside each one. A box round the group marks them, and the larger box beside it is a map: each designator sits where its capacitor sits in the group, and is turned the same way. A straight legend line joins the two boxes.*

recommendations.title: Draw the outline, slots and cut-outs as closed shapes on one layer
recommendations.page_title: Profiling: routing, scoring, slots and cut-outs
recommendations.recommendation: Draw the board outline, and every internal slot and cut-out, as closed shapes on one mechanical layer, and send that layer as its own file. Put nothing else on that layer. Draw plated slots in the drill data, not as outline.
recommendations.why: CAM builds the router path from the outline layer. Gaps, overlapping lines, dimensions or a title block on that layer make it guess where the edge is. A slot drawn only on a copper or legend layer may never be cut at all.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Fab queries and delay, or a slot or cut-out missing from the finished board.

sources.text: Fabs' published outline and Gerber guidelines; the Gerber format's guidance on profile layers. Not covered in the podcast.

recommendations.title: Allow for the router: a radius in every inside corner and slots at least 1 mm wide
recommendations.page_title: Profiling: routing, scoring, slots and cut-outs
recommendations.recommendation: Give every inside corner a radius of at least half the router bit's width, and design for 1 mm unless you need tighter. Make routed slots at least 1 mm wide. If a part needs a square inside corner, ask the fab for a smaller bit or draw small relief cut-outs at the corner.
recommendations.why: A round bit can't cut a sharp inside corner: it leaves a radius equal to its own. Fabs route outlines with bits about 2 mm in diameter, which leaves a 1 mm radius, and use smaller bits on request at extra time and risk of breakage. A slot can't be narrower than the bit that cuts it.
recommendations.typical_values: Inside corner radius 1 mm with a standard 2 mm bit; about 0.5 mm with a 1 mm bit, on request. Routed slot at least 1 mm wide; non-plated slots 1 mm, plated slots from about 0.5 mm at some fabs. Routed edge tolerance about ±0.1 mm; V-scored edges are looser.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A rectangular part that won't drop into its cut-out, a board that doesn't fit its enclosure, or a fab query.
recommendations.applies_to: Varies by manufacturer; check with yours.

A slot 1 mm wide has round ends. A cut-out for a square 8 by 6 mm part has a round relief at each corner so the part's corners fit.

recommendations.title: Dimension castellations, edge plating, countersinks and bevels on the drawing, and expect them to cost more
recommendations.page_title: Profiling: routing, scoring, slots and cut-outs
recommendations.recommendation: Treat any edge feature beyond a plain routed edge as a special: castellated (half-cut plated) holes, plated edges, countersunk or counterbored holes, and bevels. Show and dimension each one on the fabrication drawing, mention it when you order, and expect extra cost and lead time. If the feature is unusual, talk to the fab and assembler with a sketch before you commit the design.
recommendations.why: Each one needs an extra process step: castellations are drilled and plated, then routed through the middle of the holes; edge plating is plated before routing; countersinks are cut with a separate tool. None of them shows clearly in Gerber data, so a fab that isn't told may simply route a plain edge.
recommendations.typical_values: Castellated holes about 0.8 mm finished (0.5 mm the usual minimum) with 1.5 mm pads, at least 0.6 mm apart. Countersinks: give the angle (82° or 90° are common) and the top diameter.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Features left off or built wrong, half-holes that tear their plating out, or a quote that changes after you order.
recommendations.example: An open-source wrist-worn heart-rate monitor needed a notch to hold a watch band's spring pin, with no work after assembly. The designer used a castellated hole as the notch, with a zero-ohm resistor on each side to trap the pin. They talked it through with the assembler first, with drawings, to settle how close to the castellation the resistors could sit.
recommendations.applies_to: Varies by manufacturer; check with yours.

recommendations.title: Have every bare board electrically tested against your netlist
recommendations.page_title: Bare board electrical test and inspection
recommendations.recommendation: Ask for 100% electrical test of every bare board, against the netlist you supplied (see [PCB-DFM-009](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/01-fabrication-data/#pcb-dfm-009-always-send-a-netlist-made-from-the-same-revision-as-the-gerbers)). Expect a flying-probe test for prototypes and small batches, and a fixture (bed of nails) for large, repeat orders.
recommendations.why: Electrical test finds opens and shorts in the copper, including faults hidden on inner layers and in plated holes. Tested against your netlist rather than a netlist the fab extracted from your Gerbers, it also catches a Gerber that doesn't match the design. Assembly inspection can't do this: it looks at parts and solder joints, and assumes the bare board is right. A hole the plating missed, for example, fails electrical test at the fab instead of failing in the field.
recommendations.typical_values: Flying probe: no tooling, slower per board. Fixture: tooling cost and a few days to build, then fast.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A short or open found only after assembly, when the board is full of parts and the fault is much harder to find and fix.

recommendations.title: Ask for IPC Class 2 unless the product needs Class 3, and know Class 3 is a design standard too
recommendations.page_title: Bare board electrical test and inspection
recommendations.recommendation: Build to IPC Class 2, which suits nearly all products, unless the product's use truly needs Class 3 (high reliability: medical life support, aerospace, some automotive and military). If you do need Class 3, design for it from the start, not only at ordering, and call out the class instead of writing your own acceptance criteria.
recommendations.why: The IPC classes set what's acceptable in the bare board (IPC-6012) and the assembly (IPC-A-610): annular ring, plating thickness, solder fillets and much more. Class 3 limits are tighter, so they cost more to make and inspect, and some can only be met if the design allows them: a Class 3 annular ring needs pads big enough for it, for example. Ordering Class 3 for a board designed to Class 2 doesn't make it a Class 3 product.
recommendations.typical_values: Class 1, simple products, about 5% of what's built; Class 2, about 90%; Class 3, the rest, at a much higher cost (one estimate: ten times or more).
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Paying far more than you need to, or ordering Class 3 for a design that can't meet it and getting rejects or waivers.

recommendations.title: For boards that matter, ask for the fab's evidence
recommendations.page_title: Bare board electrical test and inspection
recommendations.recommendation: For Class 3 boards, impedance-controlled boards and anything safety-critical, ask the fab to ship its evidence with the boards: a certificate of conformance, the electrical test result, the impedance test report where it applies, and cross-sections (microsections) of test coupons for Class 3. Write what you need on the fabrication drawing or purchase order, so it's quoted from the start.
recommendations.why: A pass label on its own doesn't say what was tested, against which netlist, or to which limits. A cross-section of a coupon cut from the same panel shows the plating thickness in the holes and the layer build, which no electrical test can. Asking up front costs little; asking after the boards have shipped usually can't be done.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: No proof the boards meet the drawing when a customer, auditor or failure investigation asks for it.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice; report formats vary by fab.

sources.text: IPC-6012F (Sept 2023), quality conformance testing and coupons; fabs' published electrical-test and quality documents. Not covered in the podcast.

recommendations.title: Choose parts that are active, widely stocked, and made by more than one maker where you can
recommendations.page_title: Choosing parts that can be bought and built
recommendations.why: Parts stocked widely, by more than one maker, keep shipping when one source runs short. A specialty part can carry a lead time of weeks where a mainstream equivalent ships the same day. Parts reused from an old design, or an old library, may already be at the end of their life when the board reaches manufacturing. Distributors sell in small quantities; buying straight from a maker often means minimum orders of thousands.
recommendations.typical_values: Minimum: active, and in stock at two or more authorized distributors. Recommended: also available from a second maker, or listed in a common-parts library chosen for deep supply.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A build held for weeks waiting for one part, or a redesign when it can't be bought at all.
recommendations.example: For a 200-unit build, an assembler found that only about 204 of one pressure sensor existed in stock anywhere. A simple 4-pin, 0.1 in header from a specialty maker had a two-week lead time, while equivalents from other makers shipped at once.

recommendations.title: For parts at risk of shortage, give the board a way to take an alternate
recommendations.page_title: Choosing parts that can be bought and built
recommendations.recommendation:
For a part that's scarce, single-source or has been short before, plan an alternate into the layout:
1. First choice: an alternate in the same package and pinout, listed on the BOM ([PCB-DFA-069](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/03-bom/)), so the board doesn't change at all.
2. If the alternate comes in a different package: use an overlapping footprint only where the part maker publishes one, and name the package you want fitted on the BOM.
3. If the two can't overlap: draw both footprints side by side and mark the one not fitted as DNP (do not place).
recommendations.why: A board that already accepts a second part can be built from whatever is in stock, without a new revision. Some makers sell the same chip in packages of different sizes with the same pinout, and publish a layout that takes either: a tiny leadless package placed inside the footprint of a leaded one, with each pin joined to its partner by a short trace, as in D57. An overlapping footprint leaves pads unused whichever package is fitted, so the assembler needs to know which package to cut the stencil for. Drawing your own overlap risks pads too close together, the wrong pitch, and bridges.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A board respin, or a long wait, when the one part it accepts runs out.
recommendations.example: One designer used an op-amp sold in both SC-70 and SOT-23 packages, and set the board up to take either, so the assembler could fit whichever was in stock.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice; most useful for parts with a history of shortages.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale, plan views. Left: a SOT-23-6 footprint with six pads 0.6 by 1.1 mm on a 0.95 mm pitch, in two rows 2.5 mm apart; in the space between the rows sit the six pads of a 1.0 by 0.8 mm leadless package, each joined to the SOT-23 pad beside it by a short trace under the mask. Right: a SOT-23-6 footprint labeled U1 and an SC-70-6 footprint labeled U2 side by side; the BOM fits one and marks the other DNP.

recommendations.title: In production, use the original maker's part on reel, not hobby modules or reseller strips
recommendations.page_title: Choosing parts that can be bought and built
recommendations.recommendation: For anything you'll build in quantity, find the original maker and part number behind a hobby-market product, and buy that part on a reel. Avoid breakout boards, individually bagged modules, and parts sold in short strips by hobby resellers. If a module has no alternative, buy a reel of it yourself and consign it ([PCB-DFA-100](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/05-consignment-and-spares/)).
recommendations.why: Hobby resellers repackage parts in small bags or strips of ten, which can't be fed to a machine without loading every strip by hand. The original maker's part comes on continuous tape and costs far less in quantity. Hobby products are often hard for a business to buy through normal channels, or have no published maker at all.
recommendations.typical_values: Loading a strip of ten takes 20–60 seconds; a reel of 1,000 or more runs without stopping.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Hours of extra set-up on a large order, a handling charge for every strip, and parts that cost several times more than they need to.
recommendations.example: A customer specified addressable RGB LEDs sold in strips of ten and needed thousands. The assembler traced the original part, found it on reels of 1,000, and the reel worked out roughly 70% cheaper after shipping.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice; matters most above a few dozen boards.

recommendations.title: Check that board-mount connectors suit your board thickness and the product
recommendations.page_title: Choosing parts that can be bought and built
recommendations.recommendation: For every connector and mechanical part that grips or passes through the board, check its datasheet for the board thickness it's made for, and choose the version that matches your stack-up. Check too that the part is rated for the job: current, mating cycles, temperature, and any approval the product needs (medical, automotive, life-safety).
recommendations.why: Mid-mount connectors, through-hole tabs, press-fit pins and snap-in parts are designed around one board thickness, often 1.6 mm, sometimes 0.8 mm or 1.0 mm. On a thicker board the tabs don't come through far enough to solder; on a thinner one the part sits at the wrong height or rocks. Two parts that look identical can carry very different ratings.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Connectors that can't be soldered properly or sit crooked, found at first assembly; or a product that fails its approval because one part wasn't rated for it.

recommendations.title: For LEDs and other parts sold in bins, choose the bin, or test each bin and say how to handle it
recommendations.page_title: Choosing parts that can be bought and built
recommendations.recommendation: Where brightness or color matters, order the LED with a named bin in its part number, if the maker offers one. If not, get samples from several bins, test them in your circuit, and give the assembler what to do for each bin (for example, which current-limiting resistor to fit). Don't bother for indicator LEDs where brightness doesn't matter.
recommendations.why: LEDs are sorted after manufacture into bins of brightness and color, and each reel carries a bin code. Two reels of the same part number can look noticeably different side by side.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Products whose LEDs don't match each other, or vary from one batch to the next.
recommendations.example: A designer whose product depended on LED brightness bought samples of each bin, found the right resistor for each on a breadboard, and gave the assembler a table of bin to resistor.
recommendations.applies_to: LEDs and other parts sold in bins, where appearance or behavior depends on them.

recommendations.title: Don't name a brand of solder, flux or other process material unless the product needs it
recommendations.page_title: Choosing parts that can be bought and built
recommendations.recommendation: Specify process materials by type and standard (for example, "no-clean, lead-free, SAC305, per J-STD-004 and J-STD-006"), not by brand and product name, unless a qualification or customer requirement forces a particular one. If you must name one, list an approved alternative too.
recommendations.why: Named products are discontinued, reformulated or go out of stock, often after a company is bought. The assembler then can't build to your drawing without your sign-off, and a qualified product may need requalifying.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A build held while you approve a substitute, or the cost of requalifying a process.
recommendations.example: A government drawing named one flux-core solder wire, which was later discontinued; separately, a favored solder paste disappeared after its maker was acquired.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice; products with a qualified process may have to name a material.

recommendations.title: Choose tape and reel, and use tubes only as a last resort
recommendations.page_title: Packaging: reels, cut tape, tubes, trays
recommendations.recommendation: Choose parts sold on tape and reel. Treat tubes as a last resort, after every other option is exhausted: a tape-and-reel version of the same part, an equivalent part on tape, or a re-taping service at the distributor. Pay a little more for a part on tape rather than design in one that only comes in tubes. Large or delicate chips in trays are fine. On the BOM, give the maker's full part number including the packaging code (often a suffix such as R for reel or T for tube), so the right packaging is bought.
recommendations.why: Assemblers like tubes less than any other packaging. Some assemblers, Worthington Assembly among them, are asking component makers to stop using tubes altogether. Carrier tape feeds one pocket at a time, holds thousands of parts per reel, and can only be loaded one way round. Tubes hold far fewer parts, feed by vibration and gravity, and jam more often, even on the best feeders. A tube is symmetrical, so it can be loaded backwards. Its rigid ends puncture moisture barrier bags, and it's too long for most drying ovens. Parts sold only in tubes are often sent to a specialist to be re-taped before they can run well, which adds cost and time.
recommendations.typical_values: A tube holds about 50–100 parts; a reel of the same part, about 2,500. Tape from 8 mm to 24 mm wide is asymmetrical and can't be loaded backwards; wider tape marks its sides with different sprocket holes.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Slower builds, more stoppages, extra handling charges, and the occasional batch of parts placed backwards from a reversed tube.
recommendations.example: A tube loaded backwards into a feeder put a run of parts on the board the wrong way round, and every one had to be reworked.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Tubes do have one advantage: they hold heavy through-hole parts by the body, so the leads don't bend.

figures.alt: Four panels, not to the same scale. Carrier tape 8 mm wide, enlarged and drawn to scale, with sprocket holes along one edge every 4 mm, pockets every 4 mm holding chip parts lying across the tape under a clear cover tape, and empty pockets at the leading end as leader, with an arrow for the direction of feed. A 178 mm reel with tape coming off it. A tube about 500 mm long holding a row of SOIC chips, with a stopper in each end. A tray about 323 by 136 mm with a grid of pockets, each holding a large chip with pin 1 the same way.

recommendations.title: Choose connectors packaged for machine placement: on tape, with a flat top or a pick-up cap
recommendations.page_title: Packaging: reels, cut tape, tubes, trays
recommendations.recommendation: For surface-mount and hybrid connectors, choose a version supplied on tape and reel with a flat area for the machine's vacuum nozzle: either a flat top on the body, or a pick-up cap or polyimide (Kapton) pad fitted by the maker. Check the order code: the cap or pad is often a separate option, sold under its own suffix.
recommendations.why: Placement machines pick parts with a vacuum nozzle, which needs a flat, solid surface near the part's center of mass. Many connectors have open tops, slots or pins where a nozzle can't seal. Some machines have grippers that can pick a part with no flat area, and an assembler can 3D-print a custom tray for loose parts, load it by hand and let the machine place from it. Both work, but grippers are slower and harder to set up than vacuum nozzles, and a custom tray takes time to design, print and load, all of which adds cost. Otherwise, the connector is fitted by hand.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Connectors placed by hand, slowly and less accurately, or a machine that drops them.
recommendations.example: On one product, electrically identical connectors differed greatly in how quickly and accurately they could be placed, depending only on how they were packaged.

recommendations.title: Put each part's moisture sensitivity level on the BOM, from its datasheet
recommendations.recommendation: Look up every plastic surface-mount part's MSL in its datasheet or the maker's product page, not the bag or a distributor's listing. Give the BOM an MSL column, so the assembler sees the level of every part. Flag anything at MSL 3 or higher, and parts known to be moisture-sensitive even if they aren't labeled that way (some LEDs, for example).
recommendations.why: Nearly any part that isn't hermetically sealed can take on moisture. The maker's rating is the authority; packaging and listings are sometimes wrong. The assembler can only plan exposure times and baking for parts it knows about. It's very rare for a customer to say which parts are moisture-sensitive, so assemblers usually have to look up every one themselves; an MSL column on the BOM is the easiest way to hand them that information.
recommendations.typical_values: Most chips are rated MSL 3 or higher. MSL 1 parts need no special handling; MSL 2 and above are shipped in sealed bags with desiccant.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Parts that crack or delaminate in reflow, sometimes without failing until later in the field.
recommendations.example: A customer sent in moisture-sensitive LEDs in ordinary packaging, with no warning; they were reflowed as received and damaged.

recommendations.title: Prefer a lower moisture level when you have the choice, and remember a double-sided build uses one floor life for both sides
recommendations.recommendation: When two parts would do, choose the one with the lower MSL. Avoid MSL 5, 5a and 6 parts unless there's no alternative, and tell your assembler early if you use one. On a double-sided board, plan for both sides being built within one floor life.
recommendations.why: Floor life is the time a part can spend in factory air, after its bag is opened, before it's soldered. It's set at 30 °C and 60% relative humidity; warmer or damper air shortens it. The clock runs until the part's last reflow, so building the first side doesn't reset it for the second. Short floor lives force small batches, careful scheduling, or a bake.
recommendations.typical_values:
Floor life at up to 30 °C and 60% RH, from J-STD-033:

| MSL | Floor life |
|---|---|
| 1 | Unlimited (at up to 85% RH) |
| 2 | 1 year |
| 2a | 4 weeks |
| 3 | 168 hours (1 week) |
| 4 | 72 hours |
| 5 | 48 hours |
| 5a | 24 hours |
| 6 | Bake before use, then solder within the time on the label |
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Builds scheduled around one part's clock, extra baking, and higher cost.
recommendations.example: An assembler building double-sided boards with MSL 5a parts ran them in batches of 50–100 on trays, so both sides could be reflowed within 24 hours of opening the bag.

recommendations.title: Expect cheap addressable RGB LEDs and similar parts to need baking, and budget for it
recommendations.recommendation: If you use low-cost addressable RGB LEDs, or other parts known to soak up moisture, expect your assembler to bake them before reflow, even when they arrive sealed. Allow for the extra time and cost, or choose a more expensive part that doesn't need it.
recommendations.why: These LEDs absorb moisture readily, and their packaging often doesn't keep it out. Baking is an extra step outside the normal flow. Damage from moisture can be intermittent: a small delamination opens when the part warms up and closes again when it cools.
recommendations.typical_values: A low-cost addressable LED can cost a quarter of an equivalent from a mainstream maker; part of the difference comes back as baking.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: LEDs that burn out after reflow, or boards that pass a short test and fail in the field.
recommendations.example: LED matrix boards passed a 30-second bench test, then failed in the sun; the heat opened small delaminations that closed again once the boards cooled.
recommendations.applies_to: Addressable RGB LEDs and other parts with a known moisture problem.
