recommendations.title: Keep your own moisture-sensitive stock sealed, and let your assembler bake anything that's been exposed
recommendations.why: A bag opened briefly and resealed straight away doesn't start the floor-life clock: J-STD-033 lets short exposures, in air no worse than 30 °C and 60% RH, be dried out again by the desiccant in a sealed bag or a dry cabinet. This is how distributors split large packages into smaller ones without logging the few minutes the parts were out. After more than an hour in factory air, resealing doesn't necessarily stop the clock: dry storage pauses or resets it only within the limits in the table below, and beyond them only a bake resets it. The desiccant needs some air in the bag to draw moisture from the parts. Plain static bags don't block moisture, and some moisture bags aren't made for electronics. Some humidity cards change back once they dry out, so a card that looks safe may not be. Baking needs the right temperature and time for each part's level and thickness. Reels and tubes can't go above 40 °C, where a bake takes days or weeks; only trays rated for it can go in at 125 °C.
recommendations.typical_values:
For parts that have been out in air no worse than 30 °C and 60% RH (J-STD-033D Table 4-3):

| MSL | Time out of the bag | What restores the floor life |
|---|---|---|
| 2, 2a, 3 | Less than the floor life, in total | Clock paused while stored at 10% RH or less |
| 2, 2a, 3 | 12 hours or less | Reset by dry storage for 5 times the exposure, at 10% RH or less |
| 4, 5, 5a | 8 hours or less | Reset by dry storage for 10 times the exposure, at 5% RH or less |
| Any | Longer than the above, or past the floor life | Bake, then dry-pack |

Bake times for an MSL 3 part past its floor life by more than 72 hours (J-STD-033D Table 4-1):

| Package body thickness | At 125 °C | At 90 °C | At 40 °C |
|---|---|---|---|
| Under 0.5 mm | 1 hour | 3 hours | 22 hours |
| 0.8 to 1.4 mm | 8 hours | 25 hours | 8 days |
| 1.4 to 2.0 mm | 27 hours | 4 days | 37 days |
| 2.0 to 4.5 mm | 48 hours | 10 days | 79 days |

Higher levels and thicker parts take longer; large BGAs and stacked-die parts can need 96 hours at 125 °C. The floor life starts again from zero after a bake.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Parts that need baking on arrival, which delays the build, or parts damaged by the wrong bake.
recommendations.applies_to: Anyone holding or consigning moisture-sensitive parts.

figures.alt: Not to scale. A moisture barrier bag heat-sealed across the top, holding a reel of parts, a desiccant pouch and a humidity indicator card with three spots marked 60%, 10% and 5%, all blue (dry). A caution label on the outside reads: moisture-sensitive, level 3, floor life 168 hours at up to 30 °C and 60% RH, with the bag seal date.

recommendations.title: Buy parts only from authorized distributors or the maker
recommendations.recommendation: Buy from the part maker or its authorized (franchised) distributors. Don't buy from unfamiliar websites, auction sites or marketplaces, however convincing they look. If your assembler buys for you, expect them to do the same, and to tell you before using any other source.
recommendations.why: Authorized distributors buy straight from the maker, so the parts are genuine and traceable. Counterfeit parts can pass a visual check and still be wrong inside: remarked, used, or made from the wrong materials.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Parts that don't work, melt in soldering or won't take solder, found after they're on the board.
recommendations.example: A customer nearly paid a convincing fake distributor website for a hard-to-find part. Terminal blocks that looked right melted into black puddles in selective soldering, or wouldn't wet at all. One designer received 2,000 assembled units with a counterfeit LED that didn't work, and spent a day and a half reworking them by hand.

recommendations.title: If you must buy from a broker or an unfamiliar source, ask for traceability, have the parts inspected, and try them on a small build first
recommendations.why: Brokers trade excess stock, which is often genuine, but every change of hands without records adds risk. Some brokers sell only surplus bought directly from large manufacturers; others search the open market. "Available stock" may be parts someone else holds, with a delivery time the broker doesn't control. Inspection under a microscope can catch sanded and remarked markings or wrong plating that paperwork won't. Two datasheets for the "same" part number can describe different parts.
recommendations.typical_values: Inspection at 50× and 200× magnification, compared against known-good parts. One broker spends about 40 minutes inspecting each part number.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A full production run built with parts that don't match, or don't work.
recommendations.example: An assembler sourcing addressable LEDs on reel from an unfamiliar distributor found two datasheets for the same part number, in different languages and naming different makers; it got the customer's permission and tested a small build first.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Aerospace and defense work follows SAE AS5553 (buyers) and AS6081 (distributors), which require traceability, inspection and notice before any broker purchase.

recommendations.title: Find your long-lead and single-source parts early and buy them ahead, without hoarding
recommendations.recommendation: Before production, go through the BOM and find the parts with the longest lead times, a single source, or a history of shortages. Buy those ahead, enough for your next several builds if you can afford it, or arrange for a distributor or your assembler to hold them for you ([PCB-DFA-098](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/04-sourcing/#pcb-dfa-098-tell-your-assembler-or-distributor-your-expected-volumes)). If you hear a part is going out of stock, tell your assembler the same day. In a shortage, don't over-order to win a bigger share of a supplier's allocation.
recommendations.why: Parts, not boards, set the lead time for most production orders. A large order may only find part of its quantity in stock, with the rest weeks away. In a shortage, stock disappears in hours, and buying early may be the only way to get it. But orders placed in a shortage are often non-cancellable and non-returnable, and when the market turns, buyers who over-ordered are left holding years of stock.
recommendations.typical_values: These move with the market; check them when you plan. Before 2021, typical lead times were about 8–12 weeks; during the 2021–22 shortage, 18–40 weeks was common, and a quoted lead time over about 50 weeks meant the part was on allocation. Suppliers in China shut for the Lunar New Year holiday (late January or February), and lead times take one to two months to recover; order in early December what you'll need through March.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A build stopped for months by one part, or, the other way, cash tied up in stock you'll never use.
recommendations.example: During the shortage, customers who hadn't planned found 26-week lead times and couldn't build for about 20 weeks. A buyer needing 1,000 of a part found 800 in stock and waited 6–10 weeks for the rest.

recommendations.title: Tell your assembler or distributor your expected volumes
recommendations.recommendation: As soon as you know them, share your expected annual volumes and build schedule with your assembler, or with a distributor directly. For production quantities, ask for quoted prices rather than catalog prices, and for expensive parts, ask whether they can be held and released in batches.
recommendations.why: With a forecast, buyers can negotiate volume prices, place orders ahead, and warn you when a part is going on allocation. Without one, they can only buy for the job in front of them. Distributors can hold stock against a forecast and release it as you build, so you don't pay for a year of expensive parts up front.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Higher prices, surprises when parts run short, and more cash tied up than necessary.
recommendations.example: A chip quoted automatically at about $25 each for 5,000 pieces came down to about $8 each through a distributor's quote. A customer alarmed that 15 parts had been pulled from a supply program during a shortage calmed down when shown they added up to $300 a year, and that the distributor was already holding stock for them.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice; most useful once you're past prototypes.

recommendations.title: Don't set a fixed date-code limit; store parts well, and have old or doubtful stock tested for solderability
recommendations.recommendation: Don't put a blanket date-code limit (such as "no older than 2 years") on your BOM or purchase orders. Instead, store parts sealed and dry, and have the solderability of stock over about 2 years old, or of unknown history, tested to J-STD-002 before a build. If parts won't wet in assembly, suspect contamination of the leads as well as age.
recommendations.why: Solderability depends on how parts were made, packed and stored more than on their age. Properly stored parts solder well for many years, and some makers guarantee solderability for at least 2 years from shipment. Badly stored or contaminated parts can fail sooner. Makers and distributors, through their trade association (ECIA), recommend against general date-code limits: decades of process improvement removed most age-related failures, and the military specifications that started the practice have dropped it.
recommendations.typical_values: Test stock older than about 2 years, or with no storage history. J-STD-002 covers the test methods for component leads and terminations.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Good parts refused for their age, or bad ones accepted for it.
recommendations.example: A broker found 2-year-old parts that wouldn't solder because their copper had tarnished, traced in one case to sulfur contamination when they were made, while 30-year-old stock it held still soldered well. Separately, solder refused to wet a manufacturer's parts because silicone release agent from their carrier tape had transferred to the leads.

recommendations.title: Let your assembler buy the parts, and consign only the few you must
recommendations.page_title: Supplying your own parts (consignment) and spares
recommendations.recommendation: Let the assembler buy everything it can. Consign only parts it can't get: ones you've secured in a shortage, special-source parts, or parts you program or modify yourself. Don't consign resistors, capacitors and other common parts. Ask before sending a full kit or bare boards; many assemblers don't accept them.
recommendations.why: Buying, receiving and kitting parts is an assembler's everyday work, done with barcodes and systems built for it. A kit with parts from both you and the assembler on the same job is easy to mix up, especially across several orders. Cheap parts aren't worth the handling, labeling and risk of sending them in. Bare boards bought elsewhere may not suit the assembler's panel and handling needs ([PCB-DFA-001](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/01-why-panels/)).
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Slower receiving, mix-ups between your parts and theirs, and a quick-turn job that's no longer quick.
recommendations.example: Before the 2021–22 shortage, about 80–90% of one assembler's builds had no consigned parts at all; during it, that roughly reversed. Worthington Assembly and CircuitHub don't accept full consigned kits by default, and CircuitHub doesn't accept consigned bare boards.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice; policies vary by assembler. Holding stock for you between orders usually carries a fee.

recommendations.title: Send consigned parts ready for the machines
recommendations.page_title: Supplying your own parts (consignment) and spares
recommendations.why: Every strip has to be loaded into a feeder, or spliced onto the one before it, by hand. A strip too short to reach through the feeder can't be loaded at all. Cut tape nearly always arrives with a part in every pocket, and no empty leader, so the first and last part of each strip may be lost as it's loaded; the more strips, the more parts lost ([PCB-DFA-105](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/05-consignment-and-spares/#pcb-dfa-105-send-spares-plenty-of-cheap-parts-at-least-one-of-each-expensive-one-and-say-when-you-cant)). Assemblers like tubes less than any other packaging ([PCB-DFA-089](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/02-packaging/)): they feed unreliably, hold few parts and can go in backwards. A tube refilled with parts facing different ways has to be emptied and reloaded. Loose surface-mount parts can't be machine-placed at all.
recommendations.typical_values: Shortest cut strip: 50 mm minimum, 150 mm or more preferred (Worthington Assembly and CircuitHub). On 8 mm tape with a 4 mm pitch, 50 mm holds about 12 parts and 150 mm about 37. 1,000 parts sent in strips of ten means 100 strips to load or splice.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Extra handling charges, lost parts, or parts that have to be fitted by hand.
recommendations.example: A customer sent addressable LEDs as strips of ten; the assembler charged a handling fee for every strip, to cover the time spent loading them.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. EIA-481 sets leader and trailer lengths for full reels.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale, 8 mm carrier tape seen from above, with a part in every pocket. Top: one continuous strip 240 mm long, round sprocket holes along the top and the direction of feed to the right, so the right-hand end goes into the feeder first; 50 mm is marked as the shortest strip that can be handled and 150 mm as the preferred minimum, and the parts at both ends are marked as the ones that may be lost. Bottom: the same kind of parts sent as five strips of ten, each 40 mm long, shorter than the 50 mm minimum.

Drawn to scale, part of two tubes of SOIC-8 chips seen from above. Top: every chip has its pin-1 dot at the left. Bottom: a tube refilled by hand, with four of the ten chips turned end for end so their pin-1 dots are at the right.

recommendations.title: Ship consigned parts in static-shielding packaging, and moisture-sensitive ones sealed
recommendations.page_title: Supplying your own parts (consignment) and spares
recommendations.recommendation: Pack static-sensitive parts in static-shielding bags or boxes, not ordinary plastic bags or plain anti-static bags. Send moisture-sensitive parts in their sealed moisture barrier bag, or resealed with fresh desiccant and a humidity card ([PCB-DFA-094](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/03-moisture-sensitive-parts/)), and say on the packing slip that they're moisture-sensitive.
recommendations.why: Parts rattling in a plastic bag generate static, which can damage them before they reach the factory. That damage often doesn't show in test; it surfaces as field failures months later, when the cause is hard to trace. Parts that arrive with an open or badly resealed moisture bag have to be baked before use.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Field failures nobody can explain, or a build delayed while parts are baked.

recommendations.title: Label every package with its part number, and every shipment with your order details
recommendations.page_title: Supplying your own parts (consignment) and spares
recommendations.recommendation: On every bag, reel, tube and tray, put the maker's full part number (the original label is best; handwritten is fine). On every shipment, put your company name, the assembler's order number and your purchase order number, and include a packing slip listing what's inside and which order it's for. If one reel is shared between orders, say how to split it. Send the tracking number as soon as you have it. For a shipment from another country, ask the assembler first about duties, taxes and the product's end use.
recommendations.why: An assembler may receive about 100 boxes a day. A box with no order reference waits until someone works out what it is, and the job waits with it. A bag separated from its box needs its own label. Import paperwork depends on what the product is for. Unlabeled parts can hold a job up more than late ones: late parts are at least expected.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A job held up, sometimes for days, while unlabeled parts are matched; leftovers that can't be returned with the right order.

recommendations.title: Get consigned parts to the assembler at least the quoted assembly time before the ship date
recommendations.page_title: Supplying your own parts (consignment) and spares
recommendations.recommendation: Deliver consigned parts as early as you can. At the latest, they should arrive as many working days before the ship date as the quoted assembly time.
recommendations.why: The line can't be set up until every part is there. Most of a quoted lead time is preparation (buying, receiving, kitting, programming), not time on the line. A job waiting for parts can be overtaken by jobs that are ready.
recommendations.typical_values: For a 5-day assembly quote, parts at least 5 days before the ship date. Of a 15–20 day lead time, about 15 days may be preparation and about 5 on the line.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A missed ship date, often by more than the days the parts were late.

recommendations.title: Send spares: plenty of cheap parts, at least one of each expensive one, and say when you can't
recommendations.page_title: Supplying your own parts (consignment) and spares
recommendations.recommendation: Send more than the exact quantity: generous extra of small, cheap parts and at least one spare of each expensive part. If you can only send the exact number (pre-release samples, very costly parts), say so clearly. When the assembler buys for you, expect it to buy extra for the same reason.
recommendations.why: Machines reject parts they can't see clearly, lose some loading feeders, and drop parts when a nozzle clogs. The smallest parts scatter easily: an inch of tape can hold 50–100 of them. Cut tape usually has a part in every pocket, so the first and last part of each strip may be lost as it's loaded into a feeder. A board short of one part can't ship.
recommendations.typical_values: Minimum: one spare of every expensive part. Recommended: about 10–20% extra on small, cheap parts (110–120 for 100 boards); a few percent extra on costly chips. Assemblers buying for you typically add 2–3% on expensive parts and buy a full reel or more of cheap ones, since leftovers are usually scrapped.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Boards missing a part, and a wait for more.
recommendations.example: About 100 extra 10 kΩ resistors for a job needing 2,010 cost under $1. A customer sent a $5,000 FPGA with no spare and said so up front, which saved a round of emails.

recommendations.title: Tell your assembler before a substitute part number arrives
recommendations.page_title: Supplying your own parts (consignment) and spares
recommendations.recommendation: If you're sending a different part number from the one on the BOM, even an intended equivalent, tell the assembler before it arrives, and update the BOM. When the assembler asks about a mismatch, answer quickly: have an engineer reachable during the build.
recommendations.why: A part that doesn't match the BOM stops the job until someone confirms it's right. The assembler can't tell an intended substitute from a mistake.
recommendations.typical_values: Aim to answer an assembler's question within about 30 minutes.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A build stopped, or bumped behind other jobs, while a question waits.
recommendations.example: During the 2021–22 shortage, customers often sent substitutes with different part numbers; each unannounced one held its job until confirmed.

recommendations.title: Send the paste layer 1:1 with your copper pads
recommendations.recommendation: Make each pad's paste opening the same size and shape as the copper pad. Don't shrink, reshape or split paste openings yourself. If a part needs something special, say so in a note on the assembly drawing.
recommendations.why: The assembler uses your paste layer as a map of where solder goes, then redraws every opening for their own stencil thickness, paste and process (for example, cutting a small notch out of the inner edge of each chip-resistor pad). They assume your openings match the pads. If you've already reduced them, they reduce them again, and the pads get too little solder.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Starved joints, or a delay while the assembler works out what you meant.

recommendations.title: Put paste on every pad you want soldered, and only those
recommendations.recommendation: Check the paste layer pad by pad before you release the design. Remove paste from pads that must stay bare, such as test points. The exception is a board with an OSP finish, where test points should get paste (see [PCB-DFT-008](https://opendfx.org/06-test-and-programming/01-test-points/#pcb-dft-008-make-test-points-surface-mount-pads-at-least-09-mm-in-diameter-and-19-mm-apart-with-no-paste)). Add paste where library footprints leave it out, such as surface-mount standoffs and some battery contacts. For a surface-mount standoff, draw the paste openings the maker's datasheet shows; the assembler then adjusts them for its own stencil and the look you expect, often adding a lot more paste.
recommendations.why: The paste layer is the only place the assembler learns which pads get solder, and on which side of the board. Footprints downloaded from part makers often have no paste data at all; a surface-mount standoff then looks like a plain mounting hole.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Solder on test points you meant to probe, or a standoff, battery contact or pogo pin soldered on the wrong side or not at all. Assemblers catch many of these, but each catch is a question and a delay.
recommendations.example: Boards were shipped with solder on every test point. The paste layer asked for it, so that's what was built. The assembler now asks about test points on every new job.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale except copper and mask thickness, after a maker's datasheet for an M3 surface-mount standoff 5 mm long, with the plated hole most boards use. Plan views of a 7.4 mm round pad around a 4.4 mm plated hole: with no paste in the footprint the pad stays bare; with the maker's stencil, a ring of paste from 4.48 to 7.27 mm in four segments covers it. Cut-away side views after reflow: the standoff's 6 mm body rests on the pad and its 4.2 mm locating collar drops into the hole. With no paste it sits loose; with paste, solder fills under the body, forms a fillet out to the pad's edge, and some drains down the hole round the collar.

recommendations.title: Don't put one very fine-pitch part on a board of large parts
recommendations.recommendation: Keep the range of part sizes on one side of the board as narrow as you can. If the board needs one very fine-pitch part (0.4 mm pitch or finer), try to put it on the opposite side from the large, solder-hungry parts (see [PCB-DFA-024](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/03-reflow-soldering/)).
recommendations.why: One stencil prints every pad on a side, and its thickness is set mostly by the smallest openings. Large parts want a thick stencil and plenty of paste; fine-pitch parts need a thin one, or the paste won't release from their tiny openings. With both on one side, the assembler has to compromise: a thinner stencil that starves the large parts, or a stepped stencil (thicker or thinner in local patches), a special coating or finer paste, all of which cost more and take longer.
recommendations.typical_values: Stencil thickness about 5 mil (0.13 mm) for most boards, 6 mil for boards of mostly large parts, about 4 mil once 0.4 mm-pitch parts or 0.5 mm-pitch BGAs appear (one assembler's practice). The paste must release from each opening: the opening's area divided by the area of its walls (the area ratio) should be at least 0.66, and a rectangular opening's width at least 1.5 times the stencil thickness (IPC-7525). Below about 0.66 the assembler needs a coated or stepped stencil; below about 0.60, bigger changes. The paste must also fit: at least five of its largest grains across the narrowest opening, which pushes very small openings to finer, costlier paste.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A pricier stencil with a longer lead time, more defects on either the small part or the large ones, and a higher assembly price.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Exact thresholds vary by assembler, stencil and paste.

recommendations.title: Use the largest package the board has room for
recommendations.recommendation: For resistors and capacitors, use 0603 where you have room and 0402 where you need to save space. Go to 0201 or smaller only when the product truly needs it. For chips, use the larger package when the part comes in more than one and the larger one fits: an SO-8 rather than a tiny BGA, for example.
recommendations.why: Smaller parts need more accurate feeders, nozzles, printing and inspection, and slower machine speeds. They also get less solder (see [PCB-DFA-020](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/01-solder-paste-and-stencils/)) and are harder to rework and test. 0603 parts are big enough to carry printed value markings, so inspection cameras can check them; 0402 parts aren't.
recommendations.typical_values: 0603: comfortable · 0402: the everyday floor, placed by the million without trouble · 0201: workable, with more care at every step · 01005 and smaller: only when needed.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Lower yield, longer lead times and higher prices, for no benefit when the board had room.

recommendations.title: At fine pitch, choose a BGA or QFN over a leaded QFP
recommendations.recommendation: If a chip comes in a 0.4 mm-pitch QFP and a BGA, choose the BGA. Avoid 0.4 mm-pitch QFPs altogether if you can; 0.5 mm-pitch QFPs are fine. Choose the very finest packages (0.4 mm-pitch chip-scale packages and finer) only when the product needs to be that small.
recommendations.why: Fine leads are fragile: they bend in packaging and handling, they don't sit flat (poor coplanarity), and the process drifts. A BGA or QFN has no leads to damage, and once the printing process is tuned it stays tuned, so its yield is higher. The drawback is that a defect under a BGA or QFN is harder and more expensive to fix. At the finest pitches the whole job gets harder: routing needs via-in-pad, the stencil needs coatings or steps, and at about 0.3 mm pitch the part may be dipped in flux and placed with no paste at all, which requires special tools that not every assembler has.
recommendations.typical_values: 0.5 mm-pitch QFP: easy · 0.8 and 0.65 mm-pitch BGA: easy, often easier than a QFP · 0.4 mm-pitch QFP: avoid · 0.4 mm-pitch BGA or chip-scale package: expensive, only when needed · about 0.3 mm pitch: flux-dip assembly.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Defects that persist however the process is tuned, and some high-volume assemblers refuse to quote 0.4 mm-pitch QFPs at all.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Leaded parts remain the right choice for boards that will be hand-assembled.

recommendations.title: Leave room around every part, and keep tall parts away from tiny ones
recommendations.recommendation: Aim for about 1 mm from the edge of one part to the edge of the next. Where a board is too dense for that, the absolute minimums are in the table below; check with your assembler before designing to them. Keep tiny parts (0402 and smaller) away from tall ones such as aluminum electrolytic capacitors.
recommendations.why: A placement nozzle that has just put down a tall part can hit it while placing a tiny part beside it. A small part placed slightly off can end up under a large part placed next to it, such as a BGA. Tall parts also cast shadows that hide their neighbors from 3D inspection cameras, and they make rework harder.
recommendations.typical_values:
About 1 mm edge to edge, as an everyday rule of thumb (one assembler's).

| Part size (inch / metric) | Absolute minimum gap, side by side | Absolute minimum gap, end to end |
|---|---|---|
| 01005 / 0402 | 0.13 mm | 0.11 mm |
| 0201 / 0603 | 0.18 mm | 0.17 mm |
| 0402 / 1005 | 0.11 mm | 0.08 mm |
| 0603 / 1608 | 0.21 mm | 0.17 mm |

⚠️ **These minimums are hard to achieve.** They are a leading placement-machine maker's absolute minimums, published by Worthington Assembly. Use them only after you've confirmed your assembler's machines are specified for them, and agreed it with the assembler before layout.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Parts knocked off or placed on top of each other, defects that inspection can't see, and boards that are hard to rework.
recommendations.applies_to: Everyday spacing: general practice. Absolute minimums: varies by manufacturer; check with yours.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale: on the left, a top view of small capacitors 1 mm from a BGA and 1 mm from each other; on the right, a side view of a 10 mm tall aluminum capacitor whose shadow hides a small resistor right beside it from an inspection camera's angled light, while a resistor further away is in clear view.

recommendations.title: On a double-sided board, put small, light parts on one side and heavy parts on the other
recommendations.recommendation: Put the small, light and fine-pitch parts (chips, ICs, small passives) on the side built first. Put the heavy and bulky parts (large inductors, connectors, buzzers) on the side built second. Put every part whose leads or pegs go through the board, such as a USB connector with through-hole support pins, on the second side, all together. Check the datasheets of every part on the side that's reflowed twice (the side built first). Some manufacturers recommend reflowing their parts only once.
recommendations.why: During the second reflow, the first side's solder melts again with its parts hanging upside down. Surface tension holds small, light parts on; heavy parts fall off unless they're glued. Pegs that poke through the board stop the stencil lying flat on the second side, so they can't be printed around unless they're all on the side printed last. Grouping fine-pitch parts on one side also lets each side have the stencil thickness it needs (see [PCB-DFA-020](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/01-solder-paste-and-stencils/)).
recommendations.typical_values: A common rule of thumb: a part stays on during the second reflow if its weight divided by its total pad area is no more than about 30 g/in² (0.047 g/mm²). Heavier parts on the first side need glue.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Each heavy part on the first side is glued, sometimes by hand on every board, which adds labor that doesn't get cheaper with volume. Some assemblers have automated glue-dispensing equipment, but it's rare. Parts with pegs on both sides may not be buildable by normal methods at all.
recommendations.example: One design needed a spring-loaded connector on one side and a USB connector with through-hole pegs on the other, because of the enclosure. It was nearly impossible to build by normal methods; the assembler had to invent a special process.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale, side view: a 1.6 mm board on its second pass through the oven. A heavy inductor, a connector with pegs through the board and a large capacitor face up on the second side; a QFN and small resistors and capacitors hang underneath on the first side.

recommendations.title: Don't put a few parts on the second side just because there's room
recommendations.recommendation: If the board can be single-sided, keep it single-sided. If it has to be double-sided, use the same part numbers on both sides where you can.
recommendations.why: Every side is a separate pass through the printer, the placement machine and the oven, with its own stencil, program and handling. A second side that uses different parts may need a whole second machine setup.
recommendations.typical_values: A second side adds at least about 15 % to assembly cost, even when it has only two parts, both already used on the first side. A second side with entirely different parts can double it (one assembler's estimate, as of 2024).
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: You pay for a whole extra assembly pass for one or two parts.
recommendations.example: A board had one resistor on its bottom side, and plenty of room for it on the top.

recommendations.title: Check that every part can survive a standard lead-free reflow, and flag any that can't
recommendations.recommendation: Check every part's datasheet for its maximum reflow temperature and number of reflow passes, and the bare board's material too. Tell your assembler before the build about any part that can't take a standard lead-free profile, or that asks for an unusual one. Never design batteries to go through reflow, wave or selective soldering; they're soldered by hand. Through-hole parts that will be soldered in the reflow oven (pin-in-paste) need plastics rated for reflow temperatures.
recommendations.why: Lead-free solder (such as SAC305) melts at about 217 °C, and reflow profiles peak well above that, typically around 240–250 °C. Most parts are rated for it, but some sensors, microphones, LEDs, small solar cells and connector plastics aren't, and a double-sided board puts every part through at least two passes. The assembler only knows a part is special if someone reads its datasheet, and it's cheaper for that to be you.
recommendations.typical_values: Most thin lead-free packages are rated for a 260 °C peak; thicker and larger packages are often rated lower (250 °C or 245 °C), per J-STD-020. There is no single number of passes: every part sets its own, and so does the board's laminate. Count the passes your build needs (two for a double-sided board, plus any rework) and check each part and the board against it.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Parts damaged in the oven, found only when the first boards are tested, or melted connector housings.
recommendations.example: A tiny surface-mount solar cell was destroyed by a standard lead-free reflow; nobody had checked its datasheet. A lower-temperature solder fixed it, and the rest of the build went fine.

recommendations.title: Spread the heat load: don't put huge parts right beside tiny ones
recommendations.recommendation: Where you can, avoid placing a very large part, such as a big aluminum electrolytic capacitor, right beside very small parts such as 0201s. If the board needs both, expect the assembler to profile the oven with thermocouples on the largest and the smallest parts.
recommendations.why: A large part soaks up heat and acts as a heat sink, while a tiny part next to it heats much faster. The smallest parts set the highest temperature the oven may reach; the largest set how long it must soak to bring them up to soldering temperature. Modern convection ovens and a measured profile handle most boards, but the bigger the difference, the narrower the window.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A narrower process window: joints on the large part that aren't fully melted, or small parts overheated to get there.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Usually a minor concern; the assembler profiles the oven for each board.

recommendations.title: Talk to your assembler first about very thin boards and large, heavy double-sided panels
recommendations.recommendation: If the board is thinner than about 0.6 mm, especially if it's double-sided, ask your assembler before you commit whether it needs a carrier or custom support tooling. Do the same for large panels with heavy parts on both sides.
recommendations.why: Assembly equipment relies on the board being stiff enough to be its own tooling, which a standard 1.6 mm board is. A very thin board flexes under the squeegee and the placement nozzle. A single-sided thin board can often be taped to a stiff carrier; a double-sided one needs tooling shaped around the parts underneath. A double-sided board rides through the oven on its edges, so a large, heavy panel sags, and in extreme cases falls off the rails.
recommendations.typical_values: 1.6 mm: standard · under about 0.6 mm: a conversation first · 0.2–0.4 mm: custom tooling likely if double-sided.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Tooling charges and delays you didn't plan for, or poor print and placement quality.
recommendations.applies_to: Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

recommendations.title: Join neighboring pins in copper, and keep a solder mask dam between them
recommendations.recommendation: Where two neighboring pins of a part are meant to be connected, connect them in copper, and keep a solder mask dam between the two pads, as you would between any other fine-pitch pads ([PCB-DFA-032](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/04-footprints/#pcb-dfa-032-put-a-solder-mask-dam-between-every-pad-of-a-fine-pitch-part)). Avoid leaving the copper between them exposed.
recommendations.why: With no mask between the pads, solder flows across the joining copper and forms what looks exactly like a solder bridge. Operators and inspection machines are trained to treat bridges as defects, so an intended connection that looks like one causes confusion. A mask dam keeps two separate, normal-looking joints; the copper underneath still makes the connection.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Boards held while the assembler checks whether the bridge is intended, or a "defect" removed by an operator.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale, plan views of four leads of a 0.5 mm-pitch part after soldering, the middle two meant to be connected. Joined by copper under the mask with a dam between their pads, each has its own normal joint. With the copper between them left bare, solder runs across and the pair looks like a solder bridge.

recommendations.title: Use surface mount by default, and through-hole only where a part takes force
recommendations.recommendation: Choose surface-mount parts wherever they'll do the job. Keep through-hole, or hybrid parts (see [PCB-DFA-040](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/05-through-hole-soldering/#pcb-dfa-040-prefer-hybrid-parts-surface-mount-signals-with-through-hole-pegs)), for parts that are pushed, pulled or twisted sideways often, or by people who don't know the product.
recommendations.why: Surface-mount parts are placed and soldered by machine in the same pass as everything else. Through-hole parts need a separate soldering step, and loose axial and radial parts (resistors, capacitors) often need their leads bent and trimmed by hand first. A through-hole joint is stronger against sideways force, so the failure point becomes the part itself, not its solder joint.
recommendations.typical_values:
One assembler's rule of thumb:

| Usually surface mount | Usually through-hole or hybrid |
|---|---|
| Resistors, capacitors, inductors, LEDs, crystals, ICs | Connectors that untrained people plug and unplug, such as field-wired terminal blocks |
| Ribbon-cable connectors; terminal blocks wired once inside a machine | Plugs used thousands of times, such as a phone's charging port |
| Low-voltage DC power jacks plugged in rarely | Mains (AC) power connectors |
| Coin-cell clips changed every few years | Holders for batteries changed every week |
| Push buttons, DIP switches, reset switches (the force is into the board) | On/off toggle switches used often (the force is sideways) |
| Trimmers set once at the factory | Volume and gain knobs that users turn |
| Power transistors and regulators, cooled through the board's copper | |

Where an enclosure holds a connector firmly (with nuts and bolts, for example), a surface-mount connector is usually fine.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: You pay for an extra soldering step, often by hand, for parts that didn't need it, or a connector tears off the board in use.

sources.text: [“When to use through hole vs surface mount components”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8803410-when-to-use-through-hole-vs-surface-mount-components) (Jul 2021), [10:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8803410?t=600)–39:00; [“Benefits of intrusive soldering”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10791130-benefits-of-intrusive-soldering) (Jun 2022), [04:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10791130?t=240)–05:00; [“What factors influence PCB quotes w/ Brett Babilonia”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855-what-factors-influence-pcb-quotes-w-brett-babilonia) (Feb 2024), [33:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855?t=1980)–39:00.

recommendations.title: Prefer hybrid parts: surface-mount signals with through-hole pegs
recommendations.recommendation: Where a connector needs strength, look for a hybrid version: surface-mount signal pins, with through-hole pegs or pins that hold it to the board. USB-C connectors are a common example.
recommendations.why: The pegs take the force of plugging and unplugging; the signal pins only carry signals. Because the whole part can be soldered with pin-in-paste in the reflow oven, it needs no separate soldering step, and the pegs locate it so it can't be fitted crooked or backwards. Some hybrid connectors have half their signal pins as through-holes, which can be routed on inner layers.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. On a double-sided board, put hybrid parts on the side built second ([PCB-DFA-024](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/03-reflow-soldering/)).

figures.alt: Side view of a USB-C receptacle on a 1.6 mm board. Two pegs on its metal shell go through plated holes and are soldered through the board. Its signal pins come out of the back and are soldered to surface pads.

recommendations.title: Leave room around pin-in-paste parts for extra paste
recommendations.recommendation: Around any through-hole part that will be soldered in the reflow oven, leave a few millimeters clear of other parts, so the assembler can print extra paste onto the solder mask around the holes. Check the board thickness the part's maker recommends: some hybrid connectors are designed for boards no thicker than about 1.3 mm.
recommendations.why: Solder paste is only about half metal by volume, so even a hole packed full of paste gives about half a hole of solder. The assembler makes up the difference by printing paste well beyond the hole onto the mask, sometimes several millimeters; when it melts, it's all drawn into the hole. Parts placed right up against the connector leave no room for it.
recommendations.typical_values: Overprinting of up to about 5–8 mm beyond the hole has been used. Joints soldered this way often look incompletely filled from the far side, but can still meet IPC-A-610J (Table 7-4). It asks for at least 75% vertical fill for Class 2 and Class 3. For Class 2 only, 50% or 1.2 mm, whichever is less, is enough on parts with 14 or more leads, and on a lead tied to an internal plane if the solder has wetted all the way round the lead and barrel on the side the solder came from. It also notes that a pin-in-paste joint may have no fillet between the lead and the land.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Holes without enough solder, or a second print pass and extra cost to get it there.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale, cross-sections through a 1.6 mm board. After printing, paste fills the plated hole and is printed well beyond the pad, and the pin is pushed through it. After reflow, the paste has been drawn into the hole, filling it round the pin with a fillet on each side and leaving only flux residue on the mask.

recommendations.title: Choose through-hole parts rated for the soldering process they'll see
recommendations.recommendation: Check that each through-hole part's plastic is rated for the way it will be soldered: reflow temperatures for pin-in-paste, and selective or wave soldering for the others. Avoid hobby-grade and unverified parts in production; their plastics are often designed for hand soldering only.
recommendations.why: Selective and wave soldering heat plastics far more than a hand soldering iron does. High-temperature plastics cost more, so cheap parts often use plastics that soften or melt.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Melted connector housings, and a build switched to slow hand soldering.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Batteries are always soldered by hand ([PCB-DFA-026](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/03-reflow-soldering/)).

recommendations.title: Keep surface-mount parts away from through-hole pins on the solder side
recommendations.recommendation: On the side where through-hole pins come out (the side the solder is applied from), keep surface-mount pads 3 mm from the outer edge of each through-hole pad, and 5 mm on the side where the board leaves the solder wave (ask your assembler which side that is). 2 mm is the absolute minimum; more room is always better. Keep small parts especially well away from pins that will be soldered by hand.
recommendations.why: A selective soldering machine's nozzle needs room around each pin; the smaller the nozzle the board forces, the harder and slower the job. Too close, and the pins have to be soldered by hand.
recommendations.typical_values: Absolute minimum 2 mm · recommended 3 mm · 5 mm on the side where the board leaves the wave · 4–5 mm all round makes the job easy (one assembler). One selective-soldering machine maker gives 2 mm on three sides of a pin or row of pins and 5 mm on the side leaving the wave as its minimum, with a nozzle at least 3 mm in inside diameter. A second maker's minimum is 1.5 mm from the soldered area to the nearest surface-mount pad for a single pin, and 2 mm for a row of pins, with a 6 mm standard nozzle. If 2 mm isn't possible on three sides, the same maker suggests aligning nearby surface-mount parts in line with the pins.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Every board soldered by hand: higher cost, longer lead time and less consistent joints.
recommendations.example: A board had small diodes placed between its through-hole pins, so every pin had to be soldered by hand. On the next revision the diodes were moved, and the boards went through the factory on the selective soldering machine: cheaper, faster and better soldered.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Nozzle sizes vary by assembler; check with yours.

checks.check: Bottom surface-mount pads to through-hole pads, for wave or selective soldering

A white dashed line marks the recommended keep-out, 3 mm beyond the pads on three sides and 5 mm on the side leaving the wave; a red dashed line marks the 2 mm absolute minimum. A small surface-mount part sits outside it, pointing at the pins.

recommendations.title: Use thermal relief on through-hole pads connected to planes
recommendations.recommendation: Connect through-hole pads to copper pours and planes with thermal relief (a few thin spokes), not solid copper. Use thermal relief on every layer the pad connects to, inner layers as well as outer ones.
recommendations.why: A plane is a heat sink. A surface-mount part on a plane still gets hot enough in the reflow oven, but a selective nozzle, a wave or a soldering iron can't put heat into a pad faster than a solid plane draws it away.
recommendations.typical_values: Longer, narrower spokes keep more heat in the joint (a selective-soldering machine maker's guidance).
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Cold, poorly filled joints that look bad and may be weak, especially on big connectors and multilayer ground pours.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale, top side of the board. In both views the copper plane is under the solder mask and only the pad's mask opening is bare. With a solid connection, the opening shows copper right to its edge. With thermal relief, the pad sits in a clearance ring, joined to the plane by four thin spokes.

recommendations.title: Match through-hole lead length to the board and the pitch
recommendations.recommendation: Choose through-hole parts whose leads suit your board's thickness: most parts assume a 1.6 mm board. On fine-pitch through-hole connectors (about 1.27 mm pitch and finer), avoid leads that stick out a long way. If leads must be bent or formed, show the bend angle and direction on the assembly drawing.
recommendations.why: Leads too short for the board don't come through to be soldered; leads too long on a fine-pitch connector bridge to each other in selective soldering. Parts with other lead lengths exist, but often have to be special-ordered.
recommendations.typical_values: For single-nozzle selective soldering, leads sticking out about 1 mm; for multi-nozzle dip soldering, more than 2.5 mm (a selective-soldering machine maker's guidance).
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Bridged pins, leads trimmed by hand, or parts that can't be soldered.
recommendations.example: A design called for a 1.2 mm board, then used hybrid parts with leads made for 1.6 mm boards on both sides. After the first side was built, the leads stuck out through the other side, so that side's stencil couldn't lie flat to print. Later builds used the same connectors with 1.2 mm leads, made for that board thickness.

figures.alt: Side views through two neighboring leads of a 1.27 mm-pitch connector on a 1.6 mm board. Leads sticking out about 1 mm each have a full fillet. Leads that end inside the holes have no fillet on the solder side. Leads sticking out about 4 mm are bridged by solder against the board.

recommendations.title: Choose through-hole parts that hold themselves in place
recommendations.recommendation: Prefer through-hole parts that snap in or otherwise hold themselves in place. Avoid top-heavy right-angle parts, and parts that must sit at an angle or perfectly flush, unless you've agreed with your assembler how they'll be held.
recommendations.why: A part that drops loosely into its holes can tilt or lift while it's soldered. Holding it needs either a person or custom tooling.
recommendations.typical_values: A handful of boards can be held and soldered by hand; thousands justify custom tooling; a few hundred is the hardest quantity, too many for hand work and too few for tooling.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Crooked parts, tooling charges, or slow hand work.

figures.alt: Side views of the same right-angle connector at the edge of a board, before soldering, its housing reaching past the edge. With snap-in pegs it stays flat. Without them it tips forward over the edge under its own weight, lifting its pins in their holes.

recommendations.title: Talk to your assembler before designing in press-fit parts
recommendations.recommendation: Before you commit to a press-fit part, ask your assembler whether they can press it with the equipment they have, what tooling it will need and what that will cost. Leave room on the far side of the board around each press-fit part for the support tooling. If you order through an online quoting system, check that it has priced the press-fit parts; many don't detect them.
recommendations.why: Each press-fit part needs a press head shaped for it and an anvil supporting the board underneath, and the board has to be supported without crushing the surface-mount parts around it. Simple parts such as press-fit nuts are usually easy with existing equipment; large press-fit connectors may need tooling made for them.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A surprise tooling charge, a delay while tooling is made, or an assembler who can't do the job.
recommendations.applies_to: Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

recommendations.title: Give a torque for every screw and nut, and fasten hardware before soldering
recommendations.recommendation: List a torque for every screw and nut in your bill of materials or assembly drawing, not just "tight". Ask for hardware that fastens a part to the board (a connector's bolts, a regulator's heat-sink screw) to be tightened before the part is soldered.
recommendations.why:
If a part is soldered first and then bolted down, the bolt pulls the part flat against the board and strains the joints that were made while it sat slightly high. Over time, that strain fatigues and cracks the joints. Fastened first, the joints only carry signals.

*D40. The flange lift is exaggerated. If the leads are soldered first, tightening the bolts pulls the part down after the joints have set, and the joints take the strain. Tightened first, the part is already where it will stay when it is soldered.*
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Joints that pass test and crack later in the field, or hardware tightened by guesswork.

figures.alt: Side views of a connector bolted to the board, with three leads soldered through it. Soldered first and tightened afterwards, the flange is pulled down and bent, straining the solder joints. Tightened first and soldered afterwards, the flange sits flat and the joints carry no strain.

recommendations.title: Avoid soldering a connector made only for press-fit
recommendations.recommendation: If a connector is designed only to be pressed in, press it in. If you can't, and it has to be soldered, tell your assembler before the build.
recommendations.why: A press-fit connector's plastic isn't designed for soldering heat. Soldering it needs a process that gets the heat in and out quickly enough to make the joint without damaging the housing.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Melted or warped housings, or a delay while the assembler develops a special process.

recommendations.title: Choose a two-piece or clip-on RF shield for low volumes, and a one-piece shield for high volumes
recommendations.recommendation: For builds of up to a few hundred boards, use a two-piece shield (a frame soldered to the board and a separate lid) or shield clips, if you can afford them. For thousands of boards, use a one-piece shield, and agree with your assembler how it will be handled before production.
recommendations.why: A one-piece shield hides everything under it as soon as it's on, so it has to go on after the parts beneath it are soldered and inspected. That means either a second print, place and reflow pass, or hand soldering. With a two-piece shield or clips, the frame is placed and soldered with everything else, the parts inside can still be inspected, and the lid goes on at the end. A one-piece shield costs less to buy and, once the process is set up, is fully automated.
recommendations.typical_values: Two-piece or clips: about 5 to 100 boards · one-piece: thousands (one assembler's guidance).
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Extra handling and cost at low volume, or a delay while the assembler works out how to build a one-piece shield.
recommendations.applies_to: Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

figures.alt: Drawn to scale, side views of a 1.6 mm board: a one-piece shield soldered over small parts, hiding them; and a two-piece shield, an open frame soldered around the parts with a separate lid above it.

recommendations.title: Hold heavy parts down against vibration, and fit the hold-down before soldering
recommendations.recommendation: If heavy through-hole parts (large capacitors, batteries) must survive vibration, hold them to the board with something other than their solder joints. The most secure options use hardware: a hold-down bracket (injection-molded or 3D-printed) with screws through it and through holes in the board, and nuts on the other side; or a cable tie passed through two holes in the board and around the part. High-strength foam tape or room-temperature-curing (RTV) silicone also work. Plan the holes in your layout, fit screws, brackets and ties before the part is soldered, and agree the method with your assembler before you order.
recommendations.why: A heavy part shaking on its leads fatigues its solder joints until they crack. A hold-down carries the part's weight so the joints don't have to. Fitted before soldering, it leaves the joints free of strain ([PCB-DFA-048](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/06-press-fit-and-mechanical/)). Ordinary double-sided tape isn't strong or stable enough.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Joints that crack in the field, or an assembler who doesn't have the material or process.
recommendations.applies_to: Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

figures.alt: Side views of a 16 mm capacitor. A hold-down bracket fits over it and is screwed through the board, with nuts underneath. A capacitor lying on its side is held by a cable tie passed through two holes in the board and round it.

recommendations.title: Check part numbers so you don't order glue-mounted parts by mistake
recommendations.recommendation: Check the full part number of every ceramic capacitor and similar chip part to make sure it's the solder-mounted version. If your design really needs parts mounted with conductive epoxy, ask your assembler before you design them in.
recommendations.why: Some chip parts come in versions with terminations made for epoxy mounting, and the part numbers can differ by a single character. Most assemblers, Worthington Assembly and CircuitHub included, choose not to offer epoxy mounting.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Parts that won't solder properly, found at assembly, and a wait for the right parts.

recommendations.title: Expect adhesive-mounted dome switches to need tooling
recommendations.recommendation: If your design uses dome switches held by an adhesive sheet, plan for the tooling, and check that your assembler will take the job at your quantity.
recommendations.why: The adhesive sheet is usually die-cut to match your board's switch positions, which means custom tooling before the first board.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A tooling charge you didn't plan for, or a low-volume job declined.
recommendations.applies_to: Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

recommendations.title: Consider underfill or corner bonding for BGAs in products that take repeated shock
recommendations.recommendation: If the product will take heavy, repeated shock (mining equipment, for example), consider underfill under its BGAs, or corner bonding (adhesive at the BGA's corners only), and agree the process with your assembler.
recommendations.why: Repeated shock fatigues the solder balls under a BGA. Underfill fills the gap under the part and locks it to the board, so the balls don't carry the whole load.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: BGA joints that crack in service.
recommendations.applies_to: Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

figures.alt: Side and plan views of a 0.8 mm-pitch BGA. Underfill fills the whole gap under the package, round every ball, with a rounded fillet along its edges. Corner bonding puts a bead of adhesive at each corner, which wicks a little way under the package but leaves the rest of the gap open.

recommendations.title: Use no-clean flux unless your product needs cleaning, and say so if it does
recommendations.recommendation: Build with no-clean flux and no washing unless your product needs it. If it does (high reliability, high impedance, high voltage, harsh environments, or conformal coating), say so explicitly when you order; don't assume the assembler will clean.
recommendations.why: For most designs, no-clean residue is safe once it's properly heated during soldering. Cleaning adds a process step with its own risks, and many assemblers run no-clean as standard and send cleaning to a specialist. Some designs need it anyway: residue matters more in high-impedance circuits, at high voltages, on very small and dense boards, and in wearable, outdoor and other harsh uses, even for an inexpensive product.
recommendations.typical_values: Cleaning is for high-reliability uses such as aerospace, medical implants and other life-critical systems, high-voltage designs (hundreds of volts and up), and dense boards in harsh environments. How clean is "clean enough" is no longer a single pass-or-fail number: J-STD-001 now asks for objective evidence that the process is clean enough for the product, usually from surface insulation resistance (SIR) testing; ionic-contamination (ROSE) testing is a process monitor, and means little on no-clean boards.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Boards that need cleaning shipped uncleaned, or a cleaning step you didn't need, paid for and added risk to.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Whether an assembler cleans in house varies; check with yours.

recommendations.title: If a product works with no-clean, don't add cleaning or change the flux without a reason
recommendations.recommendation: If your boards are built with no-clean flux and aren't failing from residue, keep the process as it is. If you do add cleaning, add it as an extra step, and keep the same flux and soldering profile.
recommendations.why: The existing process is already qualified by its record. Changing the flux and adding cleaning at the same time changes two things at once, and a new cleaning step done poorly can leave a board less reliable than before.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: New failures, from a change made to fix a problem you didn't have.

recommendations.title: Design boards that need cleaning so the fluid can get underneath
recommendations.recommendation: On a board that will be washed, give parts as much clearance underneath as you can, especially bottom-terminated parts such as QFNs. Keep a solder mask dam around their pads ([PCB-DFA-032](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/04-footprints/)).
recommendations.why: Cleaning fluid has to reach under each part and be rinsed out again. A QFN sits only a couple of thousandths of an inch (about 0.05 mm) above the board, which is very hard to clean under; a BGA's balls leave a much bigger gap. At very high volumes, some makers go further and design so the board never needs cleaning: mask dams, controlled spacing and controlled voltages between conductors.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Residue trapped under parts that the wash can't reach.

recommendations.title: Flag parts that can't be washed, and don't wash rigid-flex boards with chemicals
recommendations.recommendation: If a board will be washed, list any parts that mustn't get wet, so the assembler can mask them or fit them after washing. Ask for rigid-flex boards not to be cleaned with chemicals.

recommendations.example: A rigid-flex board cleaned with chemicals was ruined.

recommendations.title: Clean boards before they're coated, where you can
recommendations.recommendation: If a board will be conformally coated, cleaning it first is recommended. Coating over no-clean flux residue without cleaning is common, and many boards built that way are proving reliable; if you choose it, qualify that flux and coating together for your product (for example with surface insulation resistance testing, [PCB-DFA-055](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/08-cleaning/)) rather than assuming it. Avoid treating coating as a substitute for cleaning.
recommendations.why: Electrochemical migration needs three things: a voltage, a conductive residue and moisture. Coating a board over residue seals the residue in, with any moisture already there, right where the voltage is. Properly heated no-clean residue is far less active than other fluxes' residue, which is why coating over it often works.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Residue trapped under the coating, and the failures you coated the board to prevent.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Coating over no-clean flux is not unusual; cleaning first is still the safer choice.

recommendations.title: Mark on the drawing the areas that must not be coated
recommendations.recommendation: On the assembly drawing, mark every area that must stay free of coating: connector mating areas, switches, test points you'll probe, and anything adjusted or contacted after assembly. Leave a few millimeters between keep-out areas and parts that must be coated.
recommendations.why: The coater masks or avoids exactly what the drawing shows. Selective coating machines can't hold an edge right up to a keep-out, so they need some room.
recommendations.typical_values: About 2–3 mm is usually the closest a selective coating process can reliably hold to a keep-out edge (one industry article).
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Coated connectors that won't make contact, or test points that can't be probed.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Whether test points are coated varies by customer; some require them coated.

recommendations.title: Ask how flexible boards will be separated
recommendations.recommendation: For flexible boards, agree with your assembler how they'll be separated from their panel or carrier, and design the outline to suit.
recommendations.why: Routers and V-score cutters are for rigid boards. Flexible boards are cut with scissors or a knife at low volume, and with a laser at higher volume; each needs a suitable outline and access.
recommendations.applies_to: Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

recommendations.title: Before sending boards back for repair, find the failing part and get a return number
recommendations.recommendation: Before you send failed boards back to your assembler, narrow the failure down to a part if you can, and tell them which part to replace. Get a return authorization (RMA) number first, and pack the boards the way they were sent to you, in proper static-shielding packaging.
recommendations.why: An assembler has the tools to replace parts you can't, such as a BGA, but boards that arrive with no explanation can't be fixed efficiently. If every board fails the same way, the cause has to be found before anything is replaced. Boards repacked in unshielded bags can be damaged by static on the way back.
recommendations.typical_values: For an inexpensive board (around $20), replacing a fine-pitch BGA can cost more than the board, so a refund or replacement may be offered instead.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Delays, boards repaired without the real fault being found, or new damage in shipping.

recommendations.title: Decide how each board will be tested while you design it, and test boards before they go into anything expensive
recommendations.page_title: Design for test: test points and access
recommendations.recommendation: Make testing one of the product's requirements from the first day of design. Decide who will test each board: you, your assembler or a test house. Decide how it will be tested: by flying probe, in a fixture, by a functional test or by boundary scan. Test each board before it goes into a finished product, a chassis or any other step that takes real time or money. Bring your firmware engineers in early, because the test usually needs help from the firmware.
recommendations.why: Test points, a programming connection, room for probes and tooling holes are all part of the layout. If they're missing, adding them means a new board revision. Firmware engineers write their code differently when they know from the start that it needs a test mode. Test code added at the last minute tends to have bugs, and those bugs show up as boards failing test when nothing is wrong with them. A bad board found after it's built into a product costs you the assembly time as well as the board. It's also much harder to find the fault once the board is inside the product.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: You end up with a design that works but can't be tested without a redesign. Or the test fixture costs thousands more than it needed to. Or faulty boards are found only after hours of final assembly.
recommendations.example: One customer's finished product took about 17 hours to assemble after the boards arrived, and the boards weren't being tested before that work started. Another built boards into a chassis that took about three hours to assemble before anything was powered. In both cases a simple board test first would have caught faults before the expensive part of the build. A purchasing manager once asked an assembler to guarantee that every board would work, for a design with no test of any kind. There was no way to do it.

recommendations.title: Write the test plan yourself, as numbered requirements tied to named test points
recommendations.page_title: Design for test: test points and access
recommendations.recommendation: Write a test plan for every board, even a short one, and keep it with the design files. Make each step a numbered requirement that either passes or fails. Tie each step to a named test point, connector pin or function. For example: "Step 3.1: TP4 reads 3.3 V, within 3%." "Step 4.2: firmware version 2.1 loads." "Step 5.1: LED D3 lights during boot." Write the plan as plain text that anyone can open, not only inside one test system's software. When a board fails in the field in a way the plan didn't catch, add a step that would have caught it.
recommendations.why: You know what the board is meant to do, but the assembler and the fixture builder don't. That's especially true when you've used a common part in an unusual way. A step tied to a test point can be built into any fixture, by anyone. When a board fails, the report can name the step it failed. A vague check like "it works" can't be repeated, and it doesn't tell anyone where to look. A plain-text plan is easy to review, easy to compare between revisions, and easy to move to a different tester later.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: The assembler or fixture builder has to guess what matters. They may test the wrong things, or nothing at all. Failed boards come back marked "doesn't work".
recommendations.example: One fixture builder says only about half of its customers arrive with a test plan. It would much rather start from one, because the designer knows the product best.

recommendations.title: Put a test point on every net you want to test, and on every net if you want in-circuit test
recommendations.page_title: Design for test: test points and access
recommendations.recommendation: Give every net in your test plan its own test point. If the board will get an in-circuit test, by flying probe or in a bed-of-nails fixture, aim for a test point on every net. Make a list of any nets you leave without one on purpose. Place test points while you lay out the board, not after the routing is finished. Give the fixture builder a list of the test points, with each one's net name, its X and Y position from the board's origin, and which side of the board it's on. Don't tie a part's control pins, such as enable or output-enable, straight to ground or to the supply. Connect them through a resistor, so the tester can override them.
recommendations.why: In-circuit test checks each part by measuring between nets with the power off. If the tester can't touch a net, it can't check that net or any part on it. Probing a part's own pad or lead instead is less reliable, because the probe can slip, mark the joint or miss it. Test points are cheap to place early, and very hard to squeeze into a finished, dense layout. A control pin tied straight to ground or the supply can't be changed by the tester, so it can't run its standard test on that part.
recommendations.typical_values: For full in-circuit test, one test point on every net. IPC-2221C asks for a test land on every node, and says fewer are needed when boundary scan is used. For functional test, a test point on each net the test plan measures.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Faults on nets the tester can't reach go undetected. If too many nets are missing, in-circuit test stops being worth paying for.
recommendations.example: At one consumer-products company, the boards were so small that not enough test points would fit for in-circuit test to be worth doing, so they relied on functional test alone.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. How close to full coverage is worth paying for depends on volume and on what a missed fault would cost.

recommendations.title: Make test points surface-mount pads at least 0.9 mm in diameter and 1.9 mm apart, with no paste
recommendations.page_title: Design for test: test points and access
recommendations.recommendation: Make each test point a surface-mount copper pad with the solder mask pulled back from it. Make it at least 0.9 mm in diameter, and 1.0 mm if you can. Round pads are the usual choice, but square pads are fine too and give the probe more room to land. For a square pad, use the same numbers for the length of each side. Space test points at least 1.9 mm (75 mil) apart, center to center, and 2.54 mm (100 mil) if you can. Leave paste off the test points (see [PCB-DFA-019](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/01-solder-paste-and-stencils/#pcb-dfa-019-put-paste-on-every-pad-you-want-soldered-and-only-those)). The one exception is a board with an OSP finish, where you should put paste on the test points so they're solder-coated. Print the net name in silkscreen beside each pad. If someone needs to clip a meter or scope probe on by hand, use a surface-mount test point (a small metal loop made for reflow), not a through-hole one. Tell your assembler on the assembly drawing whether the test points must stay free of flux and solder. If the test points won't be used in production, say that too.
recommendations.why: A probe never lands exactly on target, because the fixture and the board both have tolerances. A bigger pad means the probe still hits it. A square pad has about 27% more area than a round pad whose diameter equals the square's side. IPC-2221C asks for test points to be solder-coated, or to have a surface finish that doesn't oxidize. ENIG, HASL, immersion silver and immersion tin don't oxidize the way bare copper does, so on those boards the finish is enough. Solder on a test point makes a dome that a probe can slide off, so avoid it on boards with those finishes. OSP is different, because it leaves bare copper that oxidizes, and probes can't make good contact through the oxide. So on an OSP board, a thin coat of solder on each test point is better than bare copper. Spacing decides which probes will fit. At 2.54 mm, the fixture can use standard probes, which are the sturdiest and cheapest. Closer spacing needs thinner probes, which cost more, bend more easily and wear out faster. A flying-probe tester can reach much smaller pads than a fixture can. So a board laid out for a fixture can always be flying-probed, but not the other way round. A surface-mount test point is placed by the machine and soldered in reflow with everything else, so it adds almost nothing to the cost. A through-hole test point has to be fitted by hand and soldered afterwards, often by selective soldering, which is slower and harder than reflow. Test points that must stay clean also have to be protected during selective soldering, and that can get in the way of soldering nearby through-hole parts. If the assembler knows the test points won't be used, it doesn't have to protect them, and selective soldering is much easier.
recommendations.typical_values:
| Test point | Minimum | Recommended |
|---|---|---|
| Pad diameter | 0.9 mm | 1.0 mm or more |
| Center-to-center spacing | 1.9 mm (75 mil) | 2.54 mm (100 mil) |

IPC-2221C says a test land used for probing should be at least 0.9 mm in diameter. It says 0.6 mm is possible on boards smaller than 7,700 mm². It also asks for test lands on 2.5 mm centers where possible, so standard probes can be used. One test-equipment maker's fixture specification asks for test points at least 1.0 mm in diameter and at least 2.0 mm apart. The fixture builder on the podcast gives 0.8 mm as its minimum. Some published guides say 1.27 mm (50 mil) spacing is possible, but it costs more. Flying-probe testers can usually probe pads of 0.5 mm or smaller, but check with yours.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Probes miss their pads, and good boards fail the test. Or the fixture costs more because it needs fine probes.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. Check the minimum sizes with whoever builds your fixture.

recommendations.title: Keep test points on one side, clear of tall parts and the board edge, and off connector solder joints
recommendations.page_title: Design for test: test points and access
recommendations.recommendation: Put all the test points on one side of the board, top or bottom. Choose the side with fewer or shorter parts. Keep each test point at least 1 mm from the body of a short surface-mount part. Keep it 5 mm away from tall parts such as connectors, electrolytic capacitors and transformers. Keep test points at least 3 mm from the edges of the board, and 5 mm if you can, because conveyors and fixtures grip the edges (see [PCB-DFA-015](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/04-edge-clearance/#pcb-dfa-015-keep-parts-and-exposed-copper-at-least-3-mm-from-the-edges-5-mm-if-you-can)). If a signal goes to a through-hole connector, add a test point on that net instead of probing the connector's solder joint. Don't use gold edge-connector fingers as test points, because probes damage them. Avoid using vias as test points. A dedicated pad is more reliable, and a tented via can't be probed at all. Spread the test points evenly over the board, rather than bunching them in one area.
recommendations.why: A fixture that probes one side needs only one plate of probes. Probing both sides needs a second plate, lined up with the first. That costs more, and it's less reliable over the life of the fixture. A probe is a long, thin pin held in a plate. Next to a tall part, the plate has to be cut away and the probe made much longer, if it fits at all. After wave or selective soldering, the joints on a through-hole connector are covered in flux. Probes that land on flux get dirty quickly and stop making good contact. IPC-2221C allows through-hole pins to be used as test points to save space, but a dedicated pad is more reliable. When the test points are bunched in one area, the probes push harder there, so the board flexes and the vacuum seal in the fixture can leak.
recommendations.typical_values: IPC-2221C gives a simple rule for the space around a test point. The clear space should be 80% of the height of the nearest part. It should never be less than 0.6 mm, and it never needs to be more than 5.0 mm. For example, next to a part 2 mm tall, keep 1.6 mm clear. On the side being probed, IPC-2221C says parts shouldn't be taller than 5.7 mm. Taller parts need cut-outs in the fixture, and test points should be 5.0 mm away from them. Keep test points at least 3 mm from the edge of the board, and 5 mm if you can. IPC-2221C also says 3.0 mm. One test-equipment maker's fixture specification asks for at least 2 mm between a test point and any part, and between a test point and the edge of the board.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: The fixture costs more and wears out faster. Some nets may not be reachable at all.
recommendations.example: One fixture probed the flux-covered leads of through-hole parts with cup-tipped probes. It worked on the first day. Within a week, flux had built up in the probe tips, and good boards kept failing. The probes had to be wire-brushed several times a day and replaced every couple of weeks, instead of every six months.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. A flying-probe tester can reach both sides, but testing one side is still faster and cheaper.
