recommendations.title: Avoid potentiometers, DIP switches and jumpers that someone has to set by hand
recommendations.page_title: Design for test: test points and access
recommendations.recommendation: Avoid parts that someone has to adjust or set by hand during production, such as trimming potentiometers, DIP switches and jumpers. Set the value in firmware, with a fixed resistor, or with a digital potentiometer that the test can adjust. If you can't avoid a mechanical part, give its setting in the test plan and on the assembly drawing.
recommendations.why: Every hand adjustment is a step someone can forget or get wrong, and a test can't easily check it. Setting a potentiometer means probing and turning it at the same time, one board at a time. These parts are often through-hole too, which adds a soldering step. Switches can also get knocked out of position after the board has been tested.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Boards ship with switches in the wrong position, or with trimmers never set. Testing is slow, and the result depends on who did it.

recommendations.title: Choose flying probe or a bed-of-nails fixture by volume, and design for the one you'll use
recommendations.recommendation: For prototypes, small batches and designs that are still changing, plan on a flying-probe test, or none. For steady production in the thousands, consider a bed-of-nails fixture. If you do, lay the board out for it from the start. That means a test point on every net (PCB-DFT-007), pads big enough and far enough apart for a fixture (PCB-DFT-008), all on one side (PCB-DFT-009), and tooling holes in the board (PCB-DFT-001). If you're not sure which you'll use, lay the board out for a fixture anyway, because it can always be flying-probed too. Before you finish the layout, ask your assembler or test house what equipment they have and what they'd recommend for your volume.
recommendations.why: A flying-probe tester only needs a program made from your design data, so it costs little to set up. It can probe both sides of the board and reach small pads. But it moves its probes one point at a time, so it can take minutes to test each board. A fixture tests a board in seconds, because it touches every test point at once. But it has to be designed and built for one revision of the board, and changed whenever a test point moves. So a fixture is only worth its cost when it's spread over a lot of boards. Both kinds of tester learn what a good board looks like by measuring known-good boards, so they work best once the design has settled.
recommendations.typical_values: Fixtures come in two grades. A development fixture is made of acrylic or MDF and lasts for a few hundred boards. A production fixture is made of FR4 about 10 mm thick and lasts for tens or hundreds of thousands of boards. A custom production fixture can cost tens of thousands of dollars. In 2025, one test company put a fixture at about $50,000 and a high-end in-circuit tester at about $1,000,000. Prices vary widely and will change. Between a home-made fixture and a high-end tester, there are simpler production test systems built around your test plan.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: You pay for a fixture before the design has settled, and then pay again to rebuild it. Or a high-volume board spends minutes on a flying-probe tester. Or the layout doesn't allow either kind of test.
recommendations.example: One fixture builder starts by asking every customer how many boards they'll build a year. At 1,000 a year, a $100,000 fixture doesn't make sense. At a million a year, it does.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. What's available varies by assembler and test house.

recommendations.title: Where test points won't fit, use boundary scan: choose parts that support it and bring the chain to a connector
recommendations.recommendation: If the board is too dense for a test point on every net, plan for boundary scan from the start of the design. Where you have a choice, pick parts that support boundary scan. Get each part's boundary-scan description file (called a BSDL file) from its maker. Link the parts into a chain: each part's TDO pin goes to the next part's TDI pin. The TCK and TMS signals go to every part in the chain. Bring the chain out to a connector or a set of test pads, with a ground pin beside the signals. Follow each chip maker's advice on pull-up and pull-down resistors, and on terminating TCK. If the advice isn't clear, leave pads for both a pull-up and a pull-down, so either can be fitted. Make sure nothing on the board stops a chip from going into test mode, such as a pin that has to be held high or low, or a part that needs firmware before its pins work.
recommendations.why: Each boundary-scan part can drive and read its own pins. So a tester can check every connection between two of these parts without touching the nets at all. It can also check many connections to simpler parts, such as memory. That can replace some or all of an in-circuit test fixture. But it only works if the parts support it, the chain is complete and can be reached, and the board lets the chips go into test mode. None of that can be added after the layout is done. The same connector is often used for programming and debugging too (see [Programming](https://opendfx.org/06-test-and-programming/04-programming/)).
recommendations.typical_values: Boundary scan uses four signals: TCK, TMS, TDI and TDO. Some parts add a fifth, a reset called TRST. The connector also needs ground. Chip makers commonly suggest pull-up resistors of 1 kΩ to 10 kΩ on TMS and TDI. They also want TCK and TRST held at a set level, but they don't all agree on how, so follow each part's datasheet.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: On a dense board, the only way left to test the connections under the BGAs is a functional test. A functional test often can't tell you which joint has failed.
recommendations.applies_to: Boards with large digital parts that support boundary scan, such as processors, FPGAs and CPLDs. Boundary scan needs its own software and controller, and the first project takes some setting up.

figures.alt: Block diagram, not to scale. A six-pin connector carries TCK, TMS, TRST, TDI, TDO and ground. TDI runs into U1, U1's TDO into U2, U2's TDO into U3, and U3's TDO back to the connector, forming one chain; TCK, TMS and TRST run to all three chips. TMS and TDI are pulled up and TRST pulled down. A memory chip without boundary scan is wired to U1.

recommendations.title: Give every programmable part a programming connection the assembler can reach: pads for a spring-pin cable, or a test fixture
recommendations.recommendation: If the parts aren't programmed before assembly, bring the programming signals to one place on the board that can be reached after assembly. Include ground, and power and reset if the part's programming interface needs them. Use a footprint of plain pads made for a spring-pin programming cable, with its locating holes, rather than fitting a connector. Better still, put the programming signals on test points, so the test fixture programs the board as part of its test. Put the pads on the same side as the test points (PCB-DFT-009). Keep parts, tracks and vias out of the area the cable maker marks as a keep-out. Leave paste off the pads. Say on the assembly drawing or in the test plan whether the programmer powers the board, or whether the board needs its own power.
recommendations.why: A pad footprint adds nothing to the BOM and no step to assembly. The cable's locating pins line it up the same way every time. A header costs a part and a placement, often needs through-hole soldering, and stays on the board for its whole life for a job done once. A fixture that touches every test point can reach the programming pads at the same time. So the board is programmed and tested in one step, in one place, which is the quickest and most repeatable way of all. A programming connection hidden under a part, behind a tall connector, or on the other side from everything else has to be reached by hand, one board at a time.
recommendations.typical_values: Each cable maker publishes its own footprint. D63 shows one maker's six-pin footprint, for a cable without retaining legs. It has six round pads 0.787 mm in diameter, in two rows of three on a 1.27 mm (50 mil) grid. Three non-plated holes 0.991 mm in diameter locate the cable. There's one hole at one end and two at the other, so the cable only fits one way. The maker asks for no tracks or vias between the two rows of pads. Nothing else should come within 0.5 mm (0.020 in) of a pad. The pads get no paste. Use the exact footprint for the cable you'll use. List it on the BOM as do-not-fit, so nobody tries to buy a part for it.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Every board has to be programmed by hand, with a clip or flying leads. Or you pay for a connector on every board. Or nobody can reach the part once the board is built.
recommendations.applies_to: Varies by assembler, so ask yours which method and cable it uses. Parts programmed before assembly don't need a connection on the board, but one is still useful for updates and repairs.

figures.alt: Plan view, drawn to scale. Six round copper pads 0.787 mm in diameter in two rows of three on a 1.27 mm grid, numbered 1, 3, 5 along the bottom and 2, 4, 6 along the top, with traces leaving each pad outwards. Three non-plated holes 0.991 mm in diameter: one at the pin-1 end on the center line, and two at the far end, 2.03 mm apart. The area between the rows is a shaded keep-out, and a dashed circle shows the 0.5 mm clearance round one pad.

sources.text: Chris Denney (author); a spring-pin programming-cable maker's published footprint for its six-pin cable without legs (Rev B); chip makers' programming-interface guidance. Not covered in the podcast.

recommendations.title: Say where each chip gets programmed, and give the exact file, version and checksum
recommendations.recommendation: For every programmable part, say who programs it and when. That could be before assembly, on the finished board by the assembler, or by you. Give the exact file to load, its version number and its checksum. Also give any settings that go with it, such as fuse or option bytes, read-out protection, and serial numbers if each board gets its own. Mark pre-programmed parts on the BOM with the file version, so a blank part can't be fitted by mistake (see [PCB-DFA-071](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/03-bom/#pcb-dfa-071-mark-do-not-place-and-customer-supplied-lines-clearly)). Before the production run, have whoever will do the programming send you a few samples, and approve them.
recommendations.why: "Load the latest firmware" leaves the programmer guessing which file you mean. A checksum is the only quick way to prove the right file went in. Programming loose parts needs a socket made for that exact package. If the programming house doesn't have one, buying it is expensive and slow. Settings outside the main file, such as protection bits, are easy to forget, and some can't be changed once they're set. Checking a few samples before the run stops a wrong or old file being loaded into a thousand parts.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A thousand chips get the wrong file. Or read-out protection is left off. Or blank chips are fitted where programmed ones should be.
recommendations.example: One distributor's programming service checks the code first, then checks it has the right socket for the package. It programs a few samples for the customer to approve before it programs the rest. It doesn't want to program 1,000 controllers and then find out the code was wrong.

recommendations.title: Build a test mode into the production firmware rather than a separate test image
recommendations.recommendation: Give the production firmware a test mode that the test fixture can switch on. For example, the fixture could hold a pin low at power-up, or send a command. In test mode, the fixture should be able to read sensors, drive outputs and get results back. Program each board once, with the production firmware, and test it in that state. Make sure the test mode can't be switched on by accident in use.
recommendations.why: With only the normal firmware, the board does things on its own schedule. A relay switches or a sensor is read when the firmware decides, so the test can't predict what to measure, and it checks much less. Separate test firmware solves that, but then every board has to be programmed twice: once to test, and again to ship. Each pass can take 30 seconds or more in the fixture, and you pay for both. A test mode puts the board in a known state with only one programming pass. Firmware engineers need to know about it from the start, because a test mode added late tends to have bugs that make good boards fail.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: You pay for every board to be programmed twice. Or the test can't check much, because the board won't do what it's told.

recommendations.title: Make every test failure point to a place on the board
recommendations.recommendation: Write each test step so that a failure names the part of the circuit involved, not just "fail". Report the step number and where on the board the problem is. For example, "Step 3.1 failed: 3.3 V rail low, check U4, L2 and C17" is far more useful than "power failure". "USB port 3 of 12 failed" is far more useful than "USB failure". Where you can, make each step a simple electrical check, such as a voltage, a current or a reply from a chip. Don't recreate real-world conditions, such as spraying water on a water sensor, unless the product truly needs it.
recommendations.why: The person repairing a failed board needs to know where to look. If a board with 400 parts just "fails the test", the fault could be in any of them. If the failure names three parts, it can be fixed in minutes. Simple electrical checks are fast, repeatable and cheap to build into a fixture. Recreating real-world conditions is slow, and it adds more things that can go wrong in the fixture itself.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Failed boards take hours to diagnose, or get set aside and never fixed.
recommendations.example: One customer built a test fixture with a small screen that listed the parts involved in each failure, such as U1, R13, C43 and J4. The assembler called it "solid gold", because every failed board came back with the likely parts already named.

recommendations.title: Match the fixture to the volume, and send spare boards to the people building it
recommendations.recommendation: Choose the fixture to suit the number of boards it will test. Use a simple development fixture for prototypes and the first few hundred boards. Use a production fixture for steady volume. Have it built by people who build fixtures for a living. Ask for the probes to sit in sockets (receptacles), not soldered in, so worn probes can be swapped. Send the fixture builder several assembled boards, not just one. Send the schematic, the fabrication data and a 3D model of the board too. Allow time, because a custom fixture takes weeks to design and build, and often needs a revision or two.
recommendations.why: A fixture is a machine that has to work thousands of times. Its probes wear, collect flux and stick, and they need replacing. A cheap, improvised fixture works at first, but in the end it costs more in repairs and failed good boards than a well-built one. Boards sometimes get damaged while a fixture is being developed, so the builder needs spares. The same goes for other custom production tooling, such as carriers and holding fixtures for assembly. Often nobody finds out it's needed until the first larger build.
recommendations.typical_values: A development fixture is made of acrylic or MDF and lasts for a couple of hundred boards. A production fixture is made of FR4 plates about 10 mm thick and lasts for tens or hundreds of thousands of boards. Probes last about six months when they land on clean pads, but as little as two weeks on flux-covered joints. Custom tooling takes about two weeks to design, plus time to make it, try it and revise it.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Good boards fail, or bad boards pass because a probe isn't really touching them. A poor fixture can even damage the boards it tests.
recommendations.example: At one company, a spring-loaded probe in the fixture kept sticking. When it stuck, the board's ground was left floating during the test, and the same diode burned out on board after board. Once someone spotted the pattern, the repair became routine: "replace D1, check probe 13". But the fault was in the fixture, not the boards. Another customer's home-made fixtures were held together with wires and hot glue. They worked, but they needed constant repair.

recommendations.title: Agree with your assembler what happens to boards that fail
recommendations.recommendation:
Before the first production run, agree with whoever tests the boards what happens to a board that fails.
- Label it straight away with the step it failed, on a printed label rather than a note on masking tape.
- Put it in an ESD-safe bin, away from the good boards.
- Tell you about each failure straight away, not in a batch at the end of the run.
- Record every repair, even when nobody knows why replacing a part fixed the board.
- Keep any parts that were removed, so they can go back to the supplier.
- Keep a shared log of each failure and what fixed it, so the next board with the same failure is quick to repair.

When you send boards back for repair, get a return number (RMA) first. Find the cause yourself first if you can. Pack the boards as carefully as they came to you, in ESD-shielding bags (see Part 7).
recommendations.why: Anyone can diagnose a board later if it's labeled with the step it failed. Nobody can diagnose "doesn't work". One failure on its own often doesn't tell you much. Several boards with the same failure usually point to one cause, such as a wrong part value, a bad reel, a stencil problem or the fixture itself. So if failures are rare, it usually pays to let a few identical ones build up and look at them together. If a lot of boards in one batch fail, look at them straight away. A part that's replaced and thrown away without a record hides the pattern, and loses the evidence the supplier needs. Boards sent back loose, or in the wrong bag, can be damaged again on the way. The assembler then has to record that damage before it can repair them.
recommendations.typical_values: In one example, 30 failures out of a batch of 500 was enough to investigate straight away. Otherwise, collect 20 to 40 similar failures before digging in. For a cheap board with a fault that's hard to repair, such as a failed fine-pitch BGA, replacing the board may cost less than repairing it.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Failed boards get mixed back in with good ones. The same fault is diagnosed from scratch every time. Or a whole batch is sent back with no idea what's wrong with it.
recommendations.example: In one investigation, 35 of 40 failed boards turned out to have the same cause. At one contract manufacturer, technicians used to swap out a part that fixed a failing board, throw the old part away and say nothing. Nobody could spot the pattern or send the part back to the supplier. The company's rule became "share bad news immediately".
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. It matters most for repeat production. Small builds are often tested by the customer, but at larger volumes the assembler usually does the testing.

recommendations.title: Decide whether your product needs thermal cycling or burn-in, ask for it by name, and don't mistake a line test for validation
recommendations.page_title: Burn-in, stress testing and early failures
recommendations.recommendation: For each product, decide whether the boards need stress screening before they ship. If they do, decide which kind, for how long, and to what limits. Write it in the test plan, and agree it with your assembler before they quote. Thermal cycling takes boards hot and cold over and over, with a pause at each end. It's usually the better screen for assembly defects. Burn-in runs boards powered up at a raised temperature for hours. It's aimed at weak parts. Don't treat a pass on the production test as proof that the design is reliable. Proving the design, with environmental testing, life testing and qualification, is a separate job done before production. Check that boards built on the production line perform like the ones you tested in the lab.
recommendations.why: A production test checks each board for the faults in the test plan, at room temperature, for seconds or minutes. Some faults only show up after heat, cold, vibration or hours of running. Cracked joints, moisture damage inside a part and marginal parts are examples. Screening isn't included unless you ask for it. It needs test chambers, time and power, so it's quoted separately. Products used outdoors, in vehicles, in medical equipment or in industrial plants usually need it. Low-cost products used indoors often don't, but even they can benefit from a short thermal-cycling screen.
recommendations.typical_values: There's no single standard for commercial boards. The limits come from the parts' ratings and where the product will be used. Production stress screens commonly take a few hours. Burn-in commonly takes 24 to 48 hours, and longer when it's used to qualify a design. Plan for a few early failures in any batch. For example, if you need 100 good boards, order 105 to 110.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Weak boards pass the test and fail weeks later in the field. Each of those failures costs far more than one caught in the factory.
recommendations.example: A part with moisture damage passed a 30-second bench test, then failed in the field after running hot for a while. One company launched a product that had only been proven in its engineering lab. The production units shipped with problems nobody had checked them for, and the company changed how it launches products. A maker of sensors for power plants puts its boards through its own environmental testing, on top of the assembler's functional test, because a production test alone isn't enough for that use. One test engineer expects to find around ten more problems after the "golden sample" is signed off, once real production volumes start.
recommendations.applies_to: Depends on the product's use and reliability needs.

recommendations.title: Use first articles to check a proven design before a big run, not as a prototype
recommendations.recommendation: Ask for first articles when a design that already works is about to be built in quantity. That includes scaling up from prototypes, moving a product to a new assembler, and making a small change, such as adding one resistor, before a large or expensive run. For a new design or a big change, build another round of prototypes instead. Expect at least one full panel of first articles, and a set-up charge for them. After that, expect the volume to ramp up in steps, not jump straight to full volume.
recommendations.why: First articles find build problems, such as a wrong reel, a part fitted backwards, a stencil that clogs, or a footprint the assembler has to work around. They can't tell you whether the design works, because the production run follows straight after. A design problem found at that point means boards are already built. Setting up the line always builds at least one full panel, so "one first article" usually means one panel's worth. Later batches go faster as the assembler learns the board, so the first few hundred boards of a big order are the slowest.
recommendations.typical_values: At least one panel, which is often around 200 × 150 mm. A typical ramp-up is 20 boards, then 200, then 1,000 or more.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A whole run gets built with the same mistake. Or a "first article" order for an untested design turns into an expensive prototype run.
recommendations.example: A customer with a well-proven product placed a $200,000 order for 3,000 boards with several changes. The first articles showed that a resistor the customer expected was missing, and that the stencil clogged. The assembler ordered a new stencil and improved the process before building the rest.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice. An assembler may refuse first articles for an unproven design and ask for prototypes first.

recommendations.title: Check first articles against a known-good board, and don't expect the line to wait while you do
recommendations.recommendation: Test first articles the way you test your own boards. Compare them side by side with a known-good working board, not only with the drawings. Plan to have them shipped to you and test them at your own site. Don't expect the assembler to keep its line set up and waiting while you test at their factory. If you find a simple problem, send clear photos and instructions for the fix. You often won't need another full round of first articles. For a first build, send a photo of a working prototype. This matters most for parts that need a particular orientation, height or lead bend.
recommendations.why: If the silkscreen or the part's own marking is unclear, a part fitted backwards can seem to match both and pass the assembler's inspection. Only a working board shows the truth. An assembly line is set up for one job at a time. Every hour it waits for a decision is an hour of expensive equipment and people standing idle. A photo of the fix gets it right on the rest of the run without a second set-up.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A mistake that looked right to everyone gets built into the whole run. Or a line is held up for hours waiting for an answer.
recommendations.example: A customer moved a mature product to a new assembler and asked for first articles. A voltage regulator was fitted turned 180°, because both the part's marking and the board's marking seemed to agree with that way. The customer thought it looked right too. It was caught only when the customer compared it with known-good boards at its own site. About 300 boards were then built correctly. Each board had two of these regulators, so about 600 would otherwise have needed rework. The same assembler has tried four or five times to let a customer test the first board at the factory while the line waited. It went badly every time. Once, a restart agreed for 2:30 pm didn't happen until 8 pm.

recommendations.title: Ship and store assembled boards in static-shielding bags, not in plain anti-static bags
recommendations.recommendation: Put every assembled board that carries semiconductors in a static-shielding bag for shipping and storage. Use a metallized shielding bag, usually silver-gray and slightly see-through, and close it by folding the top over and taping it. Wrap the board in anti-static (usually pink) bubble wrap first, because that is safe against the board, and then put it in the shielding bag, as in D65. Don't rely on a pink or blue anti-static bag on its own. Never put boards or loose semiconductors in an ordinary plastic bag. Boards that carry no semiconductors, such as a board with only connectors and passive parts, can ship in anti-static bubble wrap alone if you agree it with your assembler.
recommendations.why: Packaging can do three different jobs. An anti-static (low-charging) material doesn't build up much charge itself when it rubs against the board. A dissipative material lets any charge drain away slowly. A shielding material has a metal layer that stops a discharge from outside reaching the board inside, like a Faraday cage. A pink anti-static bag does only the first job. If a charged hand or box touches it, the discharge goes straight through to the board. ANSI/ESD S541, the static control packaging standard, says that inside a static-controlled area, packaging must be low-charging and dissipative or conductive. Outside that area, in a warehouse, a truck or your office, it must also shield. A shielding bag only shields while it is closed and has no holes. An ordinary plastic bag is worse than nothing, because it makes static every time it moves.
recommendations.typical_values: A discharge you can see is about 3,000 V. Many semiconductors are damaged by less than 100 V, and some by far less. The ESD Association's tests for shielding bags are ANSI/ESD STM11.31 for discharge shielding and STM11.11 for surface resistance.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Boards arrive working, or seem to, and then fail weeks or months later. That kind of failure is very hard to trace back to how the boards were packed.
recommendations.example: A maker of underwater robots found that a board damaged by static in transit might work for about six months before it failed. An assembler's shipping team packs every board in anti-static bubble wrap and then a shielding bag. The only exceptions are a few customers whose boards carry only through-hole connectors and no semiconductors, and who asked for bubble wrap alone.

figures.alt: Cross-section of two packed boxes, drawn to scale. Left, marked good: a 100 mm board 1.6 mm thick with parts on top is wrapped in pink anti-static bubble wrap, then sealed in a metallized static-shielding bag whose top is folded over and taped, in a corrugated box with paper filler above and below. A spark from outside the box stops at the shielding bag. Right, marked avoid: the same board in a pink anti-static bag on its own, and the spark passes through the bag to the board.

recommendations.title: Open and handle boards only at a grounded workstation, and hold them by the edges
recommendations.recommendation: Wherever your boards are unpacked, tested or fitted into the product, set up a grounded workstation. At the least, that means a static-dissipative mat, a wrist strap and a cord to a known ground. Open the shielding bag on the mat, and keep the board on the mat until it is inside its enclosure. Keep cardboard, paper and ordinary plastic off the mat. Hold boards by their edges, and touch the plastic bodies of parts rather than their leads or solder joints. Tell everyone who handles your boards to do the same, including your own customers if they receive bare boards.
recommendations.why: A person is the most common source of a damaging discharge. A wrist strap and a grounded mat keep the person, the mat and the board at the same voltage, so no discharge can pass between them. The cord of a wrist strap has a resistor built in, most commonly 1 MΩ, so that the wearer isn't directly connected to ground. Charge reaches a part through its metal leads and the copper joined to them, so holding a board by its edges keeps your fingers away from that path. Once a board is inside its enclosure, it is far less exposed, because hands no longer touch its joints.
recommendations.typical_values: A complete mat kit with a wrist strap and grounding cord costs about $50 (2022 price). The resistor in a wrist strap cord is most commonly 1 MΩ. Don't wear a wrist strap when working on circuits at 250 V or more.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Boards your assembler built and shipped correctly are damaged on your own bench. They fail in the field, and the failure looks like a manufacturing defect.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice, wherever boards are handled outside an assembler's static-controlled area.

recommendations.title: Choose an assembler with a documented static control program, such as one that meets ANSI/ESD S20.20
recommendations.recommendation: When you choose an assembler, ask whether it runs a written static control program. Ask whether that program follows ANSI/ESD S20.20, or the equivalent IEC 61340-5-1, and how it is checked.
recommendations.why: Static control only works as a complete system. Grounded floors need grounded footwear, and wrist straps and mats need to be tested. S20.20 sets out what a program must contain: a written plan, training, grounding of people and equipment, packaging, marking and regular checks. An assembler that follows it can show you the plan and its test records.
recommendations.typical_values: In a typical program, people check their wrist straps or footwear at least once a day. Floors, mats and workstations are tested on a regular schedule.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Boards are damaged before they ever leave the factory, and nobody can tell you how or when.

recommendations.title: Put ESD protection on every connector that people or cables can touch, as close to the connector as you can
recommendations.recommendation: Give every signal that reaches a connector, button or other exposed metal its own ESD protection device, usually a TVS diode array. Place the device as close to the connector as your design rules allow. Route each protected line straight from the connector pin to the protection device's pin, with no via between them and no branch. Then route on to the chip being protected. Connect the protection device's ground pin to the ground plane through the shortest path you can, with its own via or vias. Keep unprotected traces away from the short stretch between the connector and the protection device. Choose a device rated for at least the IEC 61000-4-2 level your product must pass.
recommendations.why: Once a board is in a product, the connectors are where static gets in. A user touches a USB plug, or a cable that has picked up charge is plugged in. The protection device clamps the voltage and steers the current to ground before it reaches the chip. An ESD pulse rises in less than a nanosecond, so even a tiny inductance in the path adds a large voltage. That is why the device must be close to the connector and well grounded. If the chip is close to the connector and the protection device is further away, the current takes the path to the chip instead. This can only be done while laying out the board. A board without room for protection devices near its connectors can't have them added later.
recommendations.typical_values: IEC 61000-4-2 Level 4 is 8 kV by contact discharge and 15 kV through the air. In an 8 kV contact discharge, the current rises at about 40 A per nanosecond. At that rate, 0.25 nH of inductance in the path adds about 10 V to the voltage the chip sees. As a common rule of thumb, a thin trace has an inductance of about 1 nH for each millimeter of length. A via through a 1.6 mm board has an inductance of about 1 nH.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Products fail ESD testing for certification, or fail in the field after a user touches a connector. Moving or adding protection devices then means a new revision of the board.
recommendations.applies_to: Products with connectors, buttons or exposed metal that users touch.

sources.text: Texas Instruments, *ESD Protection Layout Guide*, SLVA680A (Feb 2015, revised Apr 2022), section 2; IEC 61000-4-2, *Electrostatic discharge immunity test*.

recommendations.title: Store spare boards and parts sealed in bags that block both static and moisture, with desiccant and a humidity card
recommendations.recommendation: Keep spare bare boards, moisture-sensitive parts and assembled boards you store for months in a moisture barrier bag made for electronics. The bag should also protect against static. Put fresh desiccant and a humidity indicator card in the bag, and heat-seal it, as in D60 in [Part 4](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/03-moisture-sensitive-parts/). Don't use a moisture barrier bag made for other goods, such as machine parts. Don't use a plain static-shielding bag for long storage, because it doesn't keep moisture out. Label each bag with what is inside and the date it was sealed. When you send stored boards or parts to an assembler, send them in the sealed bag and say on the packing slip how long they have been stored.
recommendations.why: Bags made for electronics combine a moisture barrier with a static-safe inner layer and a metal layer that shields. Moisture barrier bags made for other goods may block moisture but generate static. A plain shielding bag blocks static but lets moisture through over weeks. The humidity card shows whether the bag has kept the moisture out. Bare boards take on moisture and their finish ages, so they may need baking or a solderability check before use (PCB-DFA-080). Parts that have taken on moisture need baking before reflow (PCB-DFA-094).
recommendations.typical_values: IPC-1602A says bare boards dry-packed this way should keep for at least a year below 40 °C and 90% relative humidity. It recommends against drawing a full vacuum on the bag, because that can damage the desiccant, warp boards and puncture the bag. For moisture-sensitive parts, J-STD-033 sets the floor life and the bake times.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Stored boards or parts need baking before they can be built, which adds days to the job. Or they're built without baking, and parts crack or joints fail in reflow.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice, for anything you store for more than a few weeks.

recommendations.title: Agree with your assembler how boards will be packed: in the panel or separated, how many to a bag, and in what box
recommendations.recommendation: Before the first order ships, agree with your assembler how the boards will be packed. Say whether you want them in the panel or separated. Say how many boards go in each bag, and whether each board is wrapped on its own. For heavy boards, or boards going a long way, ask for a double-wall box and foam lining. If boards will go from the assembler to another company first, such as a coating or cleaning house, say where they go and how they should be packed for that trip. For boards with parts that hang over the edge, such as an antenna or a connector, ask whether they should ship in the panel to protect those parts. If your assembler is close by and you order often, ask about reusable static-safe boxes with partitions.
recommendations.why: The assembler packs to a standard method unless told otherwise. That suits most boards, but not all of them. Heavy parts near the edge of a board can break off in transit if the box isn't lined. A part hanging over the edge can snap off during depaneling or in the box (PCB-DFA-010). Leaving boards in the panel protects those parts, but then you must separate them yourself. Boards that go on to another company must be packed for a second trip, and it may cost less to ship them there directly. Reusable partitioned boxes protect boards well and cut out most of the single-use packing.
recommendations.typical_values: The usual pack is anti-static bubble wrap against the board, inside a static-shielding bag (PCB-DFA-109), in a box with filler, as in D65. A single-wall box is usual for light boards sent within one country.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Boards arrive with broken parts, or in a form you didn't expect, such as still in the panel when you wanted them separated.
recommendations.example: One board carried a radio module with its antenna hanging off the board edge, held to the panel only by a breakaway tab underneath. Separating it without snapping the antenna off took several people. It didn't always succeed.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice; agree it once for each product.

recommendations.title: For international shipments, give the right tariff code, a plain description of the goods and a contact telephone number
recommendations.recommendation: When boards or parts cross a border, work out the correct tariff code for them with your assembler or customs broker. Choose the code from what the boards are for in the end product, not from a quick search for "circuit board". Use a different code for boards returned for repair or under warranty. On the customs paperwork, also write a plain description of what is in the box and why it is being sent. For a return, say that it is a repair return of no commercial value, and give the tracking number of the original shipment. Give a telephone number that someone will answer. Before you send parts in from abroad, agree with your assembler who pays the duties and taxes.
recommendations.why: Customs officers read the paperwork, not just the codes. The tariff system classifies an assembled board mostly by the kind of equipment it goes into. A code chosen from a search can sit under the wrong heading, and that holds the shipment up. A repair return sent without the right code or note can be charged duty a second time. When customs has a question, they call the number on the paperwork, and an unanswered call means a held shipment.
recommendations.typical_values: Bare boards and assembled boards fall under different tariff headings. Bare boards come under heading 8534. Assembled boards usually come under the heading for parts of the equipment they go into, which depends on the product. Codes, duty rates and rules change, so check them for every new product and from time to time after that.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Shipments sit in customs for days, you pay duty you didn't owe, or a delivery date you promised is missed.
recommendations.example: An assembler once picked a code for "assembled circuit board" from a search. It later found the code sat several levels down under a heading for nuclear equipment.
recommendations.applies_to: International shipments; rules vary by country and change over time.

recommendations.title: Know what drives the price of an assembly, and design with it in mind
recommendations.page_title: What drives cost and lead time
recommendations.recommendation: Before you release a design, check it against the cost drivers in the table below. Each one has its own recommendation elsewhere in the book. Where the product needs one of them, keep it, but know that you are paying for it. Where it doesn't, design it out.
recommendations.why: An assembler's price is mostly set-up time and labor. Set-up is paid once for each batch, so it matters most on small orders. Labor is paid for every board, so it matters most on large orders. Anything that adds a machine set-up, a manual step or a slower process adds cost.
recommendations.typical_values:
| Cost driver | Why it costs more | Where it's covered |
|---|---|---|
| Many unique BOM lines | Each unique part takes about 3 to 5 minutes to load onto a feeder, however few boards you build. | [PCB-DFA-072](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/03-bom/) |
| Parts on both sides | A second side costs at least 15% more, even if it carries only two passive parts already used on the top. It can cost about twice as much if the bottom parts are all different from the top. | [PCB-DFA-024 and 025](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/03-reflow-soldering/) |
| Through-hole parts | Each one is placed and soldered by hand or on a separate machine. | [PCB-DFA-039](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/05-through-hole-soldering/) |
| Parts in tubes or loose | They're slower to load and to place than parts on tape. | [PCB-DFA-089](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/02-packaging/) |
| Very small or very fine-pitch parts | They need tighter process control and more inspection, and fail more often. | [PCB-DFA-021 and 022](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/02-component-placement/) |
| Hardware such as heatsinks, screws and brackets | Each piece is fitted by hand. | [PCB-DFA-048](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/06-press-fit-and-mechanical/) |
| Conformal coating | It needs masking, coating and inspection, usually by hand. | [PCB-DFA-061](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/09-conformal-coating/) |
| Cleaning | Many assemblers run no-clean flux only, so cleaning may be sent out to another company. | [PCB-DFA-055](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/08-cleaning/) |
| IPC Class 3 | Inspection is stricter, and some boards built to a Class 2 design can't meet it. | [PCB-DFT-003](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/11-bare-board-test/) |
| Tin-lead solder | Many assemblers now run lead-free only. One assembler solders tin-lead through-hole parts entirely by hand. | |
| Stepped or etched stencils | A simple laser-cut stencil cost about $300 in 2024. Stepped or chemically etched stencils cost more, up to about $900 or more. | [Solder paste and stencils](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/01-solder-paste-and-stencils/) |
| Small, odd or thin panels | They need special handling, carriers or extra set-up. | [Part 2](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/01-why-panels/) |
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: You get a quote far higher than you expected, for reasons that are hard to change once the board is laid out.
recommendations.example: One customer new to fine-pitch BGAs designed overlapping blind and buried vias, with laser-drilled vias much smaller than they needed to be. The assembler put them in touch with the fab's engineers, who showed them what was driving the cost. A couple of weeks later the customer sent a redesigned board. Its bare-board price came down to about $30 each, about a twentieth of what the first design would have cost.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice; prices vary by manufacturer and over time.

recommendations.title: Get your quote from real design data, and expect a repeat build to be priced differently
recommendations.page_title: What drives cost and lead time
recommendations.recommendation: Ask for a quote only when you have the real BOM and board files, or something very close to them. Don't ask for a ballpark price from a description. When you reorder, expect the price to change a little. If the board hasn't changed, programming and stencil costs drop out. If the board revision has changed, expect them to come back.
recommendations.why: An assembly quote is built from the actual parts, the number of unique lines, the number of sides and the processes the board needs. Without the real data, the assembler can only guess, and a guess is no use to you. On a first build, the assembler sometimes finds the job took longer than quoted, and the repeat price is adjusted, usually upwards. But the one-off work of the first build, such as machine programming and approving the stencil, isn't repeated for an unchanged board.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A budget built on a ballpark figure that turns out to be wrong, or surprise at a repeat price.

recommendations.title: Ask your board fab how many boards its minimum lot charge buys
recommendations.page_title: What drives cost and lead time
recommendations.recommendation: When you order a small number of bare boards, ask the fab what its minimum lot charge is and how many boards it covers. Then order that number, rather than asking for prices at several small quantities.
recommendations.why: Most board fabs charge a fixed minimum for any order, however few boards are in it. Up to some quantity, more boards cost nothing extra. Asking for prices one quantity at a time hides where that point is. Assemblers use the term less often than fabs, and some don't have a minimum lot charge at all.
recommendations.typical_values: In one example, a fab quoted $300 for 5 boards, and the same $300 for 7, 10 and 11 boards. The minimum lot charge covered 13 boards. Twenty boards cost $430.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: You pay the same price for fewer boards than you could have had.
recommendations.applies_to: Bare-board fabrication, mainly prototypes and small orders.

recommendations.title: Order a few more boards than you need: 105 to 110 when you need 100
recommendations.page_title: What drives cost and lead time
recommendations.recommendation: When you need a certain number of working boards, order about 5% to 10% more. For example, order 105 to 110 boards when you need 100. If the boards go into a test fixture, add the spares the fixture builder needs as well (PCB-DFT-017).
recommendations.why: Even a good design built well has a small failure rate. A few boards will fail test, or fail early in a stress screen (PCB-DFT-019). Some will be damaged in handling. Spares cost little when they're built with the rest of the batch. Building a handful more later costs a full set-up.
recommendations.typical_values: About 5% to 10% extra, which is 105 to 110 boards when you need 100.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: You end up a few boards short, and a small top-up order costs almost as much in set-up as the first one.

recommendations.title: Leave at least two weeks of margin in your schedule, and plan round long factory holidays
recommendations.page_title: What drives cost and lead time
recommendations.recommendation: Plan for boards to arrive at least two weeks before you need them. Ask each supplier when it will close for long holidays, and the last day it will take an order that ships before it closes. Ask domestic suppliers too, because their own suppliers may close. Place orders before that date. For the Lunar New Year, which falls in late January or February, place orders for February and March in early December where you can. When an order is urgent, tell your manufacturer so, and say why. Use holiday closures for work that doesn't need a factory, such as finishing designs and tidying your parts library.
recommendations.why: Lead times slip for reasons outside anyone's control: a late part, a question that waits, a holiday or a delay in transit. Many factories in China slow down a week or two before the Lunar New Year, because staff travel home for the longest holiday of the year. After the holiday, it takes time to clear the backlog. Domestic suppliers get busier at the same time, as customers turn to them instead. An assembler that knows an order is urgent can warn you early if something threatens the date.
recommendations.typical_values: At least two weeks of margin. Expect delays for about one to two months after the Lunar New Year.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A missed launch or delivery date, or an expensive rush order to recover it.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice; holiday dates change every year.

recommendations.title: Answer your manufacturer's questions quickly, and keep an engineer reachable by telephone
recommendations.page_title: What drives cost and lead time
recommendations.recommendation: While your order is being built, answer your manufacturer's questions within the hour, and within about 30 minutes once the job is on the assembly line. Give the manufacturer the telephone number of an engineer who knows the design, not only an email address. If you'll be away during a first or critical order, name someone who can answer for you. Keep the questions about each order in one place, such as the order's own message thread, so that everyone sees the same answers.
recommendations.why: When an assembler finds a problem, such as a part that doesn't match the BOM, the line often stops until it has an answer. If no answer comes, the job is taken off the line and has to wait for the next free slot. At the fab, an unanswered question about the panel or the drawing stops the job too.
recommendations.typical_values: Aim to answer within about 30 minutes. An idle surface-mount line costs from several hundred to several thousand dollars an hour (2021 figure). The machines on one line can cost $1 million to $2 million and are expected to last about 10 years. A 48-hour fab turn can become 3 or 4 days while questions wait for answers.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Your job comes off the line and loses days. Or the assembler has to guess, and the guess is wrong.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice; most important for first builds and fast turns.

recommendations.title: Check your order before you place it, and report a mistake at once
recommendations.page_title: What drives cost and lead time
recommendations.recommendation: Before you place an order, check that the options you choose on the order match your fabrication drawing and files. Check the board thickness, the solder mask color, the surface finish and any special processes such as via-in-pad. If you find a mistake after ordering, report it straight away. If the order was placed only minutes ago, ask whether it is simpler to cancel it and place a new one.
recommendations.why: Many manufacturers build to the options on the order, so an option that disagrees with your drawing may win. Once fabrication has started, or parts have been bought, a change costs money and time. A change made by hand on a placed order is also a chance for a new mistake. A fresh order goes through the normal checks.
recommendations.typical_values: In one assembler's experience, an order can usually be canceled and replaced at no cost within about 30 minutes, before work starts. After about 24 to 48 hours, fabrication or parts buying has usually started, and changes get harder and dearer.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Boards built to the wrong option, or a change fee that grows the longer you wait.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice; how orders are placed varies by manufacturer.

recommendations.title: Plan the move from prototype to production as a ramp, not a jump
recommendations.recommendation: Don't go straight from a few prototypes to a full production order. Build in steps, such as 20 boards, then 200, then 1,000, and then the full volume, as in D66. Before the first large build, talk to your manufacturer about your volumes and anything that was done by hand on the prototypes. Replace hard-to-find parts, hobby modules and hand-fitted parts with mainstream parts on tape where you can (PCB-DFA-083 and 085). If anything in the design or BOM has changed since the last build, expect new first articles (PCB-DFA-107). Check that boards built on the production line perform like the ones you tested in the lab. Expect the first production batch to run slower than later ones, and expect to find a few more issues. If the volume is far beyond what your manufacturer has built for you before, consider splitting the first large order between two manufacturers.
recommendations.why: Each step shows up problems while they're still cheap to fix. The first large batch is where the assembler learns the board's quirks: a via in an awkward place, a part that has to be hand-soldered because of its neighbors, a polarity mark that is easy to misread. Later batches run faster because those quirks are known. Problems that a few prototypes never showed only appear once hundreds of boards are built.
recommendations.typical_values: A typical ramp is 20, then 200, then 1,000, then 2,000 or more. After a design reaches a signed-off golden sample, expect to find about ten more issues once it reaches real production volume.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A large first order with a fault that affects every board. Or a launch that slips while the manufacturer works out how to build the board at volume.
recommendations.example: In one case, about 8 months of engineering went into reaching a golden sample. About ten more issues were still found once the product moved into production volume.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice, whenever volume rises sharply.

recommendations.title: For large orders, release boards in batches matched to the panel, and agree who holds the parts and the risk
recommendations.recommendation: For a large annual volume, agree a schedule of batch releases with your manufacturer, rather than one delivery of the whole quantity. Make each batch a whole number of panels. Agree which parts the manufacturer buys up front and which are held by a distributor and released batch by batch (PCB-DFA-098). Before a very large order, agree in writing who carries which risks. That includes insurance for parts held in the factory, and who pays if boards fail in the field months later.
recommendations.why: A batch schedule matches deliveries to how the product sells, and keeps less money tied up in parts and finished boards. A batch of whole panels uses every board the machines build. The costly part of a changeover is setting up the surface-mount machines, so batches are sized to spread that set-up over enough boards. On a large order, most of the money is in parts, and someone has to hold that stock and its risk until the boards are built.
recommendations.typical_values: In one example, a 9-up panel of 3 by 3 boards meant batches of 27 boards. Each surface-mount feeder costs about $1,000 or more (2023 figure), which is why surface-mount set-up dominates changeover cost. In one example of a $200,000 order, about $150,000 was parts and about $50,000 was labor. Orders of about $100,000 often run without a formal contract. Orders of $400,000 to $500,000 usually need one.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Cash tied up in a year of stock, partial panels that waste boards, or a dispute about who pays after a fire, a flood or a field failure.
recommendations.example: One product has been built at about 2,000 boards a year for 20 years. The customer never takes all 2,000 at once. For years it called them off in batches of 27, a whole number of its 9-up panels, every few days.
recommendations.applies_to: Production volumes; contracts and insurance vary by manufacturer and country.

recommendations.title: Bring your manufacturer into the design review before the design is final
recommendations.recommendation: Share the design with your fab and assembler while you can still change it, at about 60% to 80% complete. Ask them what will be hard to make, test or ship. Review in small steps as the design develops, rather than in one large review at the end. Before each release, compare the schematic, the board and the BOM with the previous version, so you can see exactly what changed. Let the mechanical engineers and others who depend on the board comment on the design files themselves, not only on a summary.
recommendations.why: At 60% to 80%, the layout is far enough along to show real problems, and still open enough to fix them. Small reviews get read properly, and their actions get done. A large review at the end produces a long list, and much of it never gets done. A comparison of versions catches changes nobody meant to make.
recommendations.typical_values: Review with suppliers at about 60% to 80% complete.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: Problems the manufacturer would have spotted in minutes turn into a board revision. Or a review list so long that half of it is never acted on.
recommendations.example: One design review produced 327 items and 557 actions. Only about half of them were ever dealt with.

recommendations.title: Ask for feedback after every build, and fix recurring problems before you reorder
recommendations.recommendation: After each build, ask your assembler and fab what gave them trouble. Make the changes they suggest before you reorder, not after. If the same problem comes up on more than one build, treat it as a design problem and fix it in the next revision.
recommendations.why: The people who built the board know exactly where the time went: a through-hole connector that could have been surface-mount, a part that had to be hand-soldered, a polarity mark that was easy to misread. A manufacturer will often work round a problem without telling you, and keep paying for it on every build. The next revision is the cheapest place to fix it.
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: The same problem costs you money on every build, and sometimes causes the same defect again.
recommendations.applies_to: General practice; most valuable on products that are reordered.

recommendations.title: Talk to your manufacturer before designing in anything unusual, and don't assume standard pricing
recommendations.recommendation: Before you commit to anything outside a standard surface-mount build, ask your manufacturer whether it can do it, and what it will cost. Ask every time, whether it's a first prototype or a product moving to higher volume. If you choose a very fine-pitch BGA or chip-scale package, choose a manufacturer that has built that kind of part before.
recommendations.why: Unusual processes may need tooling, a different machine, a subcontractor or skills the manufacturer doesn't have. None of that is in a standard price. Experience with a fine-pitch part comes only from building it, and a manufacturer still learning will have lower yields. The earlier you ask, the more choices you still have, including changing the design.
recommendations.typical_values:
Unusual processes covered elsewhere in this book include:
- press-fit parts (PCB-DFA-047)
- one-piece RF shields (PCB-DFA-050)
- boards thicker than about 2 mm (PCB-DFA-014)
- very thin boards and large, heavy double-sided panels (PCB-DFA-028)
- conformal coating and cleaning (PCB-DFA-055 and 061)
- adhesive-mounted parts and underfill (PCB-DFA-052 to 054).
recommendations.what_goes_wrong: A quote far above what you expected, a lead time with tooling added, or a manufacturer that can't build the board at all.
